questions.title: RAII and smart pointers in C++
questions.prompt: Explain RAII in C++ and how smart pointers apply it. Compare unique_ptr, shared_ptr and weak_ptr, give an example of each, and name a common pitfall.

expectedConcepts.label: Resource lifetime tied to object lifetime
unique_ptr: sole ownership, move-only
shared_ptr: reference counting
weak_ptr breaks cycles
Exception safety / no leaks on early return
Pitfalls: cycles, atomic refcount cost, raw new

questions.modelAnswer: RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization) ties a resource — memory, file, mutex lock — to an object: acquire in the constructor, release in the destructor. Because destructors run when scope exits, including on exceptions and early returns, resources never leak. unique_ptr expresses sole ownership, cannot be copied, only moved, and has zero overhead. shared_ptr shares ownership with an atomic reference count; the object dies when the last owner goes. weak_ptr observes without owning and breaks reference cycles (e.g. a child pointing back to its parent). Pitfalls: shared_ptr cycles leak, atomic refcounting costs, and using raw new instead of make_unique/make_shared.

questions.title: Stack versus heap allocation
questions.prompt: Compare stack and heap allocation in C++. Explain lifetime, allocation cost, size limits and cache behaviour, and when you would choose each.

expectedConcepts.label: Stack: automatic lifetime tied to scope
Heap: dynamic lifetime managed explicitly
Stack allocation is a pointer bump; heap uses an allocator
Stack size limits → overflow
Returning pointer to stack variable is dangling

questions.modelAnswer: Stack objects live in the function's frame: allocation is just moving the stack pointer, they are destroyed automatically when scope ends, and they are cache-friendly — but the stack is small (often 1–8 MB), so huge arrays or deep recursion overflow it, and returning a pointer to a local creates a dangling pointer. Heap allocation (new/make_unique) goes through an allocator — slower, can fragment, possibly contended across threads — but supports large sizes, runtime-determined sizes and lifetimes beyond the scope. Prefer stack and value semantics; use the heap via smart pointers or containers when size or lifetime demands it.

questions.title: Mutexes, atomics and race conditions
questions.prompt: Explain what a data race is, and compare protecting shared state with a mutex versus std::atomic. Mention memory ordering and when a lock-free approach is worth it.

expectedConcepts.label: Data race: concurrent unsynchronised access with a write
Data races are undefined behaviour
Mutex gives mutual exclusion over a critical section
Atomics for single variables / counters
Memory ordering: seq_cst, acquire/release, relaxed
Pitfalls: deadlock, ABA, false sharing, contention

questions.modelAnswer: A data race occurs when two threads access the same memory concurrently, at least one writes, and there is no synchronisation — in C++ that is undefined behaviour. A mutex (with lock_guard/scoped_lock RAII) serialises a critical section of any size; simple, but threads block and contention hurts latency. std::atomic makes single-variable operations indivisible (fetch_add, compare_exchange) without blocking, and memory orders control visibility: seq_cst by default, acquire/release for publish-consume handoffs, relaxed for counters. Lock-free structures (e.g. SPSC ring buffers) pay off on hot, latency-critical paths but bring ABA problems, false sharing and hard-to-verify correctness.

questions.title: Move semantics
questions.prompt: Explain move semantics in C++. Cover rvalue references, what a move constructor does, when std::move is needed, and what state a moved-from object is in.

expectedConcepts.label: Rvalue references bind to temporaries
Move steals resources instead of copying
std::move is a cast, doesn't move by itself
Moved-from object: valid but unspecified
Pitfalls: moving from const, using after move, noexcept

questions.modelAnswer: Copying a std::vector duplicates its heap buffer; moving just transfers the pointer and leaves the source empty. Rvalue references (T&&) bind to temporaries and to objects explicitly marked as movable. A move constructor takes T&&, steals the resources and resets the source. std::move is only a cast to an rvalue — the move happens in the constructor or assignment it selects. The moved-from object remains valid but unspecified: you may destroy it or assign to it. Pitfalls: std::move on a const object silently copies, using objects after moving, missing noexcept (vectors then copy on reallocation), and writing std::move on return values, which blocks RVO.

questions.title: Memory ownership and lifetime
questions.prompt: Explain how you reason about ownership and lifetime in a C++ codebase. How do function signatures communicate ownership, and what bugs result when ownership is unclear?

expectedConcepts.label: Exactly one owner responsible for destruction
Signatures express ownership: unique_ptr by value, references, raw pointers non-owning
Use-after-free, double free, leaks, dangling
Views (string_view/span) must not outlive owner
Sanitizers and static analysis

questions.modelAnswer: Every resource should have one clear owner responsible for destroying it. Signatures communicate this: passing std::unique_ptr by value transfers ownership; T& or const T& borrows; a raw T* or std::span/string_view is non-owning and must not outlive its source; returning unique_ptr hands ownership to the caller. Unclear ownership causes leaks, double frees, use-after-free and dangling views (e.g. a string_view into a temporary string). Tools: AddressSanitizer, Valgrind, clang-tidy lifetime checks, and Rust-style discipline in code review.

questions.title: Virtual functions and dynamic dispatch in C++
questions.prompt: Explain how virtual functions work in C++. Describe the vtable and vptr, why a base class needs a virtual destructor, and the cost of dynamic dispatch compared with templates.

expectedConcepts.label: Per-class vtable and a hidden vptr in each object
Dynamic dispatch / late binding through a base pointer
Indirect call, no inlining; templates give static polymorphism
Missing virtual destructor is UB; object slicing

researchContext: The C++ standard does not mention vtables; they are the usual implementation (Itanium ABI on Linux/macOS, MSVC ABI on Windows).
Calling a virtual function inside a constructor or destructor calls the version of the class currently being constructed or destroyed, not the most-derived override.
Mark overrides with `override` so the compiler catches signature mismatches, and `final` to stop further overriding (which can also enable devirtualisation).
questions.modelAnswer: When a class has virtual functions, compilers typically create a vtable for it: a per-class table of function pointers. Each object stores a hidden vptr to its class's table. Calling a virtual function through a base pointer or reference loads the vptr, looks up the slot and makes an indirect call, so the derived override runs (dynamic dispatch, or late binding). The cost is one pointer per object and an indirect call that usually cannot be inlined. Templates and CRTP give static polymorphism instead: calls are resolved at compile time and can be inlined, at the cost of code size and compile time. Pitfalls: deleting a derived object through a base pointer without a virtual destructor is undefined behaviour; passing a derived object by value slices off the derived part; and a virtual call inside a constructor does not reach the derived override.

questions.title: Undefined behaviour in C++
questions.prompt: Explain what undefined behaviour is in C++. Give three common examples, explain why the optimiser can make an undefined behaviour bug show up far from where it happens, and describe how you catch these bugs.

expectedConcepts.label: The standard places no requirements on the result
Signed overflow, out-of-bounds, dangling, null, uninitialised reads, data races
The compiler assumes UB never happens and optimises on that
Sanitizers, warnings, static analysis

researchContext: Undefined behaviour is different from unspecified behaviour (one of several allowed results, e.g. evaluation order of function arguments) and implementation-defined behaviour (documented by the compiler, e.g. sizeof(int)).
Classic optimiser example: after `int x = *p;` the compiler may delete a later `if (p == nullptr)` check, because dereferencing null would already have been UB.
Build flags: `-fsanitize=address,undefined` (ASan + UBSan), `-fsanitize=thread` (TSan, not combinable with ASan), plus `-Wall -Wextra`.
questions.modelAnswer: Undefined behaviour means the C++ standard places no requirements on what the program does: it may appear to work, crash, or produce wrong results, and the result can change with the compiler or flags. Common examples are signed integer overflow, reading or writing out of bounds, using a dangling pointer or reference after the object is destroyed, dereferencing a null pointer, reading an uninitialised variable, and data races. Because compilers may assume UB never happens, they optimise on that assumption: for example, after dereferencing a pointer they may delete a later null check, or assume a signed loop counter never overflows. So the symptom can appear somewhere else, or only in release builds. To catch it: AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer (-fsanitize=address,undefined), ThreadSanitizer for races, compiler warnings, static analysis, and safer constructs such as std::vector::at, std::span and smart pointers.

questions.title: How std::vector grows
questions.prompt: Explain how std::vector stores its elements and grows. Cover amortised constant-time push_back, capacity versus size, iterator invalidation, and when reserve helps.

expectedConcepts.label: One contiguous heap buffer; reallocation when full
Size vs capacity, geometric growth, amortised O(1)
reserve avoids reallocations; cache-friendly; noexcept moves
Reallocation invalidates iterators, pointers and references

researchContext: libstdc++ and libc++ grow capacity by 2x; MSVC grows by 1.5x. The standard only requires amortised constant time.
During reallocation, elements are moved only if the move constructor is noexcept (or the type is not copyable); otherwise they are copied to keep the strong exception guarantee.
shrink_to_fit is a non-binding request; `std::vector<bool>` is a special bit-packed case and does not behave like a normal container.
questions.modelAnswer: std::vector keeps its elements in one contiguous heap buffer and tracks size (elements in use) and capacity (slots allocated). When push_back needs more room than the capacity, it allocates a larger buffer, typically 1.5x or 2x, moves or copies the elements over, and frees the old one. Because growth is geometric, the total copying is spread over many insertions, so push_back is amortised O(1). Contiguity makes iteration cache-friendly. If you know the final size, reserve(n) avoids repeated reallocations. Elements are moved during growth only if their move constructor is noexcept; otherwise they are copied. The main pitfall is invalidation: a reallocation invalidates every iterator, pointer and reference into the vector, and insert or erase invalidate those at or after the position.

questions.title: References, pointers and const in C++
questions.prompt: Explain the difference between references and pointers in C++, and how const works with both. When should a function take a parameter by value, by const reference, or by pointer?

expectedConcepts.label: A reference is an alias that cannot be null or reseated; a pointer holds an address
Pointer to const vs const pointer; const member functions
Small types by value, large by const reference, optional by pointer
Dangling references to temporaries or locals

researchContext: Read declarations right to left: `const int* p` is a pointer to const int; `int* const p` is a const pointer to int.
A const reference can bind to a temporary and extends its lifetime to the reference's scope (only for a local const reference, not a member or a returned reference).
Core Guidelines F.16: pass cheap-to-copy types (roughly up to 2-3 words) by value, others by const reference.
questions.modelAnswer: A reference is an alias for an existing object: it must be initialised, cannot be null and cannot be reseated to refer to something else. A pointer holds an address; it can be null (nullptr), can be changed to point elsewhere, and supports pointer arithmetic. With const, read declarations right to left: const int* p is a pointer to a const int, while int* const p is a const pointer. A const member function promises not to modify the object. For parameters: pass small, cheap-to-copy types such as int or a small struct by value; pass large objects you only read by const reference to avoid a copy; use a pointer when the argument is optional and may be null. Pitfall: returning a reference or pointer to a local variable or a temporary creates a dangling reference, which is undefined behaviour.

questions.title: Rule of zero, three and five
questions.prompt: Explain the rule of three, the rule of five and the rule of zero in C++. Which special member functions do they cover, and why is the rule of zero the preferred default?

expectedConcepts.label: Destructor, copy/move constructor and assignment
Rule of three, five and zero
Let RAII members (vector, unique_ptr) manage resources
Shallow copies, double free; user destructor suppresses moves

researchContext: Declaring a destructor, copy constructor or copy assignment suppresses the implicit move operations, so the class silently copies instead of moving.
`= default` and `= delete` let you state intent explicitly; a move-only type deletes its copy operations (like std::unique_ptr).
The copy-and-swap idiom gives copy assignment the strong exception guarantee.
questions.modelAnswer: The special member functions are the destructor, copy constructor, copy assignment, move constructor and move assignment. The rule of three says that if a class needs a custom destructor, copy constructor or copy assignment, usually because it owns a raw resource, it probably needs all three. C++11 added moves, giving the rule of five: define or delete all five together. The rule of zero is the preferred default: don't manage resources by hand at all; hold them in RAII members such as std::vector, std::string or std::unique_ptr, so the compiler-generated special members are correct automatically. Pitfalls: a class owning a raw pointer with the default copy constructor makes a shallow copy and leads to a double free, and declaring a destructor or copy operation suppresses the implicit move operations, so the class silently copies instead of moving.

questions.title: Templates and compile-time programming
questions.prompt: Explain how templates work in C++. Cover instantiation, why template code usually lives in headers, how constexpr moves work to compile time, and how C++20 concepts improve template errors.

expectedConcepts.label: The compiler generates code per set of template arguments
Headers, constexpr, concepts, requires
Zero-cost generic containers and algorithms; compile-time computation
Code bloat, long compile times, unreadable errors

researchContext: Templates must be visible where they are instantiated, so definitions usually live in headers (or you use explicit instantiation).
constexpr functions may run at compile time when given constant inputs; consteval (C++20) forces compile-time evaluation.
Concepts such as `std::integral` or a custom `requires` clause constrain templates, so errors appear at the call site in readable form.
questions.modelAnswer: A template is a blueprint: when you use std::vector<int> or call max(a, b), the compiler instantiates the template, generating a separate version for that set of argument types at compile time. Because the compiler needs the full definition to do that, template code usually lives in headers. This gives zero-cost generic code: the STL's containers and algorithms are as fast as hand-written code and can be inlined. constexpr marks variables and functions that can be evaluated at compile time, so values like lookup tables are computed during the build rather than at runtime. C++20 concepts and requires clauses state what a type must support, such as std::integral, so a wrong type gives a short error at the call site instead of pages of errors from deep inside the template. Costs: code bloat from many instantiations, longer compile times and, without concepts, hard-to-read errors.

questions.title: Lambdas and captures in C++
questions.prompt: Explain lambdas in C++. Cover capture by value and by reference, what the compiler generates for a lambda, and how std::function differs from passing a lambda as a template parameter.

expectedConcepts.label: A lambda is an unnamed class with operator()
Capture by value or reference; mutable; init captures
std::function type-erases (allocation, indirect call); templates can inline
Reference captures that outlive the scope; capturing this

researchContext: [=] captures used variables by copy, [&] by reference, [x, &y] explicitly; [p = std::move(ptr)] is an init capture (C++14).
Captured-by-value members are const inside operator() unless the lambda is marked `mutable`.
Before C++20, [=] implicitly captured `this` (a pointer), not a copy of the object; use [*this] to copy the object.
questions.modelAnswer: A lambda is shorthand for a function object: the compiler generates an unnamed class whose captured variables become data members and whose body becomes operator(). The capture list controls what it stores: [x] copies x, [&x] stores a reference, [=] and [&] capture everything used by copy or by reference, and init captures like [p = std::move(ptr)] can move objects in. Captured copies are const inside the body unless the lambda is marked mutable. std::function can hold any callable with a given signature through type erasure, which is flexible but may heap-allocate and makes an indirect call; passing the lambda as a template parameter, as std::sort does, keeps its exact type so the call can be inlined. Pitfalls: capturing locals by reference in a lambda that outlives the scope, for example one stored as a callback or run on another thread, gives dangling references; capturing this has the same risk if the object is destroyed first.

questions.title: std::map versus std::unordered_map
questions.prompt: Compare std::map and std::unordered_map. Explain the data structure behind each, their time complexity, iteration order and memory use, and when you would choose one over the other.

expectedConcepts.label: map is a balanced tree (red-black); unordered_map is a hash table
O(log n) ordered vs average O(1) unordered
Ordered iteration and range queries vs fast lookup; reserve
Worst-case O(n), rehash invalidation, operator[] inserts

researchContext: std::map is usually a red-black tree: one heap node per element, so iteration chases pointers and is less cache-friendly.
unordered_map rehashes when size exceeds bucket_count * max_load_factor; rehashing invalidates iterators but not references to elements.
`m[key]` default-constructs and inserts a value when the key is missing; use find or contains (C++20) to only look.
questions.modelAnswer: std::map is a balanced binary search tree, usually a red-black tree, so keys stay sorted and lookup, insert and erase are O(log n). It supports ordered iteration and range queries with lower_bound and upper_bound. std::unordered_map is a hash table with buckets: lookups are O(1) on average, but there is no useful order, and the worst case is O(n) when many keys collide. Both allocate a node per element, so memory overhead is significant; the hash table also keeps a bucket array and rehashes when the load factor gets too high, which you can avoid with reserve. Choose unordered_map for fast lookups by key, and map when you need sorted order, range queries or predictable worst-case time. Pitfalls: operator[] inserts a default value when the key is missing, a poor hash function destroys performance, and rehashing invalidates iterators.

questions.title: Exceptions and exception safety in C++
questions.prompt: Explain how exceptions work in C++, including stack unwinding and RAII. Describe the basic, strong and nothrow exception-safety guarantees, and why noexcept matters for performance.

expectedConcepts.label: Throw unwinds the stack, running destructors
Basic, strong and nothrow guarantees
noexcept moves let vector move instead of copy
Throwing from destructors, leaks without RAII, std::terminate

researchContext: If an exception escapes a noexcept function, std::terminate is called; destructors are noexcept by default.
std::vector uses std::move_if_noexcept during reallocation to keep the strong guarantee.
Many codebases (games, embedded, Google style) disable exceptions and use error codes or std::expected (C++23).
questions.modelAnswer: When code throws, the runtime unwinds the stack: it leaves each scope in turn, running destructors of local objects, until it finds a matching catch. That's why RAII matters: resources held by objects such as unique_ptr or lock_guard are released automatically during unwinding, while raw new and delete would leak. Exception-safety guarantees describe what holds if an operation throws: the basic guarantee means no leaks and the object stays valid but possibly changed; the strong guarantee means commit or rollback, so the state is unchanged, often achieved with copy-and-swap; the nothrow guarantee means the operation never throws. Marking moves noexcept matters because std::vector moves elements during reallocation only if the move constructor is noexcept; otherwise it copies them to keep the strong guarantee. Pitfalls: throwing from a destructor during unwinding calls std::terminate, and an exception escaping a noexcept function also terminates the program.

questions.title: Compilation, linking and the one-definition rule
questions.prompt: Explain what happens when a C++ program is built: preprocessing, compilation of translation units, and linking. What is the one-definition rule, and what causes undefined reference and multiple definition errors?

expectedConcepts.label: Preprocess, compile each .cpp to an object file, link
Declarations vs definitions, ODR, inline, include guards
Headers drive rebuilds; forward declarations; static vs dynamic libraries
Undefined reference, multiple definition, ODR violations

researchContext: #include is textual copy-paste; each .cpp plus everything it includes is one translation unit compiled independently.
Functions defined in a header must be inline (templates and in-class member definitions are implicitly inline), otherwise every including file defines them.
C++20 modules aim to replace textual headers and reduce rebuild times.
questions.modelAnswer: Building C++ has three main stages. The preprocessor handles #include and macros, pasting headers in as text, so each .cpp file plus its headers becomes one translation unit. The compiler turns each translation unit independently into an object file containing machine code and a list of symbols it defines and needs. The linker then combines the object files and libraries, resolving each symbol to exactly one definition. The one-definition rule says a function or variable may be declared many times but defined once in the whole program; inline functions and templates may be defined in several translation units as long as the definitions are identical. An undefined reference error means something was declared and used but its definition was never compiled or linked, for example a missing .cpp or library. A multiple definition error usually means a non-inline function or global variable was defined in a header included by several files. Include guards stop double inclusion within one file, and forward declarations reduce rebuild times.

questions.title: string_view, span and non-owning views
questions.prompt: Explain std::string_view and std::span. Why are they useful as function parameters, and how can they lead to dangling references?

expectedConcepts.label: Non-owning pointer + length over existing data
string_view, span, contiguous range
No copies or allocations; accepts many input types
Views of temporaries dangle; string_view is not null-terminated

questions.modelAnswer: std::string_view (C++17) and std::span (C++20) are non-owning views: just a pointer and a length over data that lives somewhere else. string_view refers to characters, from a std::string, a string literal or a buffer; span refers to any contiguous sequence of elements, such as a vector, an array or a C array. As parameters they accept many input types without copying or allocating, and they are cheap to pass by value; substr on a string_view creates another view instead of a new string. The danger is lifetime: a view never keeps the data alive. Returning a string_view to a local string, storing a view of a temporary such as a function's returned std::string, or keeping a view while the underlying vector reallocates all leave it dangling. Also, string_view is not guaranteed to be null-terminated, so don't pass .data() to C functions that expect a C string.

questions.title: std::atomic and memory ordering
questions.prompt: Explain memory ordering for std::atomic in C++. Compare sequentially consistent, acquire-release and relaxed ordering, and give an example where acquire-release is needed to publish data safely.

expectedConcepts.label: Compilers and CPUs reorder memory operations
seq_cst, acquire/release, relaxed
Release store of a flag, acquire load before reading data
Data races are UB; relaxed is easy to misuse; test with TSan

researchContext: Default ordering for std::atomic operations is memory_order_seq_cst: one global order all threads agree on.
On x86, acquire and release loads/stores are plain MOVs; seq_cst stores need a full fence (XCHG or MFENCE). ARM needs barriers or special instructions for acquire/release.
Relaxed is fine for independent counters (statistics), not for flags that guard other data.
questions.modelAnswer: Compilers and CPUs reorder memory operations for speed, so without synchronisation another thread may see writes in a different order or not at all. std::atomic operations take a memory order. Sequentially consistent, the default, gives one global order of atomic operations that all threads agree on: easiest to reason about, but it needs extra fences on some hardware. Acquire-release is cheaper: a release store makes all writes before it visible to a thread whose acquire load reads that value. Relaxed guarantees only atomicity of that variable, with no ordering of other memory, which is fine for an independent statistics counter. Example: a producer fills a buffer, then does ready.store(true, memory_order_release); the consumer spins on ready.load(memory_order_acquire) and only then reads the buffer, which is guaranteed to be complete. With relaxed ordering, the consumer could see the flag but stale data. Pitfalls: plain non-atomic shared variables are a data race and undefined behaviour, and subtle ordering bugs are hard to reproduce; test with ThreadSanitizer.

questions.title: Modern C++: auto, ranges, optional and more
questions.prompt: Describe the modern C++ features you use most from C++11 to C++20, such as auto, range-based for, smart pointers, std::optional, std::variant, structured bindings and ranges, and explain what problem each one solves.

expectedConcepts.label: auto, range-for, smart pointers, move semantics
optional, variant, structured bindings, ranges
Safer, shorter code that expresses intent
auto hiding types, dangling ranges, overusing new features

questions.modelAnswer: C++11 brought auto for type deduction, range-based for loops, lambdas, move semantics and smart pointers such as unique_ptr and shared_ptr, which replaced most raw new and delete. C++17 added std::optional for a value that may be missing instead of sentinel values or null pointers, std::variant as a type-safe union handled with std::visit, structured bindings like auto [key, value] when iterating a map, and if constexpr. C++20 added concepts to constrain templates, ranges for composable pipelines like views::filter and views::transform, std::span, and the three-way comparison operator. Together they make code shorter, safer and clearer about intent: ownership is explicit and missing values are visible in the type. Pitfalls: auto can hide an important type such as a proxy or a copy instead of a reference, range views can dangle if the underlying container is a temporary, and older compilers may not support every C++20 feature.

questions.title: Goroutines and channels in Go
questions.prompt: Explain how goroutines and channels work in Go. Compare buffered and unbuffered channels, describe how the Go scheduler runs goroutines, and name a common concurrency bug.

expectedConcepts.label: Lightweight green threads with small stacks
M:N scheduler (G, M, P)
Unbuffered channels synchronise sender and receiver
Buffered channels decouple up to capacity
Share memory by communicating; select
Goroutine leaks, deadlocks, closing channels

questions.modelAnswer: Goroutines are functions running concurrently, started with the go keyword; they begin with a few KB of growable stack, so you can run hundreds of thousands. The runtime multiplexes them onto OS threads (M:N scheduling with G, M, P) and preempts long-running ones. Channels pass values between goroutines: an unbuffered send blocks until a receiver is ready (a synchronisation point); a buffered channel lets senders proceed until it is full. select waits on several channel operations. Common bugs: goroutine leaks (a goroutine blocked forever on a channel nobody reads — use context cancellation), sending on a closed channel, and deadlocks.

questions.title: Interfaces and the nil interface trap in Go
questions.prompt: Explain how interfaces work in Go. Cover implicit satisfaction, the interface value as a pair of a dynamic type and a value, and why an interface holding a nil pointer is not equal to nil.

expectedConcepts.label: Satisfied implicitly by having the methods
Interface value = dynamic type + value
Small consumer-defined interfaces; easy fakes in tests
A nil pointer inside an interface makes it non-nil

researchContext: Idiom: "accept interfaces, return structs". Define the interface where it is used, not where the type is implemented.
The empty interface `any` (interface{}) holds any value; use type switches or generics (Go 1.18+) instead of passing `any` around.
Classic bug: `func f() error { var e *MyErr = nil; return e }` returns a non-nil error. Return a literal `nil` on success.
questions.modelAnswer: A Go type satisfies an interface simply by having its methods; there is no implements keyword. So interfaces are usually small and defined by the code that consumes them, like io.Reader, which decouples packages and makes it easy to pass fakes in tests (accept interfaces, return structs). At runtime an interface value is a pair: a dynamic type and a value. It is nil only when both are nil. If a function returns a nil *MyError as an error, the interface holds the type *MyError with a nil value, so err != nil is true: the error is not nil even though the pointer inside it is a nil pointer. This is a classic bug. Return a literal nil instead. Type assertions and type switches recover the concrete type.

questions.title: Slices, append and shared backing arrays in Go
questions.prompt: Explain how slices work in Go. Describe the slice header, how append grows the backing array, and a bug caused by two slices sharing the same array.

expectedConcepts.label: Header: pointer, length, capacity over a backing array
append writes in place or reallocates; use the result
make with capacity, copy, full slice expression
Shared arrays: overwrites, silent divergence, retained memory

researchContext: Since Go 1.18, append roughly doubles capacity for small slices and grows by about 1.25x plus a constant for large ones; never rely on the exact factor.
A nil slice and an empty slice both have length 0 and work with append and range; they differ only in == nil and JSON encoding (null vs []).
Arrays ([4]int) are values and are copied on assignment; slices are references to an array.
questions.modelAnswer: A slice is a small header: a pointer into a backing array, a length and a capacity. Slicing with s[a:b] makes a new header over the same array without copying. append writes in place if len < cap; otherwise it allocates a bigger array (about double for small slices, less for large ones), copies the elements, and returns a header to the new array, which is why you must write s = append(s, x). Bug: b := a[:2]; b = append(b, 9) overwrites a[2], because both share the array, while after a reallocation the two slices silently stop sharing. Fixes: copy into a new slice, use a full slice expression a[:2:2] to limit capacity, or preallocate with make([]T, 0, n). Also, keeping a small slice of a huge array keeps the whole array in memory.

questions.title: Errors, defer, panic and recover in Go
questions.prompt: Explain error handling in Go. Cover errors as values, wrapping with %w and checking with errors.Is or errors.As, and how defer, panic and recover fit in.

expectedConcepts.label: Errors are returned values checked with if err != nil
Wrap with %w; errors.Is / errors.As; sentinel errors
defer for cleanup, runs in LIFO order
Ignored errors, panic for normal errors, defer in loops

researchContext: Deferred call arguments are evaluated when the defer statement runs, not when the deferred function executes.
recover only works when called directly inside a deferred function, and only in the goroutine that is panicking. A panic in another goroutine crashes the program.
errors.Join (Go 1.20) combines several errors; errors.Is and errors.As look through all of them.
questions.modelAnswer: Go functions return an error as a normal value, usually last, and the caller checks if err != nil right away: explicit control flow with no exceptions. Add context while keeping the cause with fmt.Errorf("reading config: %w", err); callers test with errors.Is for sentinel values like io.EOF, or errors.As to extract a typed error. defer schedules a call to run when the function returns, which is ideal for Close, Unlock and other cleanup; deferred calls run in LIFO order. panic is for truly unrecoverable programmer errors, and recover, called inside a deferred function, stops a panic, for example at a server's request boundary. Pitfalls: ignoring errors with _, using panic for ordinary failures, and defer inside a long loop, which delays every cleanup until the function returns.

questions.title: context.Context, cancellation and deadlines in Go
questions.prompt: Explain the context package in Go. How do cancellation and deadlines propagate through a call tree, why is the context the first parameter, and what goes wrong if you ignore it?

expectedConcepts.label: Carries cancellation, deadline and request-scoped values
WithCancel / WithTimeout / WithDeadline; parent cancels children
First parameter, passed to HTTP and DB calls, select on Done
Goroutine leaks, missing defer cancel, contexts in structs

researchContext: An HTTP server gives each request r.Context(), which is cancelled when the client disconnects or the handler returns.
ctx.Err() returns context.Canceled or context.DeadlineExceeded once Done is closed.
Use context values only for request-scoped data that crosses API boundaries (trace IDs, auth info), not for optional function parameters.
questions.modelAnswer: A context.Context carries a cancellation signal, an optional deadline and request-scoped values down a call tree. You derive children with context.WithCancel, WithTimeout or WithDeadline, and cancelling a parent cancels all of its children. Long-running work watches ctx.Done() in a select, and blocking calls such as HTTP requests and database queries take the ctx so they stop early and return ctx.Err(). By convention ctx is the first parameter, so it flows explicitly through every layer. Always defer cancel() after creating one, or its resources stay alive until the parent ends. If you ignore the context, goroutines keep working after the client has gone, which wastes resources and leaks goroutines. Don't store contexts in structs, and don't use context values for optional parameters.

questions.title: Maps and shared state between goroutines
questions.prompt: Explain why Go maps are not safe for concurrent use, and compare the options for sharing state between goroutines: sync.Mutex, sync.RWMutex, sync.Map and channels. When would you choose each?

expectedConcepts.label: No internal locking; concurrent writes are a race and may crash
Mutex, RWMutex, sync.Map, channels
Read-heavy, write-once caches, owner goroutine
Race detector; copying mutexes; holding locks during I/O

researchContext: The runtime detects many unsynchronised map writes and aborts with "fatal error: concurrent map writes", which cannot be recovered.
sync.Map is optimised for two cases: keys written once and read many times, and goroutines working on disjoint sets of keys. Otherwise a map plus Mutex is usually simpler and as fast.
Run tests with `go test -race`; `go vet` flags copying values that contain a sync.Mutex.
questions.modelAnswer: Built-in maps have no internal locking. Concurrent writes, or a write during a read, are a data race, and the runtime often detects this and aborts with "concurrent map writes". Options: guard the map with a sync.Mutex, the simple default; use a sync.RWMutex when reads vastly outnumber writes; use sync.Map for specific cases like caches whose keys are written once and read many times, or goroutines working on disjoint keys; or let one goroutine own the map and receive requests over channels. Find races with go test -race. Pitfalls: copying a struct that contains a mutex, forgetting to unlock (use defer), and holding a lock during slow I/O.

questions.title: Generics in Go
questions.prompt: Explain generics in Go. Cover type parameters, constraints such as comparable and union types, when generics are better than interfaces, and their current limitations.

expectedConcepts.label: Type parameters in square brackets, checked at compile time
Constraints: any, comparable, union sets, ~T
Containers and algorithms over many types; interfaces for behaviour
No generic methods; over-engineering

researchContext: Generics arrived in Go 1.18 (March 2022). Methods cannot declare their own type parameters; only the type can.
`~int` in a constraint matches any type whose underlying type is int, e.g. `type Celsius int`.
The standard library's slices and maps packages (Go 1.21) are the best examples of idiomatic generic code.
questions.modelAnswer: Since Go 1.18, functions and types can take type parameters in square brackets, such as func Map[T, U any](s []T, f func(T) U) []U, checked at compile time. Each type parameter has a constraint, which is an interface: any allows every type, comparable allows == and map keys, and constraints can list union sets like ~int | ~float64, where the tilde includes types whose underlying type matches; cmp.Ordered allows < and >. Generics fit containers and algorithms that work the same on many types, as in the slices and maps packages, giving type safety without interface{} and type assertions. Interfaces remain better when you care about behaviour, meaning what methods a value has. Limitations: methods cannot have their own type parameters, and generic code can be harder to read, so avoid it when a simple function or interface works.

questions.title: Structs, embedding and composition in Go
questions.prompt: Go has no classes or inheritance. Explain how structs, methods and embedding give you composition instead, how promoted methods work, and how this differs from inheritance.

expectedConcepts.label: Structs plus methods; composition over inheritance
Embedded fields and promoted methods
Reuse behaviour, satisfy interfaces, wrap types
No polymorphism via the embedded type; name conflicts

researchContext: A method promoted from an embedded field still runs with the embedded value as its receiver; it knows nothing about the outer struct.
Embedding an interface in a struct is a way to wrap an implementation and override only some methods.
Embedding sync.Mutex exposes Lock and Unlock as part of your type's API; often a named field is clearer.
questions.modelAnswer: Go has structs and methods but no classes or inheritance; you build types by composition. If a struct embeds another type, writing just the type name as a field, the inner type's fields and methods are promoted, so you can call outer.Method() directly, and the outer struct also satisfies any interface the inner type's methods satisfy. This lets you reuse behaviour and wrap types, for example embedding an io.Reader and overriding only Read. It is not inheritance: a promoted method still runs with the inner value as its receiver and knows nothing about the outer struct, so there is no virtual dispatch back to the outer type, and an outer struct cannot be used where the inner struct type is required. Polymorphism in Go comes from interfaces instead. Pitfalls: two embedded types with the same method name make it ambiguous, and embedding something like sync.Mutex exposes Lock and Unlock as part of your public API.

questions.title: Value and pointer receivers in Go
questions.prompt: Explain the difference between value receivers and pointer receivers on Go methods. How do they affect mutation, copying, method sets and interface satisfaction, and how do you choose?

expectedConcepts.label: Value receivers get a copy; pointer receivers can mutate
Method sets: *T has both, T only value methods
Pointer for mutation, large structs, or a mutex inside; be consistent
Changes lost on a copy; T does not implement an interface with pointer methods

questions.modelAnswer: A value receiver, func (c Counter) Inc(), gets a copy of the value, so changes inside the method are lost when it returns. A pointer receiver, func (c *Counter) Inc(), gets a pointer and can modify the original, and avoids copying a large struct. Go automatically takes the address when you call a pointer method on an addressable variable, so c.Inc() works either way. Method sets matter for interfaces: the method set of *T includes both pointer and value methods, but the method set of T only includes value methods, so if Inc has a pointer receiver, Counter does not implement an interface that requires Inc, while *Counter does. Choose pointer receivers when the method mutates, when the struct is large, or when it contains a sync.Mutex that must not be copied; use value receivers for small, immutable values. Be consistent within a type. Classic bugs: a mutation that silently does nothing, and the error that a type does not implement an interface because its methods have pointer receivers.

questions.title: select, timeouts and worker pools in Go
questions.prompt: Explain how select works in Go and how you use it for timeouts and cancellation. Then describe how to build a worker pool with a fixed number of goroutines, and how to shut it down cleanly.

expectedConcepts.label: select waits on several channel operations, picks a ready one
time.After, ctx.Done, jobs and results channels, WaitGroup
Fixed workers bound concurrency and apply back-pressure
Close the jobs channel; avoid leaks and sends on closed channels

researchContext: If several cases are ready, select picks one at random; a default case makes select non-blocking.
Only the sender should close a channel; receiving from a closed channel returns the zero value immediately, and `v, ok := <-ch` tells you it was closed.
golang.org/x/sync/errgroup with SetLimit is a common alternative to a hand-written pool.
questions.modelAnswer: select waits on several channel operations at once and runs whichever case becomes ready first, choosing randomly if several are ready; a default case makes it non-blocking. For a timeout, add a case <-time.After(2 * time.Second), or better, a case <-ctx.Done() so cancellation and deadlines come from the context. A worker pool starts a fixed number of goroutines that all range over a shared jobs channel and send to a results channel. The fixed size bounds concurrency, protecting databases or APIs, and an unbuffered or small buffered jobs channel gives natural back-pressure to the producer. To shut down cleanly, the producer closes the jobs channel when it has sent everything; each worker's range loop then ends, and a sync.WaitGroup waits for all workers before closing the results channel. Pitfalls: closing a channel from the receiving side or twice causes a panic, forgetting to close leaves workers blocked forever (a goroutine leak), and not draining results can deadlock the workers.

questions.title: WaitGroup, errgroup and sync.Once
questions.prompt: Explain how sync.WaitGroup, errgroup and sync.Once are used to coordinate goroutines in Go. How do you collect the first error and cancel the remaining work?

expectedConcepts.label: Add before starting, Done when finished, Wait blocks
errgroup.WithContext, sync.Once
First error cancels the shared context; SetLimit bounds concurrency
Add inside the goroutine, copying a WaitGroup, ignoring errors

questions.modelAnswer: sync.WaitGroup waits for a group of goroutines: call wg.Add(1) before starting each goroutine, defer wg.Done() inside it, and wg.Wait() blocks until the counter reaches zero. It does not collect errors. errgroup from golang.org/x/sync adds that: g, ctx := errgroup.WithContext(parent); each g.Go(func() error {...}) runs a task, g.Wait() returns the first non-nil error, and that first error cancels ctx so the other tasks can stop early if they watch it. g.SetLimit(n) bounds how many tasks run at once. sync.Once runs a function exactly once even when called from many goroutines, which is useful for lazy initialisation of a shared client or config. Pitfalls: calling Add inside the goroutine instead of before it (Wait may return too early), passing a WaitGroup by value so Done affects a copy, and, before Go 1.22, capturing the loop variable in goroutines started in a loop.

questions.title: Go's garbage collector and escape analysis
questions.prompt: Explain how memory is managed in Go. Cover stack versus heap allocation, escape analysis, how the concurrent garbage collector works, and how you reduce allocations in hot code.

expectedConcepts.label: Escape analysis decides stack or heap
Concurrent tri-color mark and sweep; GOGC
Preallocate, reuse buffers, sync.Pool, profile with pprof
Allocation rate drives GC CPU; pointers in interfaces escape

researchContext: `go build -gcflags=-m` prints the compiler's escape-analysis decisions.
GOGC=100 (default) starts a cycle when the heap has grown 100% since the last collection; GOMEMLIMIT (Go 1.19) sets a soft memory cap.
Go's GC is non-generational and non-moving; pauses are usually well under a millisecond, but marking uses CPU (about 25% of GOMAXPROCS during a cycle).
questions.modelAnswer: In Go you don't choose stack or heap: the compiler's escape analysis decides. A value that never outlives its function stays on the goroutine's stack, which is cheap and freed automatically; a value whose address escapes, for example returned as a pointer, stored in a global, captured by a long-lived closure or often put in an interface, goes on the heap. You can see the decisions with go build -gcflags=-m. The heap is managed by a concurrent, non-moving, tri-color mark-and-sweep collector: it marks reachable objects while your goroutines keep running, using write barriers, with very short stop-the-world pauses. GOGC controls how much the heap may grow between cycles, and GOMEMLIMIT sets a soft memory limit. The real cost is CPU: the more you allocate, the more often the collector runs. In hot code, preallocate slices and maps, reuse buffers, use sync.Pool for short-lived objects, avoid unnecessary pointers and interface conversions, and measure with pprof and benchmarks using -benchmem.

questions.title: Strings, bytes and runes in Go
questions.prompt: Explain how strings work in Go. Cover immutability, UTF-8 encoding, the difference between bytes and runes, what ranging over a string returns, and how to build strings efficiently.

expectedConcepts.label: Immutable sequence of bytes, usually UTF-8
byte vs rune (int32 code point); range decodes runes
strings.Builder, bytes.Buffer, avoid += in loops
len counts bytes; indexing gives bytes; conversions copy

questions.modelAnswer: A Go string is an immutable, read-only sequence of bytes, almost always holding UTF-8 text. A byte is a uint8; a rune is an int32 holding one Unicode code point, which may take one to four bytes in UTF-8. So len(s) counts bytes, not characters, and s[i] returns a byte, which may be the middle of a multi-byte character. Ranging over a string decodes UTF-8 for you: for i, r := range s gives the byte index and the rune at that position. To count characters use utf8.RuneCountInString, or convert to []rune. Because strings are immutable, s += x in a loop creates a new string each time; use strings.Builder, or bytes.Buffer, to build strings efficiently. Converting between string and []byte usually copies the data, so avoid doing it repeatedly in hot paths.

questions.title: Testing and benchmarking in Go
questions.prompt: Explain how you test Go code. Cover the testing package, table-driven tests, subtests, test doubles through interfaces, benchmarks, and the race detector.

expectedConcepts.label: _test.go files, TestXxx(t *testing.T), go test
Table-driven tests and subtests with t.Run
Fakes via interfaces, httptest, benchmarks, coverage
Race detector, flaky tests from timing and shared state

questions.modelAnswer: Go has testing built in: tests live in _test.go files next to the code, as functions like func TestParse(t *testing.T), and go test runs them; t.Errorf reports a failure and continues, while t.Fatalf stops the test. The idiomatic style is table-driven tests: a slice of cases with inputs and expected outputs, looped over with t.Run(name, ...) so each case is a named subtest that can run on its own. Dependencies are replaced through small interfaces, so you pass a fake store or clock instead of a real database, and net/http/httptest gives fake servers and recorders. Benchmarks are func BenchmarkX(b *testing.B), run with go test -bench and -benchmem; go test -cover reports coverage and fuzz tests find edge cases. Run go test -race in CI to catch data races. Avoid flaky tests: don't rely on time.Sleep or global state shared between tests.

questions.title: Packages, modules and visibility in Go
questions.prompt: Explain how Go organises code into packages and modules. Cover exported versus unexported names, the go.mod file and versioning, internal packages, and how you avoid import cycles.

expectedConcepts.label: A package is a directory; a module is a versioned set of packages
Capitalised names are exported; internal packages
Semantic versioning, go.sum, minimal version selection
Import cycles are errors; break them with interfaces or new packages

questions.modelAnswer: In Go, a package is a directory of .go files that share a package name; a module is a versioned collection of packages defined by a go.mod file, which names the module path and lists dependency versions. go.sum records checksums so builds are reproducible. Visibility is by capitalisation: identifiers starting with an uppercase letter are exported from the package, lowercase ones are private to it. Packages under a directory named internal can only be imported by code inside the parent of internal, which hides implementation details from other modules. Go uses semantic versioning, and from v2 onwards the major version becomes part of the import path; minimal version selection picks the lowest versions that satisfy every requirement, so builds are predictable. Import cycles are compile errors; break them by moving shared types into a separate package, or by having the lower-level package define an interface that the higher-level one implements. Avoid catch-all util packages.

questions.title: The GIL, threads, processes and asyncio in Python
questions.prompt: Explain the Global Interpreter Lock in CPython. How does it affect threads for CPU-bound versus I/O-bound work, and when would you use threading, multiprocessing or asyncio?

expectedConcepts.label: Only one thread runs Python bytecode at a time
CPU-bound vs I/O-bound work
asyncio / threading for I/O, multiprocessing for CPU
GIL is not thread safety; process overhead; free-threaded builds

questions.modelAnswer: In CPython, the Global Interpreter Lock lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time, which keeps memory management (reference counting) simple. Threads still help for I/O-bound work, because the GIL is released while a thread waits on a socket or file. For CPU-bound pure-Python code, threads give no speed-up. Use asyncio for many concurrent I/O tasks in one thread, threading for blocking I/O libraries, and multiprocessing or ProcessPoolExecutor for CPU-bound work, at the cost of process start-up and pickling data between processes. C extensions such as NumPy can release the GIL during heavy computation. The GIL does not make your code thread-safe: compound operations like counter += 1 can still race. Since Python 3.13 there is also an optional free-threaded build without the GIL.

questions.title: Generators and iterators in Python
questions.prompt: Explain generators and iterators in Python. How does yield work, why are generators memory-efficient, and how do generator expressions differ from list comprehensions?

expectedConcepts.label: yield pauses the function and resumes on next()
Iterator protocol: __iter__, __next__, StopIteration
Constant memory for large or infinite streams; pipelines
Generators can only be iterated once

questions.modelAnswer: An iterator is an object with __next__ (and __iter__) that returns the next item or raises StopIteration when it is done; a for loop uses this protocol. A generator function contains yield: calling it returns a generator object, and each next() runs the body until the next yield, hands back the value and pauses with its local state saved. Values are produced lazily, one at a time, so you can process a huge file line by line, chain processing pipelines, or represent infinite sequences in constant memory. A generator expression such as (x * x for x in data) is lazy, while a list comprehension [x * x for x in data] builds the whole list at once. Pitfall: generators are single-use, so once one is exhausted, iterating it again yields nothing.

questions.title: References, mutability and copying in Python
questions.prompt: Explain how Python variables, references and mutability work. Why does a mutable default argument cause bugs, and what is the difference between a shallow and a deep copy?

expectedConcepts.label: Names are references bound to objects; assignment does not copy
Mutable vs immutable types
Shallow copy vs deepcopy
Mutable default argument evaluated once

questions.modelAnswer: Python names are references bound to objects; assignment never copies, it binds another name to the same object. Immutable objects (int, str, tuple) cannot change, so an operation that seems to modify them creates a new object. Mutable objects (list, dict, set) change in place, and every reference sees the change; function arguments are passed as references to the same objects. A default argument is evaluated once, when the function is defined, so def f(x, items=[]) shares one list across all calls; use items=None and create the list inside the function. copy.copy makes a shallow copy: a new outer container holding the same inner objects. copy.deepcopy recursively copies nested objects too.

questions.title: Decorators and closures in Python
questions.prompt: Explain how decorators work in Python. Cover functions as first-class objects, closures, and functools.wraps, with an example such as timing or caching.

expectedConcepts.label: A decorator takes a function and returns a new one
The wrapper is a closure over the original function
lru_cache, timing, logging, retries
functools.wraps keeps the name and docstring

questions.modelAnswer: Functions in Python are first-class objects, so you can pass them in and return them. A decorator is a callable that takes a function and returns a new one: writing @timer above def f is the same as f = timer(f). The returned wrapper is a closure: it remembers the original function from the enclosing scope, usually accepts *args and **kwargs, does something before or after, and calls the original. Real uses include functools.lru_cache for memoisation, timing, logging, retries and access checks in web frameworks. Apply functools.wraps to the wrapper; otherwise the decorated function loses its __name__, docstring and signature, which hurts debugging. A decorator that takes arguments adds one more layer: a function that returns the decorator.

questions.title: How Python dictionaries work
questions.prompt: Explain how a Python dict works internally. Cover hashing, collisions, why keys must be hashable, the average and worst-case complexity, and why dicts keep insertion order.

expectedConcepts.label: Hash table: hash the key to find a slot
Hashable keys, __hash__ and __eq__, open addressing
Average O(1); compact layout keeps insertion order
Unhashable mutable keys; modifying a dict while iterating

questions.modelAnswer: A Python dict is a hash table. To store a key, Python calls hash(key), uses the hash to pick a slot, and on a collision probes other slots (open addressing) until it finds a free one; lookups repeat the probe and use == to confirm the key. That's why keys must be hashable: immutable types like str, int and tuple work, while lists and dicts don't, and custom classes need consistent __hash__ and __eq__. Lookups, inserts and deletes are O(1) on average and O(n) in the rare worst case of many collisions. The table resizes as it fills to keep probes short. Since Python 3.7, dicts keep insertion order as a language guarantee, because CPython stores entries in a compact array in insertion order with a separate sparse index table. Pitfalls: using a mutable object as a key, and adding or removing keys while iterating, which raises RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration.

questions.title: Choosing Python collections
questions.prompt: Compare Python's list, tuple, set and dict, plus collections.deque and heapq. Explain the time complexity of common operations and how you choose the right one.

expectedConcepts.label: list mutable sequence, tuple immutable, set unique, dict key-value
O(1) append and lookup by index; O(n) membership in a list
deque for queues, heapq for priority queues, Counter/defaultdict
list.pop(0) and 'in list' are O(n); sets are unordered

questions.modelAnswer: A list is a dynamic array: append and index access are O(1) (append amortised), but inserting or popping at the front and checking x in list are O(n). A tuple is an immutable list, hashable if its items are, so it can be a dict key and signals fixed records. A set stores unique hashable items with O(1) average membership tests, adds and removes, but has no order. A dict maps keys to values with O(1) average lookups and keeps insertion order. collections.deque is a double-ended queue with O(1) appends and pops at both ends, which is right for queues and BFS. heapq turns a list into a binary heap with O(log n) push and pop of the smallest item, a priority queue. Counter and defaultdict simplify counting and grouping. Common mistakes: using list.pop(0) as a queue, and testing membership in a large list inside a loop instead of converting it to a set.

questions.title: Classes, dunder methods and the MRO in Python
questions.prompt: Explain how classes work in Python. Cover __init__ and self, special dunder methods such as __repr__, __eq__ and __len__, inheritance with super(), and the method resolution order.

expectedConcepts.label: __init__ initialises; self is the instance
Dunder methods plug into built-in operations
super() and the C3 method resolution order
Class vs instance attributes; __eq__ without __hash__

questions.modelAnswer: A class defines a type; calling it creates an instance and runs __init__ to set up attributes, with self referring to that instance. Special dunder methods let your objects work with built-in syntax: __repr__ controls how they print in the console and logs, __eq__ defines ==, __lt__ supports sorting, __len__ and __getitem__ make them behave like containers, and __enter__ and __exit__ make them context managers. A subclass calls super().__init__() to reuse the parent's setup. With multiple inheritance, Python uses the C3 linearisation, the method resolution order shown by Class.__mro__, so each class appears once and super() calls the next class in that order, which makes cooperative mixins work. Pitfalls: a mutable class attribute is shared by all instances, defining __eq__ without __hash__ makes instances unhashable, and deep inheritance trees are harder to follow than composition.

questions.title: Exceptions and context managers in Python
questions.prompt: Explain exception handling in Python with try, except, else and finally, and how context managers and the with statement guarantee cleanup. How would you write your own context manager?

expectedConcepts.label: try / except / else / finally
with calls __enter__ and __exit__
Files, locks, connections; contextlib.contextmanager
Bare except, swallowing errors, catching too broadly

questions.modelAnswer: Code that may fail goes in try; except catches specific exception types; else runs only if no exception occurred; finally always runs, for cleanup. raise throws an exception, and raise ... from err chains the original cause. A context manager packages setup and cleanup: the with statement calls __enter__ at the start and __exit__ at the end, even if an exception is raised, so with open(path) as f closes the file and with lock: releases the lock. You can write one as a class with __enter__ and __exit__, or more simply with the contextlib.contextmanager decorator: a generator that does setup, yields the resource, and does cleanup in a finally block. Pitfalls: a bare except: also catches KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit; catching Exception too broadly and doing pass swallows real bugs. Catch the narrowest exception you can handle.

questions.title: Type hints and dataclasses in Python
questions.prompt: Explain type hints in Python and what tools like mypy do with them. Then explain dataclasses: what they generate for you, and when you would use them instead of a plain class, a dict or a named tuple.

expectedConcepts.label: Hints are not enforced at runtime; checked by mypy/pyright
@dataclass generates __init__, __repr__, __eq__
Structured records vs dicts; Pydantic for validation
Mutable defaults need default_factory; hints don't validate

questions.modelAnswer: Type hints, such as def total(items: list[float]) -> float, document the expected types but are not enforced when the code runs. Static checkers like mypy or pyright read them and report mismatches before runtime, and editors use them for autocompletion and refactoring. A dataclass is a class decorated with @dataclass: from annotated fields, it generates __init__, __repr__ and __eq__, and can generate ordering, immutability with frozen=True, and lighter objects with slots=True. Use it instead of a dict for structured records, so typos become errors and fields are discoverable; a NamedTuple suits small immutable tuples; Pydantic is better when you must validate untrusted data such as JSON, because dataclasses don't check types at runtime. Pitfall: a mutable default like a list must use field(default_factory=list), and Any in hints quietly switches checking off.

questions.title: async and await in Python
questions.prompt: Explain how async and await work in Python. Cover coroutines, the event loop, running tasks concurrently with gather, and what happens if you call blocking code inside a coroutine.

expectedConcepts.label: async def creates coroutines; await suspends until a result is ready
Event loop, tasks, gather
Many concurrent I/O operations: HTTP calls, sockets, web servers
Blocking calls freeze the loop; use to_thread or async libraries

questions.modelAnswer: async def defines a coroutine function; calling it returns a coroutine object that does nothing until it is awaited or scheduled. await suspends the current coroutine until the awaited operation, such as a network response, is ready, and hands control back to the event loop, which runs other coroutines in the meantime, all on a single thread. asyncio.run starts the loop; asyncio.create_task schedules a coroutine to run concurrently, and asyncio.gather or a TaskGroup waits for several at once, so ten HTTP requests take about as long as the slowest one. This suits I/O-bound work with many connections, like web servers in FastAPI or clients using httpx. The big pitfall is blocking: calling time.sleep, requests.get or heavy CPU work inside a coroutine freezes the whole loop, so every other task stops. Use await asyncio.sleep, async libraries, or asyncio.to_thread for blocking calls. Forgetting await is another common bug: the coroutine never runs.

questions.title: Memory management in CPython
questions.prompt: Explain how CPython manages memory. Cover reference counting, the cyclic garbage collector, when objects are freed, and how memory leaks can still happen in Python.

expectedConcepts.label: Reference counting frees objects at zero references
Generational cyclic garbage collector
Deterministic cleanup, weak references, profiling tools
Leaks via caches, globals, closures; __del__ surprises

questions.modelAnswer: CPython mainly uses reference counting: every object counts how many references point to it, and when the count drops to zero the object is freed immediately, which is why files are often closed as soon as the last reference goes away (though you should still use with). Reference counting cannot free cycles, such as two objects referring to each other, so CPython also has a generational cyclic garbage collector that periodically finds unreachable groups of objects and frees them; the gc module controls it. Leaks still happen when objects stay reachable by mistake: unbounded caches or global lists that keep growing, closures or callbacks holding large objects, or objects registered somewhere and never removed. Use weakref for caches and observers, and find leaks with tracemalloc or a memory profiler. Large small-object pools may also not return memory to the operating system right away.

questions.title: Scopes, args and kwargs in Python
questions.prompt: Explain how name lookup works in Python with the LEGB rule, what global and nonlocal do, and how *args and **kwargs, keyword-only and positional-only parameters work.

expectedConcepts.label: Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in lookup
global, nonlocal, *args, **kwargs
Keyword-only after *, positional-only before /
UnboundLocalError; shadowing built-ins

questions.modelAnswer: Python resolves a name using the LEGB rule: Local scope of the current function, then Enclosing functions, then the Global module scope, then Built-ins. Assigning to a name inside a function makes it local for the whole function, so reading it before the assignment raises UnboundLocalError; global makes the name refer to the module-level variable, and nonlocal to a variable in an enclosing function, which is how closures update counters. In a function definition, *args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple and **kwargs collects extra keyword arguments into a dict, which is handy for wrappers that forward everything. Parameters after a bare * are keyword-only, which makes calls clearer, and parameters before / are positional-only. Pitfalls: shadowing built-ins by naming variables list, dict or id, and overusing global state.

questions.title: Ownership and borrowing in Rust
questions.prompt: Explain ownership and borrowing in Rust. Cover move semantics, the rule of many shared borrows or one mutable borrow, and how this prevents data races and use-after-free without a garbage collector.

expectedConcepts.label: One owner; value dropped when the owner goes out of scope; moves
Many &T or one &mut T; borrow checker
No GC; prevents use-after-free and data races at compile time
Excess cloning; Rc<RefCell<T>> moves checks to runtime

questions.modelAnswer: Every value in Rust has exactly one owner, and when the owner goes out of scope the value is dropped, freeing its memory deterministically without a garbage collector. Assigning or passing a non-Copy value moves ownership, so the old variable can no longer be used. Instead of moving, you can borrow: any number of shared references (&T) or exactly one mutable reference (&mut T) at a time, and a reference can never outlive the value. The borrow checker enforces these rules at compile time, which rules out use-after-free, double free and data races, since a data race needs two aliases where at least one writes. The cost is a learning curve and sometimes restructuring code. Pitfalls are cloning everything to silence the compiler, and overusing Rc<RefCell<T>>, which moves borrow checks to runtime where they can panic.

questions.title: Option, Result and the ? operator in Rust
questions.prompt: Explain how Rust handles errors and missing values with Option and Result. Cover pattern matching, the question mark operator, and when panicking with unwrap is acceptable.

expectedConcepts.label: Option (Some/None) and Result (Ok/Err) instead of null and exceptions
Enums handled with match / if let; the ? operator
Early return with ?, From conversion, thiserror/anyhow
unwrap/expect panic; fine in tests, not on untrusted input

questions.modelAnswer: Rust has no null and no exceptions. Option<T> is either Some(value) or None, and Result<T, E> is either Ok(value) or Err(error). Both are enums, so the compiler makes you handle each case, usually with match or if let, or with combinators like map and and_then. The ? operator returns early with the error, converting it through From, or gives you the success value, which makes propagating errors concise. Libraries often define error enums (for example with thiserror), and applications often use anyhow. unwrap and expect panic on None or Err: fine in tests, prototypes, or when failure is truly impossible (document it with expect), but avoid them on input you don't control in production.

questions.title: Traits, generics and dyn in Rust
questions.prompt: Explain traits in Rust. Compare generics with trait bounds, which use static dispatch, against trait objects with dyn, which use dynamic dispatch, and describe the trade-offs.

expectedConcepts.label: A trait defines shared behaviour, like an interface
Monomorphised generics vs dyn trait objects with a vtable
Inlining and speed vs binary size and heterogeneous collections
Only dyn-compatible (object-safe) traits; code bloat

questions.modelAnswer: A trait defines shared behaviour: a set of methods a type can implement, much like an interface, optionally with default methods. Generics with trait bounds, such as fn show<T: Display>(x: T), are monomorphised: the compiler generates a specialised copy for each concrete type, giving static dispatch, inlining and no runtime cost, but larger binaries and longer compile times. A trait object, &dyn Trait or Box<dyn Trait>, is a fat pointer to the data plus a vtable, giving dynamic dispatch: one copy of the code and the ability to keep different types in one collection, at the cost of an indirect call and no inlining. Only dyn-compatible (formerly object-safe) traits can be trait objects; for example, generic methods are not allowed unless restricted with where Self: Sized.

questions.title: Send, Sync, Arc and Mutex in Rust
questions.prompt: Explain the Send and Sync traits in Rust and how they make threads safe. Why are Rc and RefCell not thread-safe, and what do Arc and Mutex provide instead?

expectedConcepts.label: Send = can move to another thread; Sync = &T can be shared
Rc/RefCell vs Arc/Mutex, atomic reference counting
thread::spawn requires Send; unsafe sharing is a compile error
Deadlocks and lock poisoning are still possible

questions.modelAnswer: Send means a value can be moved to another thread; Sync means a shared reference &T can be used from several threads (T is Sync if &T is Send). Both are auto marker traits: a type gets them automatically when all its fields have them. thread::spawn requires its closure to be Send and 'static, so unsafe sharing becomes a compile error rather than a runtime bug. Rc uses a non-atomic reference count, so it is neither Send nor Sync, and RefCell does borrow checks at runtime without synchronisation, so it is not Sync. Across threads, use Arc, an atomically reference-counted pointer, for shared ownership, and Mutex or RwLock for mutation: Arc<Mutex<T>>. Rust prevents data races, but not deadlocks or higher-level logic races, and a Mutex becomes poisoned if a thread panics while holding it.

questions.title: Lifetimes in Rust
questions.prompt: Explain lifetimes in Rust. What problem do lifetime annotations solve, how do elision rules let you omit them most of the time, and what does a signature like fn longest<'a>(x: &'a str, y: &'a str) -> &'a str mean?

expectedConcepts.label: References must not outlive the data they point to
Lifetime parameters, elision, 'static
Annotations relate lifetimes; they don't change them
Returning references to locals; structs holding references

questions.modelAnswer: A lifetime is the region of code during which a reference is valid. The borrow checker uses lifetimes to make sure no reference outlives the data it points to, which prevents dangling references. Annotations like 'a don't change how long anything lives; they describe relationships between lifetimes so the compiler can check them. In fn longest<'a>(x: &'a str, y: &'a str) -> &'a str, the returned reference is valid for no longer than the shorter of x and y, so the caller can't use the result after either input is dropped. Most of the time you don't write lifetimes because of elision rules: each reference parameter gets its own lifetime; if there is exactly one input lifetime, it is used for outputs; and for methods taking &self, outputs get self's lifetime. 'static means the data lives for the whole program, like string literals. Pitfalls: trying to return a reference to a local variable, which can never work, and putting references in structs too early; often an owned type like String is simpler.

questions.title: Box, Rc and RefCell in Rust
questions.prompt: Explain Rust's smart pointers Box, Rc and RefCell. What does each one solve, how does interior mutability work, and how can Rc create memory leaks?

expectedConcepts.label: Box: single owner on the heap; recursive types, trait objects
Rc shared ownership; RefCell interior mutability
Graphs and trees; Weak for parent links; Arc/Mutex across threads
Rc cycles leak; RefCell panics at runtime

questions.modelAnswer: Box<T> puts a value on the heap with a single owner; it is used for recursive types like linked lists and trees, for large values you want to move cheaply, and for trait objects such as Box<dyn Error>. Rc<T> gives shared ownership within one thread: cloning an Rc increments a reference count, and the value is dropped when the last Rc goes away. Because Rc only hands out shared references, you combine it with RefCell<T> for interior mutability: RefCell moves the borrow rules from compile time to runtime, so borrow() and borrow_mut() check at runtime that there is never a mutable borrow alongside others. Rc<RefCell<T>> is common for graphs and shared state; across threads the equivalents are Arc and Mutex. Pitfalls: two Rc values pointing at each other form a cycle whose counts never reach zero, leaking memory, so use Weak for back-pointers such as a child's link to its parent; and a second borrow_mut while one is active panics with "already borrowed".

questions.title: Iterators and closures in Rust
questions.prompt: Explain iterators and closures in Rust. Cover lazy iterator adapters like map and filter, consumers like collect, the Fn, FnMut and FnOnce traits, and why iterator chains are zero-cost.

expectedConcepts.label: Adapters are lazy until a consumer runs them
Fn, FnMut, FnOnce; move closures
Compiles to loops as fast as hand-written code
Unused lazy iterators; iter vs into_iter ownership

questions.modelAnswer: An iterator is anything implementing the Iterator trait, whose next() returns Some(item) or None. Adapters such as map, filter, enumerate and zip are lazy: they build a new iterator and do nothing until a consumer like collect, sum, for or count pulls items through. Closures are anonymous functions that capture variables from their environment. The compiler picks the most flexible trait: Fn if the closure only reads what it captures, FnMut if it mutates captured state, FnOnce if it consumes it; the move keyword forces captured values to be moved in, which is needed for threads. Iterator chains are zero-cost abstractions: thanks to monomorphisation and inlining, data.iter().filter(...).map(...).sum() usually compiles to the same tight loop you would write by hand, often without bounds checks. Pitfalls: building an iterator chain without consuming it does nothing (the compiler warns), and choosing between iter(), iter_mut() and into_iter() decides whether you borrow, mutably borrow or move the collection.

questions.title: Enums and pattern matching in Rust
questions.prompt: Explain enums and pattern matching in Rust. How do enums with data differ from enums in C or Java, why must match be exhaustive, and how do you use them to make invalid states unrepresentable?

expectedConcepts.label: Variants can carry data (algebraic data types)
Exhaustive match, if let, destructuring, guards
Make invalid states unrepresentable; state machines
Catch-all _ hides new variants

questions.modelAnswer: In C or Java an enum is mostly a set of named constants. In Rust each variant can carry its own data, making enums algebraic data types or tagged unions: enum Shape { Circle { r: f64 }, Rect { w: f64, h: f64 } }. Option and Result are ordinary enums. You take them apart with match, which destructures the data and can add guards like Some(x) if x > 0, or with if let for a single case. match must be exhaustive: the compiler rejects code that forgets a variant, so when you add a new variant, every place that needs updating becomes a compile error. That lets you make invalid states unrepresentable: instead of a struct with a status field plus optional fields that only make sense in some states, model each state as a variant that carries exactly its data, like a connection that is Connecting, Connected { session } or Failed { error }. Pitfall: a catch-all _ arm silences the exhaustiveness check, so new variants slip through unnoticed.

questions.title: async and await in Rust
questions.prompt: Explain how async and await work in Rust. Cover futures being lazy and polled, why you need a runtime such as Tokio, and the difference between spawning a task and awaiting a future.

expectedConcepts.label: async fn returns a lazy Future that is polled
Executor/runtime (Tokio), wakers, tasks
Many I/O-bound connections; join for concurrency
Blocking in async code; Send bounds; holding locks across await
