questions.modelAnswer: An async fn returns a Future, a value representing work that hasn't finished. Futures in Rust are lazy: nothing happens until something polls them, and the compiler turns each async fn into a state machine that can pause at every await. The standard library defines Future but no executor, so you add a runtime such as Tokio, which polls futures, parks them while they wait on I/O, and uses wakers to resume them when sockets or timers are ready. Awaiting a future runs it as part of the current task, one step after another; join! runs several futures concurrently within the task; tokio::spawn creates an independent task the runtime can run in parallel on its worker threads, which therefore requires the future to be Send and 'static. Async shines for many I/O-bound connections, such as web servers. Pitfalls: calling blocking code or heavy CPU work inside async code stalls the runtime's threads, so use spawn_blocking; and holding a std::sync::Mutex guard across an await can deadlock or make the future non-Send.

questions.title: unsafe Rust
questions.prompt: Explain what unsafe means in Rust. What extra operations does it allow, what guarantees do you take responsibility for, and how should unsafe code be wrapped in safe abstractions?

expectedConcepts.label: Raw pointer dereference, unsafe functions, FFI, mutable statics, unsafe traits
You uphold the invariants; the borrow checker still runs
Small unsafe blocks inside safe APIs, like Vec
Aliasing violations, data races; test with Miri

questions.modelAnswer: unsafe doesn't turn off the borrow checker; it unlocks a few extra operations: dereferencing raw pointers, calling unsafe functions including foreign C functions over FFI, accessing mutable statics, implementing unsafe traits like Send or Sync by hand, and accessing union fields. In return you promise to uphold the invariants the compiler can't check, such as pointers being valid and aligned, no aliasing &mut, and no data races; breaking them is undefined behaviour. The idiom is to keep unsafe blocks small, document why they are sound with a SAFETY comment, and wrap them in a safe API that cannot be misused from safe code. The standard library does exactly this: Vec, String and Mutex use unsafe internally but expose safe interfaces. Unsafe is also how Rust binds to C libraries. Risks: subtle aliasing and lifetime bugs; test unsafe code with Miri and keep it small enough to audit.

questions.title: String versus &str in Rust
questions.prompt: Explain the difference between String and &str in Rust. Cover ownership, how string slices work, UTF-8 and why you cannot index a string by position, and which type to use in function parameters.

expectedConcepts.label: String owns a growable heap buffer; &str borrows a slice
Always valid UTF-8; chars vs bytes
Take &str in parameters; deref coercion from &String
No indexing by position; slicing mid-character panics

questions.modelAnswer: String is an owned, growable, heap-allocated buffer of text: you can push to it and it is freed when its owner goes out of scope. &str is a borrowed string slice, a pointer and a length pointing into text owned by something else: a String, or the program binary for string literals, which have type &'static str. Both are always valid UTF-8, so one character can take one to four bytes. That's why Rust doesn't let you index s[3]: a position in bytes might be the middle of a character, and a position in characters would be O(n). Use .chars() for Unicode scalar values and .bytes() for raw bytes, and byte-range slicing like &s[0..4] panics if it doesn't fall on a character boundary. For function parameters, take &str: it accepts string literals and, through deref coercion, &String, without forcing callers to allocate. Return String when you create new text, and convert with to_string or to_owned.

questions.title: Copy, Clone and Drop in Rust
questions.prompt: Explain the Copy, Clone and Drop traits in Rust. Which types are Copy, why can't a type be both Copy and Drop, and when does a value get dropped?

expectedConcepts.label: Copy is an implicit bitwise copy; Clone is an explicit, possibly deep copy
Drop runs cleanup when a value goes out of scope
Integers, bools, chars, shared references are Copy; String and Vec are not
Copy and Drop are mutually exclusive; mem::forget; clone costs

questions.modelAnswer: By default, assigning or passing a value moves it. If a type implements Copy, the value is instead copied implicitly with a simple bitwise copy, and the original stays usable. Integers, floats, bool, char, shared references and tuples or arrays of Copy types are Copy; String, Vec and Box are not, because copying their bits would create two owners of the same heap buffer. Clone is an explicit .clone() that can do a deep copy, like duplicating a String's buffer, so its cost is visible in the code; you can derive both. Drop is Rust's destructor: its drop method runs automatically when a value goes out of scope, in reverse order of declaration, which is how RAII frees memory, closes files and releases locks. A type can't be both Copy and Drop, because implicit copies would make it unclear how many times cleanup runs. You can drop early with drop(x); std::mem::forget skips the destructor. Pitfall: cloning large values in hot loops just to satisfy the borrow checker.

questions.title: The JVM, JIT and garbage collection
questions.prompt: Explain how Java code runs on the JVM and how garbage collection works. Cover bytecode and JIT compilation, the heap and generational collection, and what causes GC pauses.

expectedConcepts.label: javac compiles to bytecode run by the JVM
JIT; reachability from GC roots; young and old generations
Stop-the-world pauses, G1/ZGC, heap sizing
Leaks via unintended references; OutOfMemoryError

questions.modelAnswer: javac compiles Java into platform-independent bytecode. The JVM loads classes, interprets the bytecode at first, profiles it, and JIT-compiles hot methods into optimised machine code. Objects live on the heap, and the garbage collector frees objects that are no longer reachable from GC roots such as thread stacks and static fields. Most objects die young, so collectors are generational: frequent, cheap collections of the young generation and rarer collections of the old generation. Modern collectors such as G1 (the default) and ZGC do much of their work concurrently to keep pauses short, but stop-the-world pauses still happen and grow with live data and allocation rate. Java can still leak memory: objects kept reachable by mistake, for example in static maps, caches or listeners that are never removed, until an OutOfMemoryError.

questions.title: equals, hashCode and HashMap in Java
questions.prompt: Explain the contract between equals and hashCode in Java, how HashMap uses them, and what goes wrong if you override one without the other or use mutable fields in a key.

expectedConcepts.label: Equal objects must have equal hash codes
hashCode picks the bucket, equals finds the key
Objects.hash / Objects.equals, records
Missed lookups, duplicates, mutable keys

questions.modelAnswer: The contract: if a.equals(b) is true, then a.hashCode() must equal b.hashCode(). The reverse need not hold, because collisions are allowed. HashMap and HashSet use hashCode to choose a bucket, then equals to find the matching key inside it. If you override equals but not hashCode, two equal keys usually land in different buckets, so lookups miss and a set can hold "duplicates". If a key's fields change after it is inserted, its hash changes and the entry becomes unreachable. Base both methods on the same immutable fields, use Objects.hash and Objects.equals, or use records, which generate both correctly.

questions.title: Visibility, volatile and executors in Java
questions.prompt: Explain the basics of the Java memory model: visibility, the volatile keyword, synchronized and happens-before. When would you use an ExecutorService or virtual threads instead of creating threads by hand?

expectedConcepts.label: Writes may be invisible or reordered without happens-before
volatile, synchronized, atomics
Thread pools, futures, virtual threads
volatile is not atomic; check-then-act; deadlocks

questions.modelAnswer: Without synchronisation, one thread's writes may never become visible to another, and operations can be reordered. The Java memory model defines happens-before rules: unlocking a monitor happens-before every later lock of the same monitor, and a write to a volatile field happens-before later reads of that field. volatile gives visibility and ordering, but not atomicity: count++ on a volatile int is still a race, so use AtomicInteger or a lock. synchronized gives mutual exclusion plus visibility. Rather than creating threads by hand, submit tasks to an ExecutorService, which manages a thread pool, returns futures and shuts down cleanly. Since Java 21, virtual threads make one thread per task cheap for blocking I/O. Pitfalls: check-then-act races and deadlocks from inconsistent lock ordering.

questions.title: Java collections: ArrayList, LinkedList and HashMap
questions.prompt: Compare ArrayList and LinkedList in Java, and explain how HashMap works internally, including buckets, resizing and treeification. What are the time complexities, and when would you choose each collection?

expectedConcepts.label: ArrayList is a resizable array; LinkedList is doubly linked
Buckets, load factor 0.75, resize, tree bins
ArrayList by default; ArrayDeque for queues; LinkedHashMap/TreeMap
ConcurrentModificationException; HashMap not thread-safe

questions.modelAnswer: ArrayList is a resizable array: get(i) is O(1), adding at the end is amortised O(1), and inserting or removing in the middle is O(n) because elements shift. LinkedList is a doubly linked list: adding or removing at the ends is O(1), but get(i) is O(n), and every node is a separate object, so it uses more memory and has poor cache locality. In practice ArrayList is the default, and ArrayDeque is better than LinkedList for queues and stacks. HashMap is an array of buckets: it hashes the key, picks a bucket, and stores entries there; equals finds the right key within a bucket. When the size exceeds capacity times the load factor (0.75 by default), it doubles the array and redistributes entries. Since Java 8, a bucket with many collisions turns into a red-black tree, so the worst case is O(log n) instead of O(n). Use LinkedHashMap for insertion order or LRU caches and TreeMap for sorted keys. Pitfalls: modifying a collection while iterating throws ConcurrentModificationException (use the iterator's remove), and HashMap is not thread-safe; use ConcurrentHashMap.

questions.title: Generics and type erasure in Java
questions.prompt: Explain generics in Java and type erasure. What can't you do because types are erased at runtime, and what do bounded wildcards like extends and super mean?

expectedConcepts.label: Type parameters are checked at compile time, then erased
? extends, ? super, PECS
Type-safe collections without casts; generic methods
No new T(), no instanceof List<String>, no primitives

questions.modelAnswer: Generics let classes and methods take type parameters, like List<String>, so the compiler checks types and inserts casts for you, giving type-safe collections without manual casting. Java implements them with type erasure: after checking, the compiler replaces type parameters with their bounds, usually Object, so at runtime List<String> and List<Integer> are the same class. That's why you can't write new T(), check instanceof List<String>, create a generic array, or use primitives like List<int>; you pass a Class<T> token when you need the type at runtime. Wildcards express variance: List<? extends Number> can be read as Numbers but you can't add to it, while List<? super Integer> accepts Integers but reads as Object. The rule of thumb is PECS: producer extends, consumer super, as in Collections.copy. Pitfalls: raw types and unchecked casts bypass the checks and cause ClassCastException later.

questions.title: Checked and unchecked exceptions in Java
questions.prompt: Explain Java's exception hierarchy and the difference between checked and unchecked exceptions. Cover try-with-resources, and the best practices for throwing and catching exceptions.

expectedConcepts.label: Throwable: Error and Exception; RuntimeException
Checked must be declared or caught; unchecked need not
try-with-resources closes AutoCloseable
Don't swallow; keep the cause; avoid catching Exception broadly

questions.modelAnswer: Everything thrown in Java is a Throwable, which splits into Error, for serious JVM problems like OutOfMemoryError that you normally don't catch, and Exception. Checked exceptions, such as IOException, must be either caught or declared in the method's throws clause, so the compiler forces callers to think about them. Unchecked exceptions extend RuntimeException, such as NullPointerException or IllegalArgumentException, and usually signal programming errors; they don't need declaring. try-with-resources, try (var in = Files.newInputStream(path)) { ... }, closes any AutoCloseable automatically, even on exceptions, replacing error-prone finally blocks. Best practices: catch only what you can handle, at the right level; wrap low-level exceptions in meaningful ones while keeping the original as the cause; never leave an empty catch block; don't use exceptions for normal control flow; and avoid catching Exception or Throwable broadly, which hides bugs.

questions.title: Interfaces versus abstract classes in Java
questions.prompt: Compare interfaces and abstract classes in Java. Cover default methods, multiple inheritance of type, state, and how sealed interfaces and records are used in modern Java.

expectedConcepts.label: Class can implement many interfaces but extend one class; abstract classes hold state
Default methods, sealed, records
Interfaces for contracts; abstract classes for shared implementation
Diamond conflicts with defaults; fragile base classes

questions.modelAnswer: An interface defines a contract: methods a class promises to provide. A class can implement many interfaces but extend only one class. An abstract class can hold state (fields), constructors and partly implemented methods, so it suits a family of closely related classes sharing code, as in the template method pattern. Since Java 8, interfaces can have default and static methods, which lets libraries add methods without breaking implementers, but interfaces still can't hold instance state. Modern Java adds records, concise immutable data carriers with generated constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode and toString, and sealed interfaces, which list exactly which classes may implement them; together with pattern matching in switch, the compiler can check that every case is handled. Prefer interfaces plus composition for flexibility. Pitfalls: two interfaces providing the same default method force you to override it to resolve the conflict, and deep abstract-class hierarchies become fragile when a base class changes.

questions.title: Streams and lambdas in Java
questions.prompt: Explain lambdas and the Stream API in Java. Cover functional interfaces, intermediate versus terminal operations, laziness, collectors, and when parallel streams or plain loops are a better choice.

expectedConcepts.label: Lambdas implement functional interfaces
Intermediate (lazy) vs terminal operations; collectors
Declarative pipelines; loops for simple or performance-critical code
Side effects, reusing streams, misused parallel streams

questions.modelAnswer: A lambda like x -> x * 2 is a short implementation of a functional interface, an interface with a single abstract method such as Function, Predicate, Supplier or Runnable; method references like String::length are shorthand for lambdas. The Stream API processes collections declaratively: list.stream().filter(...).map(...).collect(Collectors.toList()). Intermediate operations like filter, map and sorted are lazy and return a new stream; nothing runs until a terminal operation such as collect, forEach, count or reduce, which lets the pipeline stop early with findFirst. Collectors like groupingBy and joining build maps and strings. Streams are readable for transformations, but plain loops are fine, and sometimes faster, for simple or performance-critical code; use IntStream to avoid boxing. Pitfalls: side effects inside lambdas, reusing a stream after a terminal operation (IllegalStateException), and parallel streams, which share the common ForkJoinPool and only help for large, CPU-bound, independent work.

questions.title: The JavaScript event loop
questions.prompt: Explain the JavaScript event loop. Cover the call stack, the task queue and the microtask queue, and why a Promise callback runs before a setTimeout callback scheduled with zero delay.

expectedConcepts.label: One thread and call stack; async work handled by the runtime
Task (macrotask) queue vs microtask queue
Microtasks drain after each task, so promises run before timeouts
Long synchronous work blocks the loop; use workers

questions.modelAnswer: JavaScript runs your code on a single thread with one call stack. Slow operations such as timers, network requests and file I/O are handled by the browser or Node, which queue a callback when they finish. The event loop runs one task (macrotask) at a time, such as a setTimeout callback or an event handler, and after each task it drains the whole microtask queue: Promise reactions, queueMicrotask callbacks and code after an await. That's why Promise.resolve().then(a) runs before setTimeout(b, 0): a is a microtask processed as soon as the current script finishes, while b waits for a later task. Pitfalls: long synchronous work blocks the loop, freezing the UI or stalling a server, and endless microtask chains can starve rendering. Move CPU-heavy work to Web Workers or worker threads.

questions.title: Closures and this in JavaScript
questions.prompt: Explain closures in JavaScript and how the value of this is determined. Give an example of a closure, and explain how arrow functions differ from regular functions.

expectedConcepts.label: A function keeps access to variables of the scope where it was created
this depends on the call site; arrow functions use lexical this
Private state, counters, callbacks, event handlers
Losing this in callbacks; var in loops; retained memory

questions.modelAnswer: A closure is a function together with the variables from the scope where it was created; it can keep using them after the outer function has returned. Example: function counter() { let n = 0; return () => ++n; }. Each counter has its own private n. Closures power callbacks, event handlers, module privacy and memoisation. For regular functions, this is decided at the call site: obj.method() sets this to obj, a plain call gives undefined in strict mode, new sets it to the new object, and call, apply and bind set it explicitly. Arrow functions have no this of their own; they use the this of the enclosing scope, which makes them handy as callbacks inside methods. Pitfalls: losing this when passing obj.method as a callback, var in loops sharing one variable (use let), and closures keeping large objects alive.

questions.title: TypeScript's type system
questions.prompt: Explain TypeScript's type system. Cover structural typing, type inference, union types with narrowing, and why types are erased at runtime, including what that means for validating API data.

expectedConcepts.label: Static, structural typing checked at compile time
Inference, unions, narrowing, type guards, generics
Validate untrusted data at runtime, e.g. with Zod
Types are erased; any and as assertions hide bugs

questions.modelAnswer: TypeScript adds static types that are checked at compile time and then erased: the output is plain JavaScript. Typing is structural, so a value fits a type if it has the required shape, whatever its declared name. The compiler infers most types from initial values and return statements. Union types, such as string | number or discriminated unions like { kind: 'ok' } | { kind: 'error' }, are narrowed with typeof, in, checks on the discriminant, or custom type guards. Because types vanish at runtime, data from fetch or JSON.parse is untrusted: type it as unknown and validate it with a schema library such as Zod before using it. Pitfalls: any and as assertions silence the checker and let wrong data through.

questions.title: Prototypes and classes in JavaScript
questions.prompt: Explain prototypal inheritance in JavaScript. How does property lookup follow the prototype chain, and how do ES6 classes relate to prototypes?

expectedConcepts.label: Lookup walks the prototype chain until found or null
__proto__ / Object.getPrototypeOf, constructor .prototype, class, extends
Methods shared via the prototype save memory
Mutating built-in prototypes; class fields vs methods; this binding

questions.modelAnswer: Every JavaScript object has an internal link to another object, its prototype. When you read a property, the engine looks on the object itself, then on its prototype, then that object's prototype, up the prototype chain until it finds the property or reaches null; Object.prototype sits near the top, which is why every object has toString. Object.create(proto) makes an object with a chosen prototype, and Object.getPrototypeOf reads it. A constructor function's .prototype object becomes the prototype of instances created with new, so methods placed there are shared by all instances: one copy in memory. ES6 classes are mostly syntactic sugar over this: class methods go on the prototype, extends links the prototypes, and super calls the parent's version. Pitfalls: modifying built-in prototypes like Array.prototype breaks other code, arrow-function class fields create a separate function per instance rather than one shared method, and for...in also iterates inherited enumerable properties, so check hasOwnProperty or use Object.keys.

questions.title: Promises and async/await in JavaScript
questions.prompt: Explain promises and async/await in JavaScript. Cover promise states, chaining, error handling, and the difference between Promise.all, Promise.allSettled and Promise.race.

expectedConcepts.label: Pending, fulfilled, rejected; settles once
then/catch chaining; async functions return promises; await
all fails fast; allSettled waits for all; race takes the first
Unhandled rejections; sequential awaits in loops; forgotten await

questions.modelAnswer: A promise represents a value that will be available later. It starts pending and settles once, either fulfilled with a value or rejected with an error. then registers what to do with the value and returns a new promise, so steps chain; catch handles a rejection anywhere earlier in the chain. An async function always returns a promise, and await pauses that function until a promise settles, letting you write sequential-looking code with try/catch for errors. To run work concurrently, start the promises first and combine them: Promise.all waits for all and rejects as soon as any one fails, Promise.allSettled waits for every result and reports each outcome, and Promise.race settles with whichever finishes first, which is useful for timeouts; Promise.any takes the first success. Pitfalls: forgetting await, unhandled rejections that crash Node or are silently lost, awaiting inside a loop when the calls could run in parallel, and using async callbacks with forEach, which doesn't wait for them.

questions.title: var, let, const, hoisting and equality
questions.prompt: Explain the differences between var, let and const in JavaScript, including hoisting and the temporal dead zone. Then explain type coercion and why === is usually preferred over ==.

expectedConcepts.label: var is function-scoped; let and const are block-scoped
Hoisting and the temporal dead zone
== coerces types; === compares without coercion
const objects are still mutable; NaN; surprising coercions

questions.modelAnswer: var is function-scoped and can be redeclared; let and const are block-scoped, so a variable declared inside an if or a loop stays there. const prevents reassigning the variable, but the object it points to can still be mutated unless you freeze it. All declarations are hoisted to the top of their scope, but differently: a var is initialised to undefined, so reading it early gives undefined, while let and const sit in the temporal dead zone until their line runs, so reading them early throws a ReferenceError. That makes bugs easier to spot. == compares after type coercion, with surprising results like 0 == '' and '1' == 1 being true, while === compares value and type without coercion, so it is predictable and preferred; a common exception is x == null, which checks for both null and undefined. Also, NaN is not equal to itself; use Number.isNaN. Default to const, use let when you must reassign, and avoid var.

questions.title: ES modules versus CommonJS
questions.prompt: Explain JavaScript modules. Compare ES modules with CommonJS, covering import and export, static versus dynamic loading, tree shaking, and how Node.js decides which format a file uses.

expectedConcepts.label: ESM import/export vs CommonJS require/module.exports
ESM is static and async; CommonJS is dynamic and synchronous
Static structure enables tree shaking and code splitting
package.json type, .mjs/.cjs; interop headaches

questions.modelAnswer: CommonJS is Node's original module system: require() loads a module synchronously and returns its module.exports object, and because require is just a function call it can happen anywhere, even conditionally. ES modules are the standard: import and export declarations at the top level, so the dependency graph is known statically before the code runs; loading is asynchronous, imports are live bindings, top-level await is allowed, and import() loads a module dynamically when needed. Because the structure is static, bundlers like Vite, Rollup or webpack can tree-shake unused exports and split code into chunks. In Node, a .mjs file is always ESM and a .cjs file always CommonJS; for .js files, the nearest package.json's "type": "module" makes them ESM, otherwise CommonJS. Pitfalls: mixing the two is awkward, older Node versions can't require ESM, and __dirname doesn't exist in ESM, so you use import.meta.url instead.

questions.title: Generics and utility types in TypeScript
questions.prompt: Explain generics in TypeScript and common utility types such as Partial, Pick, Omit and Record. How do keyof and mapped types work, and when do advanced types become a problem?

expectedConcepts.label: Type parameters preserve the relationship between inputs and outputs
Partial, Pick, Omit, Record, keyof, mapped types
Derive types from one source of truth; constraints with extends
Unreadable types, slow compiles, any leaking

questions.modelAnswer: Generics let a function or type work with many types while keeping the relationship between them: function first<T>(items: T[]): T | undefined returns the same type the array holds, unlike returning any. Constraints narrow what T can be, as in <T extends { id: string }>. keyof T is the union of T's property names, and a mapped type like { [K in keyof T]?: T[K] } builds a new type by transforming each property; that is exactly how Partial<T> works. Built-in utility types cover common needs: Partial<T> makes all fields optional (good for update payloads), Required<T> the opposite, Pick<T, 'a' | 'b'> and Omit<T, 'password'> select fields, Record<K, V> types dictionaries, and ReturnType extracts a function's result type. They let you derive types from one source of truth instead of copying them. Pitfalls: deeply nested conditional and mapped types become unreadable, produce confusing error messages and slow the compiler; prefer simple, explicit types where possible.

questions.title: Forwarding references and perfect forwarding
questions.prompt: Explain forwarding (universal) references and perfect forwarding in C++. How do reference collapsing and template deduction make T&& bind to both lvalues and rvalues, why is std::forward needed instead of std::move, and where does it go wrong?

expectedConcepts.label: T&& in a deduced context is a forwarding reference
Reference collapsing rules
std::forward restores the value category
Used in factories and emplace to avoid copies
Pitfalls: forwarding twice, greedy overloads, auto&& vs const&

questions.modelAnswer: A parameter of type T&& where T is deduced (or auto&&) is a forwarding reference. If an lvalue of type X is passed, T deduces to X&, and reference collapsing turns X& && into X&; if an rvalue is passed, T deduces to X and the parameter is X&&. Inside the function the parameter has a name, so it is always an lvalue; std::forward<T>(arg) casts it back to an rvalue only when T was deduced as a non-reference, preserving the caller's value category. std::move would unconditionally cast and steal from lvalues. This is how make_unique, emplace_back and generic wrappers pass arguments through without extra copies. Pitfalls: forwarding the same argument twice (the second use may see a moved-from object), forwarding-reference constructors that greedily beat the copy constructor for non-const lvalues, and confusing a forwarding reference with a plain rvalue reference like std::vector<T>&&.
researchContext: Scott Meyers coined "universal reference"; the standard term is forwarding reference.
Constrain greedy forwarding constructors with concepts or enable_if.

questions.title: SFINAE versus C++20 concepts
questions.prompt: Explain SFINAE in C++ and how it was used to constrain templates with enable_if and void_t. Then explain C++20 concepts and requires-clauses. Why are concepts better, and what still trips people up?

expectedConcepts.label: Substitution failure removes a candidate instead of erroring
enable_if / void_t / detection idiom
Concepts and requires-clauses name constraints
Readable errors, subsumption, overload ordering
Pitfalls: hard errors outside immediate context, syntactic-only checks

questions.modelAnswer: SFINAE: when substituting deduced template arguments produces an invalid type or expression in the immediate context of the declaration, that overload is silently dropped from the candidate set rather than causing a compile error. Libraries exploited this with std::enable_if in a return type or template parameter, decltype expressions and void_t-based detection to say "only if T has begin()". C++20 concepts make constraints first-class: template<std::integral T> or requires requires(T t) { t.begin(); }. Benefits: constraints are named and reusable, errors say which constraint failed, and the compiler can order overloads by subsumption (a more constrained template wins). Pitfalls: errors inside a function body are hard errors, not SFINAE; concepts only check syntax, not semantics (a type can satisfy sortable but have a broken operator<); and subsumption only works when constraints are built from the same named concepts.

questions.title: Object layout, vtables and multiple inheritance
questions.prompt: Walk through how a C++ object with virtual functions is laid out in memory. Explain the vptr and vtable, what changes with multiple inheritance and virtual inheritance (the diamond), and the cost of dynamic dispatch compared with a direct call.

expectedConcepts.label: Hidden vptr per object points at a per-class vtable
Multiple inheritance: several vptrs, this-pointer adjustment, thunks
Virtual inheritance shares one base subobject via an offset
Indirect call, blocks inlining, branch prediction, cache misses
Pitfalls: non-virtual destructor, slicing, virtual calls in constructors

questions.modelAnswer: With the Itanium ABI used by GCC and Clang, a polymorphic object starts with a hidden pointer (vptr) to its class's vtable, an array of function pointers plus RTTI and offset data, shared by all instances. A virtual call loads the vptr, indexes the slot and calls indirectly. With multiple inheritance an object contains one base subobject per base, each with its own vptr; converting Derived* to the second base adds an offset, and calls through that base go via thunks that adjust this. Virtual inheritance (the diamond) keeps one shared base subobject and stores its offset in the vtable, so access costs an extra indirection. Cost: the call itself is cheap, but it usually prevents inlining, can mispredict, and touches extra cache lines; final and whole-program optimisation enable devirtualisation. Pitfalls: deleting through a base without a virtual destructor, object slicing on copy, calling virtuals in constructors (they dispatch to the current class), and memset or memcpy on polymorphic objects.

questions.title: Cache lines, false sharing and data layout
questions.prompt: Explain how CPU caches affect C++ performance. Cover cache lines, spatial and temporal locality, array-of-structs versus struct-of-arrays, and false sharing between threads. How would you detect and fix false sharing?

expectedConcepts.label: 64-byte cache lines, locality, prefetching
Array of structs vs struct of arrays
False sharing: independent data on one line ping-pongs between cores
Fix with alignas(64) padding or per-thread data
Detect with perf c2c / VTune; pitfalls of padding everything

questions.modelAnswer: Memory moves between RAM and the CPU in 64-byte cache lines. Sequential access (spatial locality) and reuse (temporal locality) let the hardware prefetcher hide latency: an L1 hit is about 1 ns, a DRAM miss around 80-100 ns. Layout matters: if a hot loop only reads positions, a struct-of-arrays keeps those values contiguous, while an array-of-structs drags cold fields into the cache. False sharing happens when two threads write different variables that sit on the same cache line; the coherence protocol (MESI) keeps invalidating the line in the other core, so "independent" counters scale negatively. Fix it by aligning hot per-thread data to the line size (alignas(std::hardware_destructive_interference_size) or 64), using per-thread accumulators and combining at the end. Detect it with perf c2c, VTune or by seeing throughput drop as threads are added. Do not pad everything: padding increases memory footprint and can hurt locality elsewhere, so measure.

questions.title: A lock-free single-producer single-consumer queue
questions.prompt: Design a lock-free single-producer single-consumer ring buffer in C++. Explain the head and tail indices, which memory orders you need on each load and store and why, how you avoid false sharing, and why multi-producer queues are much harder (including the ABA problem).

expectedConcepts.label: Fixed-size ring buffer with head/tail indices, power-of-two mask
Release on publish, acquire on consume
Separate cache lines for head and tail, cached copies
MPMC needs CAS; ABA problem and solutions
Full/empty detection and one slot or counters

questions.modelAnswer: Use a fixed array of power-of-two capacity, a tail index written only by the producer and a head index written only by the consumer. Push: load tail relaxed (only the producer writes it), load head with acquire to check for space, write the element, then store tail+1 with release so the element write is visible before the new tail. Pop: load head relaxed, load tail with acquire, read the element, store head+1 with release so the producer knows the slot is free. Because each index has a single writer, no compare-and-swap is needed. Put head and tail on separate cache lines and let each side keep a cached copy of the other index to avoid constant coherence traffic. Distinguish full from empty with monotonically increasing counters masked on access, or by keeping one slot empty. Multi-producer queues need CAS loops on shared indices, which brings contention and the ABA problem: a pointer or index is changed and changed back between a read and a CAS, so the CAS wrongly succeeds; solutions are sequence numbers per slot, tagged pointers, hazard pointers or epoch-based reclamation.
researchContext: Rigtorp SPSCQueue and the LMAX Disruptor are well-known reference designs.
On x86 acquire/release loads and stores compile to plain moves; on ARM they need barriers or ldar/stlr.

questions.title: Custom allocators, arenas and std::pmr
questions.prompt: Why would a C++ program replace the default allocator? Explain arena (bump) allocators, pool allocators and std::pmr memory resources, the problems they solve such as fragmentation and allocation latency, and the risks they introduce.

expectedConcepts.label: malloc cost, lock contention, fragmentation, latency spikes
Arena/bump allocation, free all at once
Fixed-size pools / free lists
std::pmr memory_resource and polymorphic_allocator
Risks: lifetime bugs, dangling after reset, allocator propagation

questions.modelAnswer: General-purpose malloc must handle any size from any thread, so it can take locks, call into the kernel, and fragment the heap over time; for a hot path that means unpredictable latency. An arena or bump allocator grabs one big block and hands out memory by advancing a pointer; individual frees are no-ops and everything is released at once, perfect for per-request or per-frame data. Pool allocators keep free lists of fixed-size blocks, giving O(1) allocate/free and no fragmentation for same-sized objects like order nodes. C++17 std::pmr lets containers take a memory_resource at runtime (monotonic_buffer_resource, unsynchronized_pool_resource) without changing the container type's template parameter. In low-latency systems you typically pre-allocate everything at startup and never touch the global heap on the hot path. Risks: objects outliving their arena (dangling pointers after reset), destructors not running if you just drop the arena, allocator propagation rules on copy/move/swap, and the virtual-call overhead of pmr.

questions.title: Iterator invalidation in STL containers
questions.prompt: Explain iterator and reference invalidation for std::vector, std::deque, std::list, std::map and std::unordered_map. Give a concrete bug caused by invalidation and how to write the code safely, for example erasing while iterating.

expectedConcepts.label: vector: reallocation invalidates all; insert/erase invalidates after the point
Node-based list/map keep others valid
unordered_map rehash invalidates iterators but not references
Use the iterator returned by erase / erase-remove / erase_if
Bug: push_back while holding a reference or iterator

questions.modelAnswer: std::vector stores elements contiguously: any insertion that exceeds capacity reallocates and invalidates every iterator, pointer and reference; insert or erase without reallocation invalidates everything at or after the position. std::deque invalidates iterators on most insertions but keeps references valid when inserting at the ends. Node-based containers (list, map, set) only invalidate iterators to erased elements. unordered_map invalidates iterators on rehash but references and pointers to elements stay valid. Classic bug: holding int& first = v[0] and then calling v.push_back, which reallocates, so first dangles - undefined behaviour that often works in tests and crashes in production. Erasing in a loop must use it = container.erase(it) rather than ++it after erase, or better std::erase_if (C++20) or the erase-remove idiom for vectors. Reserve capacity up front if you need stable addresses, or store indices instead of iterators.

questions.title: Copy elision, RVO and NRVO
questions.prompt: Explain copy elision in C++: return value optimisation, named return value optimisation and what C++17 guaranteed. When does the compiler fall back to a move or a copy, and why is return std::move(local) usually a mistake?

expectedConcepts.label: RVO constructs the result directly in the caller's storage
C++17 guarantees elision for prvalues
NRVO for named locals is optional
Implicit move on return when elision does not happen
return std::move blocks NRVO; returning members/params

questions.modelAnswer: Copy elision lets the compiler build a returned object directly in the caller's storage, so no copy or move constructor runs. Returning a prvalue (return Widget{...};) is guaranteed elision since C++17 - it works even for non-movable types, because no temporary is materialised. NRVO, returning a named local (Widget w; ...; return w;), is permitted but not required; compilers usually do it when every return path returns the same object. If elision does not happen - for example two different named locals returned on different paths - the standard applies an implicit move, treating the local as an rvalue first. Writing return std::move(w) is a pessimisation: it turns the expression into an xvalue, which disables NRVO and forces a move. Function parameters and members are not eligible for NRVO, and returning a member by value copies unless you explicitly move it.

questions.title: CRTP and static polymorphism
questions.prompt: Explain the curiously recurring template pattern in C++. How does it give static polymorphism without virtual functions, where is it used in practice, and what are its downsides compared with virtual dispatch or C++20 concepts?

expectedConcepts.label: Base<Derived> calls static_cast<Derived*>(this)
Compile-time dispatch, inlinable, no vptr
Uses: mixins, enable_shared_from_this, hot loops
Downsides: no heterogeneous containers, code bloat, errors
Alternatives: deducing this (C++23), concepts

questions.modelAnswer: In CRTP a class derives from a template instantiated with itself: struct Order : Base<Order>. Base calls into the derived class with static_cast<Derived&>(*this).impl(), so the target is known at compile time - no vptr, no indirect call, and the compiler can inline everything. It is used for mixins (adding comparison operators or counters to many classes), std::enable_shared_from_this, expression templates, and in low-latency code where a strategy or handler is chosen at compile time. Downsides: every Base<X> is a different type, so you cannot store mixed types in one container or choose behaviour at runtime; each instantiation adds code; mistakes like passing the wrong Derived compile silently; and errors are verbose. C++23 deducing this (explicit object parameters) replaces many CRTP uses, and concepts express "has impl()" without inheritance.

questions.title: C++20 coroutines
questions.prompt: Explain how C++20 coroutines work. Cover co_await, co_yield and co_return, the promise type and coroutine handle, where the coroutine frame lives, and what makes them hard to use correctly compared with threads or callbacks.

expectedConcepts.label: Stackless: state stored in a heap-allocated frame
co_await / co_yield / co_return
promise_type, coroutine_handle, awaiter protocol
Uses: generators, async I/O without callbacks
Pitfalls: dangling references, lifetime, no standard task type

questions.modelAnswer: A C++20 coroutine is any function using co_await, co_yield or co_return. It is stackless: locals that live across a suspension are stored in a coroutine frame, usually heap-allocated (the compiler may elide it), and suspension returns control to the caller or resumer. The return type must provide a promise_type that controls initial and final suspension, how values are yielded or returned and how exceptions propagate; std::coroutine_handle resumes or destroys the frame. co_await expr uses the awaiter protocol: await_ready (skip suspension?), await_suspend (schedule resumption, e.g. register with an I/O reactor) and await_resume (produce the result). This lets you write async I/O and generators as straight-line code without callback chains or a thread per request. Hard parts: reference parameters and lambdas captured by reference dangle once the caller's frame is gone; who destroys the frame; per-call allocation; and the standard ships the machinery but (until std::generator in C++23) no ready-made task types, so you depend on libraries like cppcoro or asio.

questions.title: Type erasure and std::function
questions.prompt: Explain type erasure in C++ using std::function and std::any as examples. How is it implemented internally, what is the small buffer optimisation, and what does it cost compared with templates or virtual interfaces?

expectedConcepts.label: Uniform interface over unrelated types without inheritance
Internal concept/model with virtual call or function-pointer table
Small buffer optimisation avoids heap for small objects
Costs: indirect call, possible allocation, no inlining
Alternatives/pitfalls: function_ref, move_only_function, copyability

questions.modelAnswer: Type erasure gives one concrete type that can hold any object satisfying an interface, without those objects sharing a base class. std::function<int(int)> can hold a lambda, a function pointer or a functor. Internally it stores the object behind an abstract "concept" with a templated "model" implementing call, copy and destroy - either via a virtual base or a hand-rolled table of function pointers. Small buffer optimisation keeps small callables (typically up to two or three pointers) in an inline buffer, falling back to the heap for bigger captures. Costs: each call is an indirect call that the compiler usually cannot inline, large captures allocate, and copying copies the callable. Templates (passing F&&) are zero-overhead but leak into every signature; virtual interfaces need inheritance. Pitfalls: std::function requires a copyable callable (use std::move_only_function in C++23), and for non-owning callbacks function_ref-style views avoid both allocation and ownership.

questions.title: shared_ptr internals and thread safety
questions.prompt: Explain how std::shared_ptr is implemented: the control block, strong and weak counts, make_shared versus shared_ptr(new T), the aliasing constructor and custom deleters. What exactly is and is not thread-safe about shared_ptr?

expectedConcepts.label: Control block with strong and weak counts and deleter
make_shared: one allocation, but memory held until weak refs die
Aliasing constructor shares ownership but points elsewhere
Count updates are atomic; the pointee and the same shared_ptr object are not
Pitfalls: two control blocks from one raw pointer, cycles, passing by value

questions.modelAnswer: A shared_ptr holds two pointers: one to the object and one to a control block containing the strong count, the weak count, the deleter and allocator. Copying increments the strong count atomically; when it reaches zero the object is destroyed, and when the weak count also reaches zero the control block is freed. make_shared allocates object and control block together - one allocation and better locality - but the memory is only released after the last weak_ptr goes, which matters for large objects. The aliasing constructor shares one control block while pointing at a member or sub-object. Thread safety: the reference counts are atomic, so different shared_ptr copies pointing at the same object can be used from different threads; but concurrent writes to the same shared_ptr instance race (use std::atomic<std::shared_ptr<T>> in C++20), and the pointee itself is not synchronised. Pitfalls: creating two shared_ptrs from the same raw pointer gives two control blocks and a double delete (use enable_shared_from_this), reference cycles leak, and passing shared_ptr by value on hot paths costs atomic increments.

questions.title: Static initialisation and the initialisation order fiasco
questions.prompt: Explain how and when C++ initialises globals and static variables: zero, constant and dynamic initialisation, function-local statics and their thread safety, and the static initialisation order fiasco across translation units. How do you avoid it?

expectedConcepts.label: Zero, constant, then dynamic initialisation
Order across translation units is unspecified
Function-local statics are thread-safe since C++11
Fixes: constinit/constexpr, construct-on-first-use, inline variables
Pitfalls: destruction order, hidden lock on hot path

questions.modelAnswer: Objects with static storage are first zero-initialised, then constant-initialised if their initialiser is a constant expression (baked into the binary), and otherwise dynamically initialised at startup before main. Within one translation unit dynamic initialisation follows declaration order, but across translation units the order is unspecified, so a global in a.cpp that uses a global in b.cpp may see it uninitialised - the static initialisation order fiasco. Fixes: make it constexpr or constinit (C++20) so it is constant-initialised; wrap it in a function returning a reference to a function-local static (construct on first use), which since C++11 is initialised exactly once and thread-safely; or remove global state. Pitfalls: destruction runs in reverse order at exit, so a static used by another static's destructor can already be dead; and function-local statics check a guard variable on every call, a small cost in very hot loops.

questions.title: Condition variables, spurious and lost wakeups
questions.prompt: Explain how std::condition_variable works with a mutex in C++. Why must you wait with a predicate, what are spurious wakeups and lost wakeups, and should you notify while holding the lock? Sketch a bounded blocking queue.

expectedConcepts.label: wait atomically unlocks, sleeps and relocks
Always wait with a predicate / while loop
Spurious and lost wakeups
Bounded queue: not_full and not_empty conditions
Pitfalls: changing state without the lock, notify_one vs notify_all

questions.modelAnswer: A condition variable lets a thread sleep until another thread changes shared state. You lock a std::unique_lock<std::mutex>, check the condition, and call cv.wait(lock, pred); wait atomically releases the mutex and sleeps, then reacquires the mutex before returning. Always wait with a predicate (or a while loop) because wakeups can be spurious, and because another consumer may have taken the item between the notify and your wake. A lost wakeup happens if the producer changes state and notifies without holding the mutex at the moment between the consumer's check and its sleep - so the state must always be modified under the mutex, even if the variable is atomic. Notifying after unlocking avoids waking a thread that immediately blocks on the mutex; notifying while locked is also correct. A bounded queue uses a deque, a mutex and two condition variables: push waits on not_full while size == capacity, pushes, notifies not_empty; pop waits on not_empty, pops, notifies not_full. Use notify_one when any one waiter can proceed and notify_all for shutdown or when waiters wait on different predicates.

questions.title: The Go scheduler: G, M and P
questions.prompt: Explain how the Go runtime schedules goroutines. Describe the G, M and P model, local and global run queues, work stealing, what happens when a goroutine makes a blocking syscall, and how preemption works. What does GOMAXPROCS control?

expectedConcepts.label: G goroutine, M OS thread, P processor/context
Local run queues per P, global queue, work stealing
Blocking syscall hands off the P; netpoller for network I/O
Asynchronous preemption since Go 1.14
GOMAXPROCS = number of Ps; container CPU limits
Pitfalls: cgo/syscalls creating threads, lock contention

questions.modelAnswer: Go multiplexes many goroutines (G) onto a few OS threads (M). A thread must hold a P (logical processor) to run Go code; there are GOMAXPROCS Ps, defaulting to the number of CPUs. Each P has a local run queue of runnable Gs, plus there is a global queue; an idle P steals half of another P's queue (work stealing), keeping all cores busy without a central lock. Network I/O does not block threads: the netpoller (epoll/kqueue) parks the goroutine and wakes it when the socket is ready. A blocking syscall or cgo call does block the M, so the runtime detaches its P and hands it to another thread so other goroutines keep running. Since Go 1.14 preemption is asynchronous (signal-based), so a tight loop without function calls can no longer starve the scheduler. Practical notes: in containers GOMAXPROCS used to see host CPUs rather than the cgroup quota, causing throttling (newer Go versions respect cgroup limits; previously automaxprocs was used); lots of blocking cgo or syscalls can create many threads; and runtime.LockOSThread pins a goroutine to an M.
researchContext: Go 1.25 made GOMAXPROCS container-aware by default.
go tool trace visualises scheduling latency per P.

questions.title: The Go memory model and happens-before
questions.prompt: Explain the Go memory model. What does happens-before mean, which operations create synchronisation (channels, mutexes, sync/atomic, sync.Once), and why is a program with a data race wrong even if it seems to work? How does the race detector find races?

expectedConcepts.label: Happens-before defines when a write is visible to a read
Channel send before receive completes; unlock before lock; atomics
Data race: concurrent access, at least one write, no sync
Compiler/CPU reordering, torn reads, hoisted loads
go test -race: vector clocks, only finds executed races

questions.modelAnswer: The memory model says when a read is guaranteed to observe a write: only if the write happens before the read. Within one goroutine program order applies; across goroutines you need synchronisation. A send on a channel happens before the corresponding receive completes; closing a channel happens before a receive that returns because it is closed; for an unbuffered channel the receive happens before the send completes; Unlock happens before the next Lock; sync/atomic operations are sequentially consistent; the function passed to once.Do completes before any Do returns. A data race is two concurrent accesses to the same memory, at least one a write, with no happens-before between them. Racy programs can appear fine but the compiler may hoist a load out of a loop (spin forever on a flag), the CPU can reorder stores, and multi-word values like interfaces, slices and strings can be torn, which can even break memory safety. The race detector (go test -race / go build -race) instruments accesses and uses vector clocks to report races that actually execute, at roughly 5-10x CPU cost, so it only catches what your tests exercise.

questions.title: How channels work inside the Go runtime
questions.prompt: Explain how a Go channel is implemented and how it behaves. Cover the hchan structure, buffered versus unbuffered channels, the send and receive queues, what closing does, and the behaviour of nil and closed channels in send, receive and select.

expectedConcepts.label: hchan: ring buffer, lock, sendq and recvq
Waiting goroutines parked on sendq/recvq; direct handoff
Unbuffered channel is a rendezvous
Close: receivers get zero value and ok=false; send panics
nil channel blocks forever; disable a select case
Pitfalls: closing twice, closing from receiver, leaks

questions.modelAnswer: A channel is a pointer to an hchan: a lock, an optional circular buffer with send and receive indices, the element type, a closed flag, and two queues of parked goroutines (sendq and recvq). On send the runtime locks the channel; if a receiver is waiting it copies the value directly to that goroutine's stack and wakes it; else if the buffer has space it enqueues; else the sender parks on sendq. Receive mirrors this. An unbuffered channel has no buffer, so every send waits for a receiver - a rendezvous that also synchronises. close sets the flag and wakes all waiters: receivers drain the remaining buffer then get the zero value with ok == false; sending on or closing a closed channel panics. A nil channel blocks forever on send and receive, which is useful in select to disable a case once its input is exhausted. Conventions: only the sender (owner) closes, never close twice, and make sure every blocked goroutine can eventually proceed or it leaks.

questions.title: Goroutine leaks and how to prevent them
questions.prompt: What is a goroutine leak in Go? Give three realistic ways a goroutine can leak, explain how you would detect leaks in a running service and in tests, and describe the patterns that prevent them.

expectedConcepts.label: Blocked forever, never collected, holds memory
Causes: unread channel, missing cancel, abandoned result
Fix with context cancellation and select on ctx.Done
Buffered result channel of size one; errgroup
Detect with runtime.NumGoroutine, pprof goroutine profile, goleak

questions.modelAnswer: A goroutine leak is a goroutine that is blocked forever (or loops forever), so it is never collected along with its stack and everything it references; in a long-running service the count grows until memory runs out. Common causes: (1) a function starts a goroutine to compute a result on an unbuffered channel, but the caller returns early on timeout so nobody ever receives and the sender blocks forever; (2) a worker ranges over a channel that is never closed; (3) a goroutine waits on network I/O or a lock with no deadline or cancellation. Prevention: pass a context.Context and select on ctx.Done() in every blocking send or receive; make one-shot result channels buffered with capacity one so the sender never blocks; have the owner close channels; use errgroup.WithContext so siblings stop on first error; and set deadlines on I/O. Detection: watch runtime.NumGoroutine as a metric, grab /debug/pprof/goroutine?debug=2 to see thousands of goroutines parked at the same line, and run go.uber.org/goleak in tests.

questions.title: Reducing allocations: sync.Pool and escape analysis in practice
questions.prompt: A Go service spends 30 percent of CPU in the garbage collector. Explain how you would find and reduce allocations: profiling, escape analysis output, preallocating slices and maps, sync.Pool, and GOGC or GOMEMLIMIT tuning. What are the risks of each?

expectedConcepts.label: Alloc profile with pprof, benchmarks with -benchmem
Escape analysis: -gcflags=-m, pointers escaping to heap
Preallocate capacity, reuse buffers, avoid interface boxing
sync.Pool for short-lived reusable objects
GOGC and GOMEMLIMIT trade memory for CPU
Pitfalls: pooled objects not reset, retaining huge buffers, OOM

questions.modelAnswer: First measure: run a CPU profile to confirm GC time, then a heap profile with -sample_index=alloc_space to find the call sites allocating most, and write benchmarks with -benchmem to track allocs/op. Use go build -gcflags=-m to see why values escape to the heap - returning pointers to locals, storing in interfaces, closures capturing variables, or slices whose size is unknown at compile time. Fixes: preallocate slices and maps with make(..., 0, n), reuse byte buffers, avoid converting between string and []byte in hot loops, avoid boxing small values into interfaces, and use strings.Builder. sync.Pool caches temporary objects per P so they can be reused between GC cycles; always reset an object before putting it back and do not pool huge buffers (one large request can make every pooled buffer large). GOGC controls how much the heap grows before the next cycle - raising it trades memory for less GC CPU; GOMEMLIMIT sets a soft memory cap so you can run with GOGC=off or high values safely, but a limit set too low can make the GC run continuously (a death spiral).

questions.title: How interfaces are represented in Go
questions.prompt: Explain how Go represents interface values at runtime: the two-word layout, itab and eface, how method calls and type assertions work, and what this means for performance and nil comparisons. When does storing a value in an interface allocate?

expectedConcepts.label: Two words: type/itab pointer and data pointer
eface for empty interface, iface with method table
Method call via itab function pointer; assertion compares type
Non-pointer values are boxed and usually escape
Typed nil pointer inside interface is not nil

questions.modelAnswer: An interface value is two machine words. For a non-empty interface (iface) the first word points to an itab, which records the interface type, the concrete type and a table of function pointers for the interface's methods; for interface{} / any (eface) the first word is just the concrete type descriptor. The second word points to the data. Calling a method loads the function pointer from the itab and calls it indirectly, which usually prevents inlining (profile-guided optimisation can devirtualise hot sites). A type assertion compares the type word; asserting to another interface looks up or builds an itab, cached in a global table. Because the data word is a pointer, storing a non-pointer value such as a struct or int in an interface generally copies it to the heap (the runtime avoids this for small integers and zero-sized values). The famous pitfall: returning a nil *MyError as an error produces an interface with a non-nil type word, so err != nil is true.

questions.title: How Go maps work internally
questions.prompt: Explain how Go maps are implemented and how that shows up in behaviour: hashing, buckets or Swiss-table groups, growth and incremental evacuation, randomised iteration order, why you cannot take the address of a map element, and why concurrent writes crash the program.

expectedConcepts.label: Hash table with seeded hash, buckets/groups
Growth when load factor exceeded; incremental migration
Randomised iteration order
Elements move, so not addressable
Concurrent map writes are a fatal error, not a panic
Maps never shrink; delete keeps memory

questions.modelAnswer: A Go map is a hash table using a per-map random seed so attackers cannot craft collisions. Until Go 1.24 it used arrays of 8-slot buckets with overflow chains and tophash bytes; Go 1.24 switched to a Swiss-table design with groups of slots and control bytes probed in parallel. When the load factor is exceeded the table grows, and migration is incremental - spread across later writes - to avoid long pauses. Iteration order is deliberately randomised so nobody depends on it. Because entries move during growth, you cannot take &m[k]; store pointers as values if you need to mutate in place, or reassign the struct. Maps are not safe for concurrent use: the runtime detects concurrent writes and aborts with "fatal error: concurrent map writes", which cannot be recovered - protect with a mutex or RWMutex, or use sync.Map for append-mostly or disjoint-key workloads. Maps never shrink, so a map that once held millions of entries keeps its memory after deletes; copy into a new map to release it.

questions.title: sync.Mutex fairness, starvation and RWMutex
questions.prompt: Explain how sync.Mutex behaves under contention in Go: spinning, normal versus starvation mode, and why it is not a fair lock by default. When is RWMutex faster and when is it slower than Mutex, and what alternatives exist for very hot shared state?

expectedConcepts.label: Normal mode lets newcomers barge; starvation mode after 1 ms
Brief spinning before parking
RWMutex helps read-heavy long critical sections; costs more per op
Alternatives: sharding, atomics, copy-on-write, channels
Pitfalls: copying a mutex, recursive locking, writer blocking readers

questions.modelAnswer: Go's Mutex first tries a CAS; under contention it spins briefly on multicore machines, then parks the goroutine on a runtime semaphore. In normal mode a woken waiter competes with newly arriving goroutines, which usually win because they are already running on a CPU - good throughput, but unfair. If a waiter fails to acquire for more than 1 ms the mutex switches to starvation mode, handing ownership directly to the waiter at the head of the FIFO queue, and switches back once the queue drains. RWMutex lets many readers in at once, which helps when reads dominate and critical sections are long; but each RLock touches a shared counter, so for short sections under heavy multi-core load it can be slower than a plain Mutex, and a waiting writer blocks new readers. For very hot state: shard the data with one lock per shard, use atomics or atomic.Pointer with copy-on-write for read-mostly configuration, or give ownership to one goroutine. Pitfalls: copying a struct that contains a mutex (go vet catches it), Go mutexes are not reentrant so recursive locking deadlocks, and holding a lock across I/O.

questions.title: Profiling a Go service with pprof and trace
questions.prompt: A Go API has high p99 latency. Walk through how you would investigate it with Go tooling: CPU, heap, goroutine, block and mutex profiles via net/http/pprof, reading flame graphs, and go tool trace. What does each profile tell you that the others do not?

expectedConcepts.label: CPU profile: sampling where on-CPU time goes
Heap profile: inuse vs alloc space
Block and mutex profiles show waiting, not CPU
Execution trace: scheduler latency, GC pauses, per-request timelines
Pitfalls: off-CPU latency invisible in CPU profile, exposing pprof publicly

questions.modelAnswer: Import net/http/pprof on an internal admin port and capture profiles from production-like load. The CPU profile samples stacks about 100 times a second while goroutines run on CPU; a flame graph shows which call paths burn time. The heap profile shows inuse_space (what is live now - leaks) and alloc_space (total allocated - GC pressure). The goroutine profile dumps every goroutine stack, revealing leaks or thousands of goroutines stuck on one lock or channel. Block and mutex profiles (enabled with runtime.SetBlockProfileRate and SetMutexProfileFraction) record time spent waiting on channels, selects and contended mutexes - crucial because tail latency is often off-CPU waiting that a CPU profile cannot see. go tool trace records an execution trace: per-P timelines, GC phases, scheduler delays and network blocking, ideal for explaining a single slow request. Use pprof -diff_base to compare before and after. Pitfalls: never expose pprof on a public port, keep block/mutex sampling rates modest, and remember slow downstream calls appear as waiting rather than CPU.

questions.title: Graceful shutdown of a Go HTTP server
questions.prompt: Explain how to shut down a Go HTTP service gracefully in Kubernetes. Cover signal handling, http.Server.Shutdown, draining in-flight requests, stopping background workers with context, readiness probes and timeouts. What goes wrong if you just call os.Exit?

expectedConcepts.label: Catch SIGTERM with signal.NotifyContext
Server.Shutdown stops accepting and waits for in-flight requests
Fail readiness first so the load balancer stops routing
Cancel context for workers, WaitGroup, flush, close DB
Pitfalls: os.Exit skips defers, grace period exceeded, hijacked conns

questions.modelAnswer: Kubernetes sends SIGTERM, waits terminationGracePeriodSeconds (30 s by default), then SIGKILLs. Use ctx, stop := signal.NotifyContext(context.Background(), syscall.SIGTERM, os.Interrupt) and run ListenAndServe in a goroutine. On signal: first mark the readiness probe as failing and wait a few seconds, because endpoint removal propagates to load balancers asynchronously and new requests may still arrive. Then call srv.Shutdown(ctxWithTimeout): it closes listeners, closes idle keep-alive connections and waits for active requests to finish, returning when they are done or the timeout hits. Cancel the root context so background workers and consumers stop, wait for them with a WaitGroup or errgroup, flush logs, metrics and buffered messages, and close database pools. os.Exit or an unhandled kill skips deferred calls, drops in-flight requests (clients see 502s or resets), and can lose buffered data. Also: Shutdown does not wait for hijacked connections such as WebSockets - track and close those yourself with RegisterOnShutdown - and keep the total under the grace period.

questions.title: Error wrapping, errors.Is and errors.As
questions.prompt: Explain idiomatic error handling in Go beyond if err != nil. Cover wrapping with fmt.Errorf and %w, errors.Is and errors.As, sentinel errors versus custom error types, errors.Join, and how to decide what to expose to callers.

expectedConcepts.label: fmt.Errorf with %w adds context and keeps the chain
errors.Is compares against sentinels through the chain
errors.As extracts a typed error
Wrapping makes the inner error part of your API
Pitfalls: log and return, comparing with ==, losing context, typed nil

questions.modelAnswer: Errors are values; good code adds context as they propagate: return fmt.Errorf("load user %d: %w", id, err). The %w verb wraps, so the original stays reachable through Unwrap. errors.Is(err, sql.ErrNoRows) walks the chain looking for a sentinel value; errors.As(err, &target) walks it looking for a type, e.g. *net.OpError or your own *ValidationError with fields. Go 1.20 added errors.Join and multiple %w for combining errors. Sentinels are simple but couple callers to a value; custom types carry structured data; behaviour interfaces (Temporary(), Timeout()) are the most decoupled. Wrapping with %w makes the inner error part of your API contract - use %v when you do not want callers depending on an implementation detail such as which database driver you use. Pitfalls: comparing with == breaks once anything wraps, matching on error strings, logging and also returning the same error (duplicate logs), and returning a typed nil pointer as error.

questions.title: Pipelines, fan-out and bounded concurrency in Go
questions.prompt: Design a Go pipeline that reads a million URLs, fetches them with at most 50 in flight, parses the results and writes to a database in batches. Explain the stages, channels, fan-out and fan-in, cancellation on error, backpressure and ordering.

expectedConcepts.label: Stages connected by channels, each owned and closed by its producer
Fan-out to N workers, fan-in to one channel
Bound concurrency: worker count, semaphore, errgroup.SetLimit
errgroup.WithContext cancels everything on first error
Backpressure via unbuffered/small buffers; batching
Pitfalls: ordering lost, leaks on early exit, closing too early

questions.modelAnswer: Stage 1: a producer goroutine reads URLs and sends them on a channel, closing it at EOF. Stage 2: fan out to 50 fetcher goroutines ranging over that channel - the worker count is the concurrency bound (alternatively errgroup.SetLimit(50) or a buffered-channel semaphore). Each fetch uses the shared context and an HTTP client with timeouts, and sends results to an output channel; a separate goroutine waits on the workers' WaitGroup and then closes the output channel (fan-in). Stage 3: parsers, then a single writer that accumulates rows into batches of, say, 1000 or flushes every second. Run everything under errgroup.WithContext so the first fatal error cancels the context and every stage's select on ctx.Done() returns. Backpressure is automatic: small channel buffers mean a slow database blocks the writer, which fills buffers and stalls fetchers rather than piling up memory. Ordering is lost with fan-out; if needed, tag items with sequence numbers and reorder. Pitfalls: closing a channel from the consumer side or before all senders finish (panic), stages that keep sending after cancellation (leaks), and unbounded goroutine creation per item.

questions.title: Loop variables, closures and the Go 1.22 change
questions.prompt: Explain the classic Go bug where goroutines or closures created in a loop all see the last value of the loop variable. What changed in Go 1.22, what still surprises people with range loops, such as copying values and ranging over integers or functions?

expectedConcepts.label: Before 1.22 one variable shared across iterations
Go 1.22: per-iteration variables (go.mod version)
range copies values; modifying v does not change the slice
range over int and iterator functions (1.23)
Still matters for older modules; vet loopclosure

questions.modelAnswer: Before Go 1.22 a for loop declared one variable reused across iterations, so for _, v := range items { go func() { use(v) }() } often had every goroutine see the last item, and taking &v gave the same address each time; the workaround was v := v inside the loop. Go 1.22 changed semantics: each iteration gets a fresh variable, but only for modules whose go.mod declares go 1.22 or later, so older modules keep the old behaviour and go vet still has a loopclosure check. Still surprising: range copies each element, so v.count++ modifies the copy - use items[i].count++ or a slice of pointers; ranging over a large array (not slice) copies the whole array; Go 1.22 added range over integers (for i := range 10) and Go 1.23 added range-over-func iterators (iter.Seq), where breaking out of the loop must be respected by the yield function.

questions.title: Value categories: lvalues, prvalues and xvalues
questions.prompt: Explain C++ value categories: lvalue, prvalue and xvalue, and the umbrella terms glvalue and rvalue. How do they decide which overload is called and when an object can be moved from? Give examples of each.

expectedConcepts.label: lvalue has identity and can be named / addressed
prvalue is a pure temporary value
xvalue: expiring object, e.g. std::move(x)
Overload resolution: T& vs T&& binding
Pitfalls: named rvalue references are lvalues; moving from const

questions.modelAnswer: Every expression has a type and a value category. An lvalue has identity: you can take its address and it persists beyond the expression (a variable name, *ptr, a function returning T&). A prvalue is a pure value with no identity, such as 42, a + b or a function returning T by value; since C++17 it initialises its result object directly. An xvalue is an expiring object: it has identity but its resources may be reused, produced by std::move(x), a cast to T&&, or a member of an rvalue. glvalue = lvalue or xvalue; rvalue = prvalue or xvalue. Overload resolution uses this: a T&& overload binds rvalues and is preferred for them, const T& binds anything, so foo(std::move(v)) calls the move version. Pitfalls: inside a function, a parameter declared T&& has a name and is therefore an lvalue, so you must std::move it again to pass it on; std::move on a const object yields const T&&, which silently selects the copy constructor.

questions.title: Comparisons and the spaceship operator
questions.prompt: Explain how comparison operators work in modern C++. What does the three-way comparison operator <=> do, what are strong_ordering, weak_ordering and partial_ordering, how does defaulting comparisons work, and what are the pitfalls with floating point and mixed types?

expectedConcepts.label: <=> returns an ordering object; compiler rewrites < > <= >=
strong vs weak vs partial ordering
Defaulted == and <=> compare members in order
== is separate from <=> for efficiency
Pitfalls: NaN, mixed signed/unsigned, pointer members

questions.modelAnswer: Before C++20 a type needed up to six hand-written operators that easily drifted out of sync. C++20 adds a <=> b, which returns an ordering object comparable with 0; the compiler rewrites a < b as (a <=> b) < 0 and also tries reversed arguments, so one operator gives all four relational comparisons. strong_ordering means equal values are interchangeable (integers); weak_ordering allows equivalent but distinguishable values (case-insensitive strings); partial_ordering allows unordered values, as with floating-point NaN. Writing auto operator<=>(const T&) const = default; compares members lexicographically in declaration order, and a defaulted operator== is generated separately because equality can often short-circuit, for example by comparing sizes first. Pitfalls: doubles give partial_ordering, so NaN compares unordered and sorting with it breaks strict weak ordering; mixing signed and unsigned values still converts surprisingly (use std::cmp_less); defaulted comparison of pointer members compares addresses, not pointees.

questions.title: std::optional, std::variant and std::visit
questions.prompt: Explain std::optional and std::variant in C++. When would you use them instead of null pointers, sentinel values, unions or inheritance, how does std::visit work, and what are their costs and pitfalls?

expectedConcepts.label: optional: maybe-a-value without heap allocation
variant: type-safe tagged union
std::visit with overloaded lambdas, exhaustive handling
Closed set vs open inheritance hierarchy
Pitfalls: valueless_by_exception, size of largest member, bad_optional_access

questions.modelAnswer: std::optional<T> stores either a T or nothing, inline without heap allocation, replacing sentinel values like -1 or nullable pointers used only to mean "absent". Access with has_value(), value() (throws bad_optional_access) or *opt (undefined if empty). std::variant<A, B, C> is a type-safe tagged union: it holds exactly one alternative and knows which, so reading the wrong one throws bad_variant_access instead of silently reinterpreting bytes like a raw union. std::visit calls a callable with the active alternative; with an "overloaded" set of lambdas the compiler checks that every alternative is handled. Choose variant for a closed set of types known up front (messages in a protocol, AST nodes, states) - value semantics, no virtual calls or heap; choose inheritance for an open set that plugins extend. Costs: a variant is as large as its largest alternative plus a tag; visit is usually a jump table. Pitfalls: a variant can become valueless_by_exception if an assignment throws; dereferencing an empty optional is UB; optional<T&> did not exist before C++26.

questions.title: std::thread, std::async, futures and jthread
questions.prompt: Compare the ways to run work concurrently in standard C++: std::thread, std::jthread, std::async, std::promise and std::future, and packaged_task. How do you get results and exceptions back, how do you stop a thread cooperatively, and what goes wrong with each?

expectedConcepts.label: std::thread must be joined or detached
jthread joins automatically and has stop_token
future/promise transport results and exceptions
std::async launch policy; blocking future destructor
Pitfalls: detached threads with dangling refs, no thread pool, oversubscription

questions.modelAnswer: std::thread starts an OS thread running a callable; before its destructor runs it must be joined or detached, otherwise std::terminate is called. C++20 std::jthread joins automatically in its destructor and passes a std::stop_token so the function can poll stop_requested() or register a stop_callback, giving cooperative cancellation. To get a value back, a std::promise sets a value or exception in a shared state and the matching std::future::get() blocks until it is ready, rethrowing any exception in the caller. packaged_task wraps a callable so its result goes into a future. std::async(policy, f) is the shortcut: launch::async runs on a new thread, launch::deferred runs lazily on get(), and the default lets the implementation choose. A future returned by std::async blocks in its destructor until the task finishes, which surprises people who discard it. Pitfalls: detached threads that reference stack data that has gone, creating a thread per task instead of using a pool, and oversubscribing cores.

questions.title: Deadlocks and lock ordering in C++
questions.prompt: Explain how deadlocks happen in multithreaded C++ code. Describe the four conditions for deadlock, how std::scoped_lock and std::lock avoid lock-ordering deadlocks, lock hierarchies, and how you would debug a deadlock in production.

expectedConcepts.label: Coffman conditions: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait
Consistent global lock order
std::scoped_lock / std::lock lock several mutexes deadlock-free
