Debug with thread dumps / gdb thread apply all bt, TSan
Pitfalls: calling callbacks under a lock, recursive locking, condition variable misuse

questions.modelAnswer: A deadlock needs four conditions at once: mutual exclusion, hold and wait (holding one lock while waiting for another), no preemption, and circular wait. The classic case is thread 1 locking A then B while thread 2 locks B then A. The main cure is breaking circular wait with a consistent global lock order, enforced with a lock hierarchy (each mutex has a level and you may only acquire lower levels). When you must take several mutexes together, std::scoped_lock(a, b) (or std::lock) uses a deadlock-avoidance algorithm that tries and backs off, so the order you list them in does not matter - useful for swap(a, b) between two objects. Also keep critical sections small and never call unknown code (callbacks, virtual functions, logging that locks) while holding a lock. Debugging: attach gdb to the hung process or take a core dump and run thread apply all bt to see which threads wait on which mutex; ThreadSanitizer detects lock-order inversions in tests even when no deadlock happened. Other pitfalls: locking a non-recursive mutex twice in one thread deadlocks immediately.

questions.title: Sanitizers and debugging memory bugs in C++
questions.prompt: A C++ service crashes randomly in production. Explain how you would find memory and threading bugs using AddressSanitizer, UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer, ThreadSanitizer, MemorySanitizer, Valgrind and core dumps. What does each catch and what does it cost?

expectedConcepts.label: ASan: use-after-free, buffer overflow, leaks
UBSan: signed overflow, misaligned access, bad shifts
TSan: data races
Core dumps and gdb for post-mortem in production
Costs: 2x slowdown for ASan, 5-15x TSan; cannot combine ASan and TSan; CI usage

questions.modelAnswer: Start by reproducing under sanitizers in CI and staging. AddressSanitizer (-fsanitize=address) instruments memory accesses with shadow memory and catches heap/stack/global buffer overflows, use-after-free, double free and, with LeakSanitizer, leaks - roughly 2x slowdown and extra memory. UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer catches signed overflow, invalid shifts, misaligned or null dereferences and bad casts at low cost. ThreadSanitizer finds data races and lock-order inversions with 5-15x slowdown. MemorySanitizer (Clang) reports reads of uninitialised memory. ASan and TSan cannot be combined in one build, so run separate jobs. Valgrind needs no recompilation but is 20-50x slower. In production, enable core dumps, keep separate debug symbols for each release, and analyse crashes with gdb (bt, frame, info locals, thread apply all bt). Random crashes far from the bug usually mean memory corruption, which is exactly what ASan pinpoints at the moment of the bad access rather than at the later crash. Also compile with warnings as errors and _GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS for bounds checks in debug builds.

questions.title: std::string internals and small string optimisation
questions.prompt: Explain how std::string is implemented in modern standard libraries. What is the small string optimisation, how big is the inline buffer, what does this mean for copying, moving and string_view, and how would you avoid unnecessary string allocations in hot code?

expectedConcepts.label: Pointer, size, capacity; contiguous null-terminated buffer
SSO stores short strings inline (about 15-22 chars)
Moving a short string copies bytes; long string moves pointer
Avoid allocations: reserve, string_view, append, reuse buffers
Pitfalls: COW is banned since C++11, dangling string_view, c_str lifetime

questions.modelAnswer: A std::string owns a contiguous, null-terminated character buffer and tracks its size and capacity. Libraries use the small string optimisation: the object (typically 24 or 32 bytes) reuses its own storage as an inline buffer, so strings up to about 15 characters (libstdc++, MSVC) or 22 (libc++) need no heap allocation at all. Larger strings allocate and grow geometrically like vector. Consequences: copying a short string is just a memcpy; moving a long string steals the pointer, but moving a short one copies its bytes; pointers into a short string are invalidated by moving it. Copy-on-write implementations are not allowed since C++11 because of iterator and thread-safety rules. In hot code: take std::string_view parameters for read-only access, reserve() before building strings in loops, append instead of repeated operator+ temporaries, reuse a buffer across iterations, and use std::to_chars/fmt for formatting. Pitfalls: string_view to a temporary string dangles, and c_str() pointers die when the string is modified or destroyed.

questions.title: Struct layout, alignment and padding
questions.prompt: Explain how the compiler lays out a struct in C++. What are alignment requirements and padding, how do you compute sizeof for a struct of mixed members, how can reordering members save memory, and when are alignas or packed structs useful or dangerous?

expectedConcepts.label: Each type has an alignment; members placed at multiples of it
Padding between members and at the end for arrays
Order members largest to smallest to reduce padding
alignas for cache lines / SIMD
Packed structs cause misaligned access; layout differs across ABIs

questions.modelAnswer: Each type has an alignment requirement (alignof), usually its size for primitives: a double needs an address divisible by 8 on mainstream 64-bit ABIs. The compiler places members in declaration order, inserting padding so each starts at a multiple of its alignment, and pads the end so the struct's size is a multiple of its largest member alignment - otherwise elements of an array would be misaligned. Example: struct { char a; double b; char c; } is 24 bytes (1 + 7 padding + 8 + 1 + 7 padding), but ordering it double, char, char gives 16. In memory-heavy or cache-sensitive code, ordering members from largest to smallest and grouping hot fields together reduces size and cache misses. alignas(64) aligns hot data to cache lines to avoid false sharing or meets SIMD requirements. Packed structs (#pragma pack, __attribute__((packed))) remove padding to match wire formats, but cause slow or even faulting misaligned accesses and break taking references to members; prefer explicit serialisation with memcpy. Layout, padding and endianness differ across compilers and platforms, so never send raw structs over the network.

questions.title: Strict aliasing, type punning and std::bit_cast
questions.prompt: Explain the strict aliasing rule in C++. Why is reinterpreting a float as an integer through a pointer cast undefined behaviour, how does the optimiser exploit the rule, and what are the correct ways to do type punning, including memcpy and std::bit_cast?

expectedConcepts.label: Objects may only be accessed through compatible types, char/byte exempt
Compiler assumes differently typed pointers do not alias
Use memcpy or std::bit_cast
Union punning is UB in C++ (allowed in C)
Real bugs under -O2; -fno-strict-aliasing; UBSan does not catch it

questions.modelAnswer: The strict aliasing rule says an object may only be accessed through a glvalue of its own type (or a similar/signed-unsigned variant), or through char, unsigned char or std::byte. So float f; int i = *reinterpret_cast<int*>(&f); is undefined behaviour. The optimiser relies on the rule: if a function receives an int* and a float*, it assumes writes through one cannot change what the other points to, so it may keep values in registers or reorder loads and stores. Code that "works" at -O0 then breaks at -O2. Correct punning: std::memcpy(&i, &f, sizeof i) - compilers turn it into a single move - or C++20 std::bit_cast<std::uint32_t>(f), which is constexpr-friendly and checks sizes and trivial copyability. Reading the inactive member of a union is allowed in C but undefined in C++ (though GCC documents it as an extension). Parsing network buffers by casting a char buffer to a struct pointer is also wrong because no struct object exists there; memcpy into a real struct or use std::start_lifetime_as (C++23). Some projects compile with -fno-strict-aliasing (the Linux kernel) at a performance cost.

questions.title: Writing a low-latency hot path in C++
questions.prompt: You are writing the order-handling hot path of a trading system in C++ where every microsecond matters. Explain the techniques you would use and avoid: memory allocation, virtual calls, exceptions, branches, cache behaviour, logging, system calls and compiler optimisations, and how you would measure tail latency.

expectedConcepts.label: No heap allocation on the hot path: preallocate, pools
Cache-friendly data, avoid pointer chasing, warm caches
Predictable branches, [[likely]], branchless code, PGO
Avoid syscalls and locks: async logging, kernel bypass, core pinning
Measure percentiles with rdtsc/histograms, not averages
Pitfalls: hidden allocations, page faults, frequency scaling, false sharing

questions.modelAnswer: Principle: do as little unpredictable work as possible between packet in and order out. Memory: allocate everything at startup (object pools, ring buffers, reserved vectors) so the hot path never calls malloc; pre-fault and lock pages (mlock) to avoid page faults. Data layout: keep hot data contiguous and small, avoid linked structures and pointer chasing, and keep caches warm by touching the path even when idle. Dispatch: prefer templates or CRTP over virtual calls where types are known; avoid std::function and hidden allocations from std::string or exceptions; exceptions are fine if never thrown on the hot path. Branches: make the common case predictable, use [[likely]] hints, branchless arithmetic where it helps, and profile-guided optimisation. System: no syscalls or locks on the hot path - log by writing compact binary records to a lock-free queue drained by another thread; use kernel-bypass NICs; pin threads to isolated cores with busy-polling; disable frequency scaling and hyper-threading siblings. Measure with rdtsc-based timestamps into histograms and track p99/p99.9 and max, not averages; test with realistic bursts. Common traps: false sharing, denormal floats, logging formatting on the hot thread, and STL containers that reallocate.

questions.title: C++20 ranges and views
questions.prompt: Explain C++20 ranges. How do range algorithms differ from iterator-pair algorithms, what are views and why are they lazy, how does pipe composition work, and what pitfalls exist around dangling, performance and caching in views like filter?

expectedConcepts.label: Range algorithms take the range directly, with projections
Views are lazy, non-owning, cheap to copy
Composition with the pipe operator
Avoid temporary containers; ranges::to in C++23
Pitfalls: dangling, filter caches begin, const iteration, compile times

questions.modelAnswer: Ranges let algorithms take a whole range instead of a begin/end pair: std::ranges::sort(v) or ranges::sort(people, {}, &Person::age), where the projection sorts by a member without a custom comparator. They are constrained with concepts, giving clearer errors. Views are lightweight, usually non-owning adaptors that compute elements lazily when iterated: v | views::filter(is_even) | views::transform(square) | views::take(10) builds a pipeline with no intermediate containers and only does work for elements actually consumed, which also allows infinite ranges like views::iota(0). C++23 adds ranges::to<std::vector>() to materialise results. Pitfalls: a view referencing a temporary container dangles (ranges algorithms return std::ranges::dangling for rvalue ranges to catch some cases); filter_view caches its first begin() for amortised O(1), so it cannot be iterated as const and mutating the underlying data after iteration can give wrong results; deeply nested pipelines increase compile times and may not optimise as well as hand-written loops in debug builds.

questions.title: C++20 modules
questions.prompt: Explain C++20 modules. What problems with header files do they solve, how do module interface units, export and import work, how do they interact with macros and the build system, and why has adoption been slow?

expectedConcepts.label: Headers are textually included, reparsed, leak macros, ODR issues
Module interface units, export, import, BMI
Isolation: macros and non-exported names do not leak
Build systems must scan dependencies and build in order
Adoption issues: tooling, mixed headers, import std in C++23

questions.modelAnswer: With #include the preprocessor pastes header text into every translation unit, so the same declarations are parsed thousands of times, macros leak in both directions, include order can change meaning, and inline definitions must obey the one-definition rule across copies. Modules replace textual inclusion with compiled interfaces. A module interface unit starts with export module net; and marks what it exports; importers write import net; and the compiler reads a precompiled binary module interface instead of reparsing source. Non-exported names stay private, macros do not leak out of a module, and import order does not matter, giving faster and more hygienic builds. Legacy headers can be pulled in via the global module fragment or header units, and C++23 adds import std;. The catch is the build: a module must be compiled before its importers, so build systems need dependency scanning (CMake 3.28+ with Ninja), BMIs are compiler-specific, and IDEs, package managers and mixed header/module codebases lagged for years, so many teams still use headers with precompiled headers.

questions.title: Object lifetime, placement new and std::launder
questions.prompt: Explain object lifetime in C++ at a low level. What does placement new do, how do you correctly construct and destroy objects in raw storage such as a custom container or pool, what are std::launder and std::construct_at for, and what undefined behaviour is easy to trigger here?

expectedConcepts.label: Storage vs object lifetime: begins at construction, ends at destructor
Placement new constructs in existing aligned storage
Explicit destructor call / std::destroy_at
std::launder for reusing storage with const/reference members
UB: misaligned storage, double destroy, accessing before construction

questions.modelAnswer: Allocating memory is not the same as creating an object: an object's lifetime begins when its constructor completes and ends when its destructor starts, and storage can outlive it. Containers like vector separate the two: they allocate raw, suitably aligned storage (operator new, std::allocator) and construct elements in place with placement new - new (ptr) T(args...) - or std::construct_at (C++20, usable in constexpr). Destruction is explicit: p->~T() or std::destroy_at(p), then the storage is released separately. Rules: storage must be aligned for T (alignas or std::aligned_alloc); never access an element before constructing or after destroying it; destroy exactly once; and handle exceptions during construction by destroying the already-built elements (std::uninitialized_copy does this). If you construct a new object in storage previously occupied by an object with const or reference members, old pointers may not be used to reach the new object; std::launder(ptr) gives a pointer the compiler must treat as possibly pointing to the new object. In pools, forgetting destructors leaks resources, and reinterpret_cast-ing raw bytes to T without constructing is UB.

questions.title: Error handling: exceptions, error codes and std::expected
questions.prompt: Compare the ways to report errors in C++: exceptions, error codes, std::optional and C++23 std::expected. Discuss performance, readability, noexcept, how errors cross library and thread boundaries, and which you would pick for a low-latency system versus a business application.

expectedConcepts.label: Exceptions: zero-cost happy path, expensive throw, separate control flow
Error codes / std::error_code must be checked explicitly
std::expected carries value or error, monadic and_then
noexcept and move operations; terminate on throw
Choice by context: hot paths, -fno-exceptions, boundaries

questions.modelAnswer: Exceptions separate error handling from the normal path; with table-based unwinding the non-throwing path costs essentially nothing, but a throw is slow (microseconds, allocation, unwinding) and makes control flow invisible at call sites. They are natural for constructors and rare, unrecoverable-at-this-level failures. Error codes (int, enum, std::error_code) are explicit and cheap but easy to ignore - mark functions [[nodiscard]] - and clutter code. std::optional says "maybe a value" but cannot say why. C++23 std::expected<T, E> holds either a value or an error, is explicit and cheap, and supports and_then/transform/or_else chaining. noexcept matters: if a noexcept function throws, std::terminate is called, and containers only move elements during reallocation if the move constructor is noexcept, otherwise they copy. Boundaries: exceptions must not cross C APIs or callbacks from other languages, and across threads they must be captured with std::exception_ptr or a future. Many low-latency and embedded codebases compile with -fno-exceptions and use expected or error codes on hot paths; business applications usually benefit from exceptions plus RAII for clean, less error-prone code.

questions.title: Designing a thread pool in C++
questions.prompt: Design a general-purpose thread pool in C++. Explain the task queue, worker loop, how tasks return results, shutdown, exception handling, and how work-stealing pools reduce contention. What problems arise when tasks block or submit other tasks and wait for them?

expectedConcepts.label: Shared queue with mutex and condition variable
Return futures via packaged_task; capture exceptions
Graceful shutdown: stop flag, notify_all, join, drain or cancel
Work stealing: per-thread deques reduce contention
Deadlock when tasks wait on tasks; blocking I/O starves pool; sizing

questions.modelAnswer: Core design: N worker threads (roughly std::thread::hardware_concurrency() for CPU-bound work) loop waiting on a condition variable for tasks in a shared queue protected by a mutex. submit(f, args...) wraps the callable in a std::packaged_task, pushes a type-erased move-only function onto the queue, notifies one worker and returns the std::future, so results and exceptions propagate to whoever calls get(). Workers catch nothing themselves beyond what packaged_task stores, so one failing task never kills a thread. Shutdown sets a stop flag under the mutex, notify_all wakes everyone, workers finish (or drop) the remaining tasks and exit, and the destructor joins them - choose and document drain-versus-cancel semantics. A single queue becomes a contention point at high task rates; work-stealing pools give each worker its own deque (push/pop at one end locally, others steal from the opposite end), improving locality and scalability, as in TBB or Folly. Pitfalls: a task that submits subtasks and blocks waiting for them can deadlock when all workers are blocked the same way - run pending tasks while waiting, or use continuations; blocking I/O inside CPU pools starves other work, so use a separate I/O pool; and unbounded queues hide overload, so consider bounded queues with backpressure.

questions.title: High-performance hash maps in C++
questions.prompt: Why is std::unordered_map often slow, and how do open-addressing hash maps such as Abseil flat_hash_map or Robin Hood hashing do better? Explain node-based chaining versus open addressing, probing, load factor, tombstones, SIMD metadata, and the trade-offs including pointer stability.

expectedConcepts.label: unordered_map uses separate chaining with a node per element
Open addressing stores elements in one array and probes
Swiss tables: control bytes and SIMD group probing
Load factor, tombstones on erase, rehash
Trade-offs: no pointer stability, bad hashes cluster, iteration

questions.modelAnswer: The standard requires unordered_map to keep references stable across rehash and to expose a bucket interface, which effectively forces separate chaining: every element lives in its own heap-allocated node linked from a bucket array. That means an allocation per insert and a pointer chase (likely a cache miss) per lookup. Open addressing stores elements directly in one contiguous array; on a collision it probes other slots (linear, quadratic, or Robin Hood, which moves "rich" elements to keep probe lengths even). Abseil's Swiss table keeps one control byte per slot holding 7 bits of the hash; it compares 16 control bytes at once with SIMD to find candidate slots, so most lookups touch one cache line of metadata and one slot. Deletion uses tombstones (or backward-shift in Robin Hood) so probe chains are not broken, and the table rehashes when load factor or tombstones exceed a threshold (around 87.5% for Swiss tables). Trade-offs: elements move on rehash, so no pointer or reference stability (node_hash_map provides it at a cost); poor hash functions cause clustering, so use a good mixing hash; large values make the array big, so store pointers or indices for them.

questions.title: ABI stability and the pimpl idiom
questions.prompt: Explain the difference between API and ABI compatibility in C++. What changes break ABI in a shared library, why did the std::string change in GCC 5 cause problems, how do the pimpl idiom and inline namespaces help, and what does this cost?

expectedConcepts.label: API = source compatibility; ABI = binary layout and calling conventions
ABI breaks: changing members, layout, virtual functions, inline code
GCC 5 std::string dual ABI
Pimpl hides members behind a pointer to an implementation
Costs: extra allocation and indirection; inline namespaces for versioning

questions.modelAnswer: API compatibility means code still compiles against the new headers; ABI compatibility means already-compiled binaries still work with the new library without recompiling. The ABI covers object layout, vtable order, name mangling and calling conventions. Breaking changes include adding or reordering data members (sizeof and offsets change in client code that allocated the object), adding or reordering virtual functions, changing inline functions or templates that clients compiled into their binaries, and changing function signatures. GCC 5 had to change std::string from copy-on-write to an SSO implementation to satisfy C++11, which changed its layout; libstdc++ shipped both behind the _GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI macro and an inline namespace (__cxx11), and mixing libraries built with different settings caused link errors. The pimpl idiom keeps only a std::unique_ptr<Impl> in the public class and defines Impl in the .cpp, so private members can change without breaking ABI and headers recompile less often; the cost is an allocation and pointer indirection per object, and you must define the destructor out of line. Libraries also expose extern "C" interfaces or versioned inline namespaces to control ABI.

questions.title: Debugging a segmentation fault in C++
questions.prompt: Walk through how you would debug a segmentation fault in a C++ program, from reproducing it to finding the root cause. Cover what a segfault actually is, reading a backtrace in gdb, common causes, and how the crash location can differ from the bug.

expectedConcepts.label: Segfault: invalid memory access caught by MMU, SIGSEGV
gdb: run, bt, frame, print, core dumps
Causes: null/dangling pointers, overflows, stack overflow
Corruption crashes later elsewhere; use ASan/watchpoints
Pitfalls: optimised builds hide variables, heisenbugs, missing symbols

questions.modelAnswer: A segfault happens when the process touches memory it may not: an unmapped page or a write to read-only memory. The MMU raises a fault and the kernel delivers SIGSEGV, which by default kills the process. First make it reproducible, build with -g (and ideally -O0 or -Og), and run under gdb or enable core dumps (ulimit -c unlimited) and load the core with gdb ./app core. bt shows the call stack; frame N, info locals and print inspect state; for threaded programs use thread apply all bt. Common causes: dereferencing null or uninitialised pointers, dangling pointers or references after the object died, iterator invalidation, out-of-bounds writes, and stack overflow from deep recursion or huge stack arrays. If the backtrace points into malloc or unrelated code, memory was probably corrupted earlier - rebuild with AddressSanitizer, which stops at the first invalid access, or use a hardware watchpoint (watch *addr) to catch who overwrites a value. Optimised builds may show "value optimized out" and reorder code, and timing-dependent crashes often indicate data races, so also try ThreadSanitizer.

questions.title: Why goroutines are cheap: growable stacks
questions.prompt: Explain why you can run hundreds of thousands of goroutines but not hundreds of thousands of OS threads. Describe how goroutine stacks start small and grow, what stack copying implies, and what the real limits on goroutine count are.

expectedConcepts.label: Goroutine stacks start at a few KB vs ~1-8 MB thread stacks
Stacks grow by copying to a bigger allocation; shrink during GC
User-space scheduling: cheap creation and switches
Copying works because the runtime adjusts pointers into the stack
Real limits: memory held by goroutines, blocked resources, leaks

questions.modelAnswer: OS threads reserve a fixed stack (often 1-8 MB of virtual memory) and every switch goes through the kernel. A goroutine starts with a tiny stack (2 KB today) managed by the Go runtime and is scheduled in user space, so creating one costs about a microsecond and a few KB, and switches are cheap. When a function prologue detects that the stack is about to overflow, the runtime allocates a stack twice as large, copies the old one over and adjusts every pointer that points into the stack - possible because the compiler knows where pointers are and escape analysis guarantees no heap object points into a stack. The garbage collector can shrink stacks that use little of their space. So the practical limit is memory: a million idle goroutines need a few GB, plus whatever each one references. Real systems hit other limits first: file descriptors, downstream connections, or goroutines leaked by blocked channels. Deep recursion grows a stack up to the max (1 GB on 64-bit by default) before crashing with "goroutine stack exceeds limit".

questions.title: select semantics, time.After and timer pitfalls
questions.prompt: Explain how select works in Go when several cases are ready, what default does, and how to implement timeouts. Why was time.After in a loop a classic memory problem, what changed for timers in Go 1.23, and how should you use time.Ticker and context deadlines correctly?

expectedConcepts.label: Ready cases chosen uniformly at random
default makes select non-blocking
Timeouts via time.After, timers or context
time.After in a loop allocated timers not collected until fired (pre-1.23)
Stop tickers; Reset semantics; priorities need nested select

questions.modelAnswer: select blocks until one of its cases can proceed; if several are ready it picks one uniformly at random, so no case can starve the others, but you also cannot express priority directly - use a nested select or check the high-priority channel first. A default case makes the select non-blocking; putting one in a for loop without sleeping creates a CPU-burning busy loop. Timeouts: case <-time.After(2 * time.Second) works for a one-off wait, but before Go 1.23 each call created a timer that was not garbage collected until it fired, so calling it in a hot loop with a long duration accumulated memory. Go 1.23 made unreferenced timers collectable and made timer channels unbuffered so Stop/Reset no longer leave stale values (for modules declaring go 1.23+). Better patterns: create one time.NewTimer and Reset it, or pass a context.WithTimeout and select on ctx.Done(), which also propagates cancellation to callees. Always defer ticker.Stop() for tickers you create, and remember a ticker drops ticks if the receiver is slow rather than queuing them.

questions.title: Using net/http clients safely in production
questions.prompt: Explain how to use Go's net/http client correctly in a production service. Cover why http.DefaultClient has no timeout, the different timeouts, connection pooling in Transport, closing and draining response bodies, retries, and context propagation.

expectedConcepts.label: Default client has no timeout; set Client.Timeout or context deadline
Transport pools connections; reuse one client
Always close and drain the body to reuse connections
NewRequestWithContext propagates cancellation
Pitfalls: client per request, retrying non-idempotent calls, MaxIdleConnsPerHost=2

questions.modelAnswer: http.DefaultClient and a zero-value http.Client have no timeout, so a slow or stuck server can hold a goroutine and connection forever. Set Client.Timeout for the whole exchange, and/or create requests with http.NewRequestWithContext so a deadline or cancellation from the incoming request propagates downstream; finer Transport settings (DialContext timeout, TLSHandshakeTimeout, ResponseHeaderTimeout) control individual phases. The Transport owns a pool of keep-alive connections, so create one client (or Transport) and reuse it across requests; creating a client per request defeats pooling and can exhaust ephemeral ports. Always defer resp.Body.Close(), and read the body to EOF (io.Copy(io.Discard, resp.Body)) before closing if you do not need it, otherwise the connection cannot be reused. The default MaxIdleConnsPerHost is 2, which causes connection churn when a service talks heavily to one host - raise it. Retries should use backoff with jitter, respect Retry-After, and only retry idempotent requests or ones with idempotency keys; check resp.StatusCode, since non-2xx responses are not errors.

questions.title: sync/atomic versus mutexes in Go
questions.prompt: When should you use sync/atomic instead of a mutex in Go? Explain the typed atomics added in Go 1.19, atomic.Pointer and atomic.Value for copy-on-write configuration, compare-and-swap loops, alignment issues on 32-bit platforms, and why atomics do not make compound operations safe.

expectedConcepts.label: Atomics for single-word counters/flags; mutex for invariants across fields
Typed atomics: atomic.Int64, atomic.Bool, atomic.Pointer[T]
Copy-on-write config with atomic.Pointer swap
CompareAndSwap loops
Pitfalls: check-then-act races, 64-bit alignment on 32-bit, mixing atomic and plain access

questions.modelAnswer: A mutex protects any invariant spanning several fields; atomics only make individual loads, stores, adds and compare-and-swaps on one word indivisible, but they avoid blocking and are much cheaper under contention for things like request counters, flags and sequence numbers. Go 1.19 added typed atomics (atomic.Int64, atomic.Uint32, atomic.Bool, atomic.Pointer[T]) that prevent accidental non-atomic access and are automatically 64-bit aligned - with the old functions, 64-bit fields on 32-bit platforms (ARM, 386) had to be manually placed first in a struct or the program crashed. A powerful pattern is copy-on-write: keep configuration in an atomic.Pointer[Config]; readers Load() with no locking, writers build a new Config and Store() it, never mutating the old one. For conditional updates use a CompareAndSwap loop: load, compute, CAS, retry on failure. Pitfalls: "if counter.Load() < max { counter.Add(1) }" is still a race between the check and the act; mixing atomic and plain accesses to the same variable is a data race; and contended atomics still bounce cache lines between cores, so shard hot counters per CPU.

questions.title: Reflection, struct tags and encoding/json
questions.prompt: Explain how Go reflection works with reflect.Type and reflect.Value, how encoding/json uses struct tags, the rules about exported fields, and the performance and correctness pitfalls of reflection-based serialisation, including omitempty, unknown fields and numbers.

expectedConcepts.label: reflect.TypeOf/ValueOf inspect types at runtime
Struct tags like json:"name,omitempty"
Only exported (capitalised) fields are visible
Reflection is slow: allocations; code generation alternatives
Pitfalls: numbers into float64, omitempty on zero values, unknown fields, nil vs empty slice

questions.modelAnswer: Reflection lets code inspect values whose types are unknown at compile time: reflect.TypeOf(x) gives the type (fields, methods, tags, Kind) and reflect.ValueOf(x) the value, which can be read and, if addressable and exported, set. encoding/json walks struct fields by reflection and reads struct tags such as `json:"user_id,omitempty"` to choose names and options; it caches per-type encoders so the walk is not repeated. Only exported fields (starting with a capital letter) are visible to other packages, so lowercase fields are silently skipped - a common "why is my JSON empty" bug. Performance: reflection allocates and prevents inlining; for hot paths use code-generated encoders, or newer faster libraries, and benchmark. Correctness pitfalls: decoding into interface{} turns all numbers into float64, losing precision for large integers (use Decoder.UseNumber or concrete types); omitempty drops legitimate zero values like 0 or false (use pointers when "unset" matters); unknown fields are ignored unless you call DisallowUnknownFields; and a nil slice encodes as null while an empty slice encodes as [].

questions.title: cgo and unsafe: costs and risks
questions.prompt: When would you use cgo or the unsafe package in Go, and why do experienced Go engineers avoid them? Explain the cost of crossing the cgo boundary, the rules for passing Go pointers to C, the effect on the scheduler and builds, and what unsafe.Pointer conversions are valid.

expectedConcepts.label: cgo calls C libraries; each call costs tens of ns
Pointer passing rules: C must not keep Go pointers
cgo calls block an OS thread; thread growth
Builds lose easy cross-compilation and static binaries
unsafe.Pointer: valid conversion patterns, GC and memory safety risks

questions.modelAnswer: cgo lets Go call C (and vice versa), useful for mature C libraries like SQLite, codecs or hardware SDKs. But every call crosses a boundary that switches stacks and coordinates with the scheduler, costing tens of nanoseconds versus about one for a Go call, so chatty fine-grained calls are slow - batch work per call. A goroutine in a C call occupies an OS thread the runtime cannot preempt, so many concurrent blocking C calls create many threads. Pointer rules: C may receive a Go pointer only for the duration of the call, must not store it, and the pointed-to memory must not contain other Go pointers (runtime.Pinner relaxes this); violations corrupt memory when the GC moves or frees objects. cgo also complicates builds: you need a C toolchain for each target, lose trivial cross-compilation and fully static binaries, and get slower builds. The unsafe package bypasses the type system - converting between pointer types, doing pointer arithmetic via uintptr, or zero-copy string/[]byte conversions (unsafe.String, unsafe.Slice). Only the documented conversion patterns are valid, and storing a uintptr instead of a pointer lets the GC free the object. go vet catches some misuse; prefer neither unless profiling proves the need.

questions.title: Designing interfaces in Go
questions.prompt: Explain idiomatic interface design in Go. Why are Go interfaces implicitly satisfied, what does "accept interfaces, return structs" mean, why should interfaces be small and defined by the consumer, and how does this help testing? When is an interface premature?

expectedConcepts.label: Implicit satisfaction: no implements keyword, structural typing
Accept interfaces, return concrete types
Small interfaces like io.Reader; composition
Define interfaces where they are used; easy fakes in tests
Premature interfaces, interface pollution, returning interfaces hides types

questions.modelAnswer: In Go a type satisfies an interface simply by having the right methods; there is no implements declaration. That decoupling means the package that needs a behaviour can declare the interface itself, with only the methods it uses, and any type from anywhere satisfies it - including types written before the interface existed. Hence the proverb "accept interfaces, return structs": functions take the narrowest interface they need (an io.Reader instead of *os.File), which makes them reusable and testable with simple fakes, while constructors return concrete types so callers get the full API and can add their own interfaces. The best interfaces are tiny - io.Reader, io.Writer, fmt.Stringer, error - and bigger ones are composed by embedding. Defining a large interface next to its only implementation "for mocking", Java-style, is interface pollution: it adds indirection, hides documentation and forces every change through two places. Introduce an interface when there are two implementations or a real need to substitute one (tests against an external API). Also remember the typed-nil trap when returning interfaces.

questions.title: singleflight and protecting backends from stampedes
questions.prompt: A Go service caches expensive database results. When a hot key expires, thousands of goroutines miss at once and overload the database. Explain how golang.org/x/sync/singleflight solves this, how it differs from a mutex or sync.Map, and what pitfalls exist with errors, cancellation and slow calls.

expectedConcepts.label: Cache stampede / thundering herd on expiry
singleflight.Group.Do deduplicates concurrent calls per key
Differs from a mutex: per-key and shares the result
Combine with stale-while-revalidate, jittered TTLs
Pitfalls: shared errors, one caller cancelling, slow calls block all; Forget, DoChan

questions.modelAnswer: When a popular cache entry expires, every request that arrives before it is refilled misses and calls the database at the same moment - a cache stampede. singleflight.Group.Do(key, fn) ensures only one execution of fn is in flight per key: the first caller runs it, concurrent callers with the same key block and receive the same result (with shared == true). A global mutex would serialise all keys and still make each waiter re-query afterwards; sync.Map only stores values and does nothing about concurrent misses. Combine it with jittered TTLs so keys do not expire together, and stale-while-revalidate or probabilistic early refresh so most requests never wait. Pitfalls: if the single call fails, every waiter gets the same error; if it hangs, everyone hangs, so the inner call needs its own timeout; the inner call should not use the first caller's request context, because that caller cancelling would fail everyone - use a detached context with a timeout (context.WithoutCancel in Go 1.21+). DoChan lets callers select on their own context, and Forget(key) lets you stop deduplicating after an error. Returned values are shared, so treat them as read-only.

questions.title: database/sql: pooling, transactions and leaks
questions.prompt: Explain how Go's database/sql package manages connections. Cover the connection pool settings, why rows.Close and rows.Err matter, using contexts for timeouts, transactions with Tx, prepared statements, and the common bugs that exhaust the pool in production.

expectedConcepts.label: sql.DB is a pool; SetMaxOpenConns, SetMaxIdleConns, SetConnMaxLifetime
rows.Close (defer) and rows.Err after iteration
QueryContext/ExecContext timeouts
Tx pins a connection; commit or rollback always
Pitfalls: leaked rows, unbounded max open, holding Tx across calls, N+1 queries

questions.modelAnswer: sql.DB is not a connection; it is a concurrency-safe pool meant to be created once and shared. Tune it: SetMaxOpenConns caps concurrent connections (the default is unlimited, which can overwhelm the database), SetMaxIdleConns keeps warm connections, and SetConnMaxLifetime/SetConnMaxIdleTime recycle connections so load balancers and failovers are respected. Each Query borrows a connection until the Rows are closed, so always defer rows.Close() and check rows.Err() after the loop to catch errors that ended iteration early; forgetting Close leaks connections until the pool is exhausted and every request blocks. Use QueryContext/ExecContext with the request context so slow queries are cancelled when the client goes away. db.BeginTx pins one connection for the transaction; always defer tx.Rollback() (a no-op after Commit) and never call the plain db methods from inside a transaction expecting them to be part of it - they use another connection and can even deadlock against your own locks. Prepared statements are per connection and re-prepared transparently. Watch for N+1 query loops and use pool metrics (db.Stats()) to detect waiting.

questions.title: Memory leaks in garbage-collected Go programs
questions.prompt: Go has a garbage collector, yet services still leak memory. Explain the common causes: goroutine leaks, slices and substrings retaining large backing arrays, maps that never shrink, unbounded caches, timers and finalizers. How would you confirm a leak with pprof and fix each case?

expectedConcepts.label: GC frees only unreachable memory; leaks are unintended references
Small slice or substring keeps a huge backing array alive
Goroutine leaks, maps not shrinking, unbounded caches, global registries
Compare inuse_space heap profiles over time
Pitfalls: RSS vs heap, GOGC headroom looks like a leak, finalizers

questions.modelAnswer: The GC only frees memory that is unreachable, so a "leak" in Go is memory that stays reachable by accident. Classic causes: goroutines blocked forever keep their stacks and everything they reference; taking a small slice of a large buffer (buf[:10]) or a substring of a huge string keeps the whole backing array alive - copy the bytes or use strings.Clone; maps keep their bucket memory after deletes, so a map that once held millions of keys stays big until rebuilt; caches and global registries without eviction grow forever (add size limits or TTLs); and in older Go versions, many outstanding time.After timers. To confirm, capture heap profiles with sample_index=inuse_space some time apart and compare them with pprof -diff_base; the growing allocation sites point to the owner. Also check the goroutine profile count. Be careful what you measure: RSS can stay high because the runtime returns memory to the OS lazily, and with GOGC=100 the heap legitimately grows to about twice the live data before collecting, which is not a leak. GOMEMLIMIT helps containers stay under their limit.

questions.title: Go compiler optimisations: inlining, bounds checks and PGO
questions.prompt: Explain which optimisations the Go compiler performs and how you can see and influence them. Cover inlining and its budget, bounds-check elimination, escape analysis, devirtualisation, and profile-guided optimisation. How do you write hot loops the compiler can optimise?

expectedConcepts.label: Inlining with a cost budget; -gcflags=-m shows decisions
Bounds-check elimination, hints like _ = s[n]
Escape analysis keeps values on the stack
PGO: default.pgo profile enables hot-path inlining and devirtualisation
Pitfalls: micro-optimising without benchmarks, interfaces in hot loops, defer cost myths

questions.modelAnswer: The Go compiler favours fast compilation, so it does fewer optimisations than C++ compilers, but the important ones are visible. Inlining copies small functions into callers when their cost is under a budget (around 80 nodes); go build -gcflags=-m prints what was inlined and why not, and -m -m gives more detail. Inlining also enables escape analysis to keep values on the stack. Every slice and array index is bounds-checked; the compiler removes checks it can prove safe, for example after a len check, ranging over the slice, or with a hint like _ = b[7] before accessing b[0..7]; -gcflags=-d=ssa/check_bce shows the remaining ones. Calls through interfaces cannot be inlined unless devirtualised. Since Go 1.21, profile-guided optimisation uses a CPU profile saved as default.pgo in the main package to inline hot functions more aggressively and devirtualise hot interface calls, typically giving 2-14% gains. For hot loops: keep functions small, avoid interface calls and allocations inside, iterate with range, and reuse buffers. Always confirm with go test -bench, -benchmem and benchstat across several runs; defer is now nearly free, so avoiding it is usually pointless.

questions.title: Observability in Go services: slog, metrics and tracing
questions.prompt: Explain how you would make a Go service observable. Cover structured logging with log/slog, passing request-scoped values through context, exposing Prometheus metrics, OpenTelemetry tracing across HTTP and gRPC calls, and the performance pitfalls of logging and high-cardinality metrics in hot paths.

expectedConcepts.label: log/slog structured logging with levels and attributes
Request ids and trace context carried in context.Context
Prometheus counters, gauges, histograms; RED metrics
OpenTelemetry instrumentation for HTTP/gRPC
Pitfalls: logging in hot loops, allocations, label cardinality, PII in logs

questions.modelAnswer: Since Go 1.21 the standard library includes log/slog for structured logging: you log a message with key-value attributes (slog.Info("order created", "order_id", id, "amount", amt)) and a handler renders JSON for log pipelines, with levels so debug logs can be disabled in production. Request-scoped data such as the request id and trace context travels in context.Context; middleware extracts or generates them, and a handler or helper attaches them to every log line so logs from one request can be found together. Metrics come from a Prometheus client: counters for requests and errors, histograms for latency (from which you compute p95 and p99), and gauges for things like queue depth or goroutine count, exposed on /metrics and scraped. OpenTelemetry instrumentation (otelhttp middleware, gRPC interceptors, database wrappers) creates spans and propagates the W3C traceparent header to downstream services, so a slow request can be followed across the system. Pitfalls: logging inside tight loops, or building expensive arguments for disabled log levels, costs CPU and allocations - use slog's LogAttrs or check Enabled; putting unbounded values such as user ids or URLs with ids into metric labels creates high cardinality that can overwhelm Prometheus; logging personal data or tokens is a privacy risk; and tracing every request at high volume needs sampling.

questions.title: Undefined, unspecified and implementation-defined behaviour
questions.prompt: What is the difference between undefined, unspecified, and implementation-defined behavior?

expectedConcepts.label: Three categories defined by the C++ standard
Implementation-defined must be documented; unspecified need not be; undefined has no requirements
UB lets the optimiser assume it never happens, so whole programs break

questions.modelAnswer: Implementation-defined behaviour is something the standard leaves to each compiler, which must document its choice, such as the size of int or whether char is signed. Unspecified behaviour also allows several valid outcomes, but the implementation need not document or be consistent, such as the order in which function arguments are evaluated; the program is still valid, it just must not depend on the order. Undefined behaviour means the standard places no requirements at all: signed integer overflow, dereferencing a null or dangling pointer, out-of-bounds access, or data races. Compilers optimise on the assumption that undefined behaviour never happens, so it can silently delete checks and break code far away from the bug.

questions.title: When std::move does not move
questions.prompt: When can std::move fail to move an object?

expectedConcepts.label: std::move is only a cast to an rvalue reference
Const objects and types without move constructors fall back to copying
Moving on return can block copy elision; moved-from objects are valid but unspecified:return std:

questions.modelAnswer: std::move does not move anything; it is just a cast that turns an expression into an rvalue, telling overload resolution that the object may be moved from. The actual move happens only if a move constructor or move assignment is selected. If the object is const, the result is a const rvalue, which cannot bind to the move constructor's non-const parameter, so the copy constructor is silently used. The same happens for types whose move operations are deleted or not declared because a user-declared destructor or copy suppresses them. Another pitfall is writing return std::move(local), which prevents copy elision and can make code slower. After a real move, the source is valid but in an unspecified state.

questions.title: Dangling references from returned locals
questions.prompt: How can a dangling reference arise from a returned local object?

expectedConcepts.label: A dangling reference refers to an object whose lifetime has ended
Returning a reference or pointer to a local or temporary leaves it dangling
Using it is undefined behaviour that often appears to work; return by value instead

questions.modelAnswer: Local variables live on the stack and are destroyed when the function returns. If a function returns a reference or pointer to one, such as const std::string& name() { std::string s = ...; return s; }, the caller receives a reference to an object that no longer exists. Subtler versions return a string_view or span into a local string or vector, or bind a reference to a member of a temporary, such as auto& x = makeObject().field. Using the dangling reference is undefined behaviour: it often seems to work until the stack memory is reused, then produces garbage or crashes. The fix is usually to return by value, which is cheap thanks to copy elision and move semantics. Compiler warnings and sanitizers catch many cases.

questions.title: std::vector versus std::deque
questions.prompt: What are the trade-offs between std::vector and std::deque?

expectedConcepts.label: vector is one contiguous array; deque is a sequence of fixed-size blocks
deque supports fast insertion at both ends and never relocates elements on growth
vector has better cache locality, contiguity for C APIs and usually wins

questions.modelAnswer: A std::vector stores elements in one contiguous block, so iteration is extremely cache-friendly, element access is a single pointer offset, and you can pass data() to C APIs. Appending at the end is amortised constant time, but inserting at the front is linear, and growth reallocates, invalidating all pointers and references. A std::deque stores elements in a series of fixed-size blocks with an index of pointers to them. It supports constant-time push and pop at both ends, and growing at the ends never moves existing elements, so references to them stay valid. The costs are an extra indirection on every access, worse locality, no contiguous storage and higher memory overhead for small deques. vector is the default; choose deque for queue-like use at both ends.

questions.title: noexcept move constructors and container performance
questions.prompt: How do noexcept move constructors affect container performance?

expectedConcepts.label: noexcept declares that a function will not throw
vector moves elements on reallocation only if the move constructor is noexcept; otherwise it copies
Mark move operations noexcept or default them so containers can move

questions.modelAnswer: When a std::vector grows, it allocates a larger buffer and transfers the existing elements. It must keep the strong exception guarantee: if anything throws, the original vector is unchanged. Moving elements destroys the originals' contents, so if a move threw halfway, the vector could not roll back. Therefore vector uses std::move_if_noexcept: it moves elements only if their move constructor is noexcept, or if the type cannot be copied, and otherwise copies them. A class with a perfectly good move constructor that is not marked noexcept will be copied on every reallocation, which can be dramatically slower for strings or large objects. So declare move operations noexcept, or let the compiler default them, and verify with static_assert and std::is_nothrow_move_constructible.

questions.title: Virtual destructors
questions.prompt: How do virtual destructors prevent resource leaks through base pointers?

expectedConcepts.label: A virtual destructor makes delete dispatch to the derived destructor
Without it, deleting through a base pointer is undefined behaviour and skips derived cleanup
Polymorphic base classes need a public virtual or protected non-virtual destructor

questions.modelAnswer: When you delete an object through a pointer to its base class, as happens with std::unique_ptr<Base> holding a Derived, the compiler needs to know which destructor to call. If the base destructor is virtual, the call is dispatched dynamically: the derived destructor runs first, releasing the derived class's members and resources such as files or buffers, then the base destructor. If it is not virtual, the behaviour is undefined, and in practice only the base destructor runs, leaking whatever the derived part owned. The rule: a class designed to be used polymorphically should have a public virtual destructor, or a protected non-virtual one if deletion through the base should not be allowed.

questions.title: Object slicing
questions.prompt: What is object slicing, and how can it surprise a C++ developer?

expectedConcepts.label: Slicing copies only the base part of a derived object
Happens when passing or storing polymorphic objects by value
Derived data and overrides are lost; use references, pointers or delete copying

questions.modelAnswer: Object slicing happens when a derived object is copied into a variable of its base class type: only the base subobject is copied, and the derived members and dynamic type are lost. It is easy to do accidentally, for example by passing a Derived to a function taking Base by value, storing derived objects in a std::vector<Base>, or assigning a derived object to a base variable. The surprise is that virtual calls on the copy now run the base implementation, and derived data is gone without any error. Avoid it by passing polymorphic objects by reference or pointer, storing them as std::unique_ptr<Base>, and making polymorphic base classes non-copyable, or providing a virtual clone function.

questions.title: Templates versus runtime polymorphism
questions.prompt: How do templates differ from runtime polymorphism?

expectedConcepts.label: Templates: compile-time; virtuals: runtime dispatch
Per-type instantiation versus vtable calls
Inlining and speed versus code bloat and flexibility

questions.modelAnswer: Both let one piece of code work with many types. Templates are resolved at compile time: the compiler generates a separate, specialised version of the code for each type used, so calls can be inlined and optimised with zero runtime overhead, and constraints are checked statically, especially with concepts. The costs are larger binaries, longer compile times, harder error messages and implementation in headers. Runtime polymorphism uses virtual functions: the actual function is chosen at runtime through the vtable. That allows heterogeneous collections, such as a vector of shapes of different types, choosing behaviour from configuration, and plugins loaded at runtime, at the cost of an indirect call that usually cannot be inlined.

questions.title: constexpr versus consteval
questions.prompt: How do constexpr and consteval differ?

expectedConcepts.label: constexpr allows compile-time evaluation; consteval requires it
A constexpr function can also run at runtime with runtime arguments
Use consteval for things that must never cost runtime, such as validating format strings

questions.modelAnswer: A constexpr function may be evaluated at compile time when it is called with constant arguments in a context that needs a constant, such as an array size or a template argument, but the same function can also be called at runtime with ordinary values. So constexpr means "can be used at compile time", not "is always computed at compile time". A consteval function, introduced in C++20, is an immediate function: every call must produce a compile-time constant, and calling it with runtime values is a compile error. That gives a guarantee, useful for building lookup tables or validating things like format strings at compile time, as std::format does. constinit is a related keyword that ensures a variable is initialised at compile time.

questions.title: Atomics versus volatile
questions.prompt: How do atomics differ from volatile in C++?

expectedConcepts.label: volatile stops optimising away accesses
std::atomic: indivisible ops and ordering
volatile is not thread-safe

questions.modelAnswer: volatile tells the compiler that every read and write of a variable is observable and must actually happen, so it is not cached in a register or removed; it exists for memory-mapped hardware registers and certain signal-handling cases. It gives no guarantees about threads: a volatile increment is still a separate read, add and write, which can interleave with other threads, and it imposes no ordering on other memory operations, so concurrent unsynchronised access is still a data race and undefined behaviour. std::atomic provides indivisible operations such as fetch_add and compare_exchange, and memory-ordering guarantees that make writes visible to other threads correctly. Unlike in Java or C#, volatile in C++ is not a synchronisation tool.

questions.title: std::variant versus virtual dispatch
questions.prompt: How do std::variant and virtual dispatch compare for representing alternatives?

expectedConcepts.label: Closed set of types versus open hierarchy
Inline storage and std::visit versus heap and vtables
New operations versus new types

questions.modelAnswer: Both model "one of several kinds", such as shapes or messages. std::variant is a closed set of types fixed at compile time; the value is stored inline without heap allocation, and you handle it with std::visit, where the compiler can check that every alternative is covered. Adding a new operation is easy, just write another visitor, but adding a new type means changing the variant and every visitor. Virtual dispatch through an inheritance hierarchy is open: new derived types can be added later, even in plugins, without touching existing code, but adding an operation means changing the base class, and objects usually live on the heap behind pointers. This is the classic expression problem: choose based on which kind of change is more likely.

questions.title: Fast in debug but slow in release
questions.prompt: How would you diagnose a C++ program that is fast in debug but slow in release?

expectedConcepts.label: Builds differ in flags, macros and libraries
UB, different code paths or contention
Profile the release build and compare flags

questions.modelAnswer: It is unusual, so treat it as a clue that the two builds differ in more than optimisation. First compare the configurations: flags, defined macros such as NDEBUG, linked libraries and allocators; sometimes a debug-only code path or setting is accidentally faster, or the release build enables extra logging, validation or a different implementation. Undefined behaviour can also change meaning under optimisation, for example turning a loop into an infinite one or removing a check, so run the code with sanitizers. In multithreaded code, faster release code can change timing and increase lock contention or false sharing. Then profile the release build itself with perf or a similar tool to see where time goes, and bisect flag differences until the slowdown appears.

questions.title: How sanitizers miss concurrency bugs
questions.prompt: How can sanitizers miss a concurrency bug?

expectedConcepts.label: ThreadSanitizer is a dynamic tool: it only sees executions that actually happen
Races on paths or interleavings not exercised in tests go unnoticed
Logic bugs like deadlocks or atomicity violations with correct locking are not data races

questions.modelAnswer: Sanitizers instrument the program and check what happens while it runs, so they only find bugs in executions that actually occur. ThreadSanitizer detects data races when two threads access the same memory without synchronisation in a run, but if the racy code path is not covered by tests, or the threads never overlap in that run, nothing is reported. Its history window is also limited, so long-separated accesses can be missed. Many concurrency bugs are not data races at all: check-then-act atomicity violations where each access is properly locked, deadlocks that did not occur in this schedule, wrong memory-ordering assumptions on atomics, and lost wakeups. So combine sanitizers with stress tests, varied schedules, code review and design simplicity.

questions.title: Designing a thread-safe cache in C++
questions.prompt: How would you design a thread-safe cache in C++?

expectedConcepts.label: Protect shared state with a mutex or shared_mutex
Reduce contention by sharding the cache into independently locked segments
Avoid returning references to entries; handle eviction and avoid computing under the lock

questions.modelAnswer: Start simple: an std::unordered_map guarded by a std::mutex, with every lookup and insertion done under std::lock_guard. If reads dominate, a std::shared_mutex allows many concurrent readers. To scale further, shard the cache: split it into, say, 16 or 64 independent maps, each with its own lock, choosing the shard by the key's hash, so threads rarely contend. Never return a reference or iterator into the map, because another thread may erase or rehash it; return a copy or a std::shared_ptr to an immutable value. Do not compute expensive values while holding the lock, and handle the case where two threads miss at the same time, and design eviction, such as LRU, so it does not become a global bottleneck.

questions.title: Nil slices versus empty slices
questions.prompt: What is the difference between a nil slice and an empty slice in Go?

expectedConcepts.label: A nil slice has no backing array; an empty slice has length zero with a non-nil pointer
Both have len 0, can be ranged over and appended to
They differ in nil checks, reflect.DeepEqual and JSON encoding as null versus empty array

questions.modelAnswer: A nil slice, declared with var s []int, has a nil pointer, zero length and zero capacity. An empty slice, created with []int{} or make([]int, 0), also has length zero but a non-nil pointer. In most code they behave identically: len returns 0, ranging over them does nothing, and append works on both, so idiomatic Go treats them the same and checks len(s) == 0 rather than s == nil. The differences show up at boundaries: s == nil is true only for the nil slice, reflect.DeepEqual considers them unequal, and encoding/json marshals a nil slice as null but an empty slice as [], which can break API clients expecting an array.

questions.title: How defer evaluates its arguments
questions.prompt: How do defer arguments get evaluated, and when does the deferred call run?

expectedConcepts.label: Arguments are evaluated when the defer statement executes
Deferred calls run in LIFO order when the function returns, even on panic
Use a closure to see later values; deferred calls in loops pile up

questions.modelAnswer: When a defer statement runs, Go evaluates the function value and its arguments immediately, but delays the call until the surrounding function returns, whether normally or through a panic. Deferred calls run in last-in, first-out order. So defer fmt.Println(x) prints the value x had at the defer statement, not at return. If you want the latest value, defer a closure, defer func() { fmt.Println(x) }(), which reads x when it runs. Closures can also modify named result values, which is how deferred code adjusts returned errors. A common pitfall is deferring inside a loop, for example closing files, since nothing is released until the whole function returns.

questions.title: Buffered channels and their trade-offs
questions.prompt: When should a channel be buffered, and what trade-offs follow?

expectedConcepts.label: Unbuffered syncs; buffered decouples
Use for bounded work, bursts or semaphores
Buffers hide backpressure and deadlocks

questions.modelAnswer: An unbuffered channel is a rendezvous: a send blocks until a receiver takes the value, so the two goroutines synchronise and the sender knows the value was handed over. A buffered channel lets senders proceed until the buffer is full, decoupling producer and consumer. Buffers are appropriate when the number of sends is known, such as collecting results from N goroutines so none blocks forever, when smoothing short bursts, or when using the channel as a counting semaphore to limit concurrency. The risks: a buffer delays backpressure, so a slow consumer is noticed later, memory grows with capacity, and adding a buffer to make a deadlock disappear usually just hides a design bug that returns under load.

questions.title: Who closes a channel
questions.prompt: How do you decide which goroutine owns closing a channel?

expectedConcepts.label: Closing signals that no more values will be sent
The sender, specifically the single owner of sending, closes it; receivers never close
Sending on or closing a closed channel panics; multiple senders need a WaitGroup or done channel

questions.modelAnswer: Closing a channel tells receivers that no more values will come, so a for range loop ends. The rule is that the sender closes, never the receiver, because sending on a closed channel panics, and only the sender knows when it has finished. More precisely, the goroutine that owns the channel, usually the one that created it and does all the sending, closes it, often with defer close(ch). When there are multiple senders, none of them can safely close it alone; instead, use a sync.WaitGroup and a separate goroutine that waits for all senders and then closes the channel. To tell senders to stop, use a separate done channel or context, not closing the data channel.

questions.title: Misusing context values
questions.prompt: What problems can arise from using context values for ordinary function parameters?

expectedConcepts.label: context.WithValue carries request-scoped data across API boundaries
Hidden dependencies, no type safety and runtime failures when values are missing
Pass required inputs as explicit parameters; use unexported key types

questions.modelAnswer: context.Context can carry values, intended for request-scoped data that crosses API and process boundaries, such as a trace ID, the authenticated user or a request deadline. Using it to pass ordinary parameters, such as a database handle, a logger configuration or business inputs, causes problems. Dependencies become invisible in function signatures, so readers and tests cannot see what a function needs. Values are untyped, so retrieving them needs type assertions that fail at runtime instead of compile time, and missing values cause surprising behaviour deep in the call stack. Keys can collide unless you use unexported key types. Pass required inputs explicitly and reserve context values for genuinely cross-cutting request metadata.

questions.title: Mutexes versus channels for shared state
questions.prompt: How do mutexes and channels compare for protecting shared state?

expectedConcepts.label: Mutexes guard memory; channels move ownership
Mutex for caches; channels for pipelines
Channel state can be slower and more complex

questions.modelAnswer: Go's proverb is "share memory by communicating", but both tools are idiomatic. A mutex protects data that several goroutines access directly, such as a cache, counter or map: lock, read or modify, unlock. It is simple and fast, but you must remember to lock everywhere and avoid holding locks too long. Channels transfer data, and with it ownership, from one goroutine to another, or let a single goroutine own the state while others send it requests. That fits pipelines, work distribution, signalling and event loops. Using channels just to guard a simple map is usually more code and slower than a mutex. Choose the mechanism that makes ownership and data flow clearest.

questions.title: sync.Once versus package initialisation
questions.prompt: What is the difference between sync.Once and package initialization?

expectedConcepts.label: init functions and package variables run once at program start before main
sync.Once runs a function lazily on first use, safely across goroutines
Prefer lazy Once for expensive or failure-prone setup; init cannot return errors

questions.modelAnswer: Package-level variables and init functions run automatically, once, when the program starts, in dependency order, before main. That is simple, but it runs even if the code is never used, slows startup, cannot return errors, so failures mean a panic, and makes tests harder because side effects happen on import. sync.Once runs a function exactly once, the first time it is needed, and guarantees that concurrent callers wait for it to finish and then see its results. It is ideal for lazily initialising expensive or optional resources, such as a client or a compiled template. Since Go 1.21, sync.OnceValue and OnceValues also return the value and error neatly.

questions.title: Avoiding import cycles in Go
questions.prompt: How can a package avoid import cycles as a codebase grows?

expectedConcepts.label: Go forbids import cycles between packages at compile time
Break cycles by depending on interfaces defined by the consumer
Layer packages by responsibility; move shared types into a lower package

questions.modelAnswer: Go refuses to compile if package A imports B and B imports A, directly or through a chain. Cycles usually signal that responsibilities are tangled. Common fixes: define a small interface in the package that needs a behaviour, so it depends on the interface rather than importing the concrete implementation, and wire the implementation in from main; move types that both packages need into a lower-level package, such as a domain or model package that imports nothing internal; or merge two packages that really are one concept. Structuring code in layers, with dependencies always pointing one way, such as handlers to services to storage, prevents most cycles from appearing.

questions.title: Testing concurrent code without sleeps
questions.prompt: How would you test a concurrent component without relying on sleeps?

expectedConcepts.label: Sleeps make tests slow and flaky because timing varies
Synchronise explicitly with channels, WaitGroups or hooks
Inject fake clocks, run with -race and use testing/synctest

questions.modelAnswer: Using time.Sleep to wait for goroutines makes tests both slow and flaky: on a loaded CI machine the sleep may not be long enough. Instead, synchronise explicitly. Have the component signal events on channels, or expose hooks so the test knows exactly when work has happened; wait with WaitGroups or with a select on the result channel plus a generous timeout only as a failure guard. Inject a clock interface or fake timers instead of calling time.Now and time.After directly, so the test can advance time instantly. Go 1.25 added the testing/synctest package, which runs goroutines in a bubble with a fake clock. Always run concurrent tests with -race, repeated with -count.

questions.title: The Go scheduler and network poller
questions.prompt: How do Go's goroutine scheduler and network poller cooperate?

expectedConcepts.label: Many goroutines on few OS threads
Blocked goroutines parked; netpoller uses epoll
Blocking-style code with event-loop efficiency

questions.modelAnswer: Go lets you write simple blocking code, such as one goroutine per connection calling conn.Read, while performing like an event-driven server. When a goroutine reads from a socket that has no data, the runtime does not block an operating system thread. It registers the socket with the network poller, which uses epoll on Linux or kqueue on macOS, parks the goroutine, and the scheduler runs another goroutine on that thread. When the poller reports the socket is readable, the goroutine is marked runnable and put back on a run queue. This is why a Go server can hold tens of thousands of connections with only a few threads, without callbacks or async syntax.

questions.title: JSON decoding and silent zero values
questions.prompt: How can JSON decoding silently produce zero values for missing fields?

expectedConcepts.label: Missing JSON fields leave struct fields at their zero value with no error
Zero cannot be distinguished from absent, such as 0 or false or empty string
Use pointer fields, validation, or DisallowUnknownFields to catch mistakes

questions.modelAnswer: encoding/json fills in only the fields that appear in the input. If a field is missing, or its name is misspelled in the JSON or the struct tag, the struct field keeps its zero value: 0, false, an empty string or nil, and Unmarshal returns no error. So a request without "quantity" looks identical to one with "quantity": 0, which can cause real bugs, such as treating a missing discount as zero or a missing flag as false. Ways to detect it: use pointer fields such as *int, where nil means absent; validate required fields explicitly after decoding, often with a validation library; and call DisallowUnknownFields on a Decoder to reject misspelled or unexpected keys.

questions.title: is versus == in Python
questions.prompt: What is the difference between is and == in Python?

expectedConcepts.label: is compares identity; == compares equality via __eq__
Two equal objects can be different objects; use is for None and sentinels
Small int and string caching makes is appear to work by accident

questions.modelAnswer: The == operator checks equality: whether two objects have the same value, as defined by their __eq__ method. The is operator checks identity: whether both names refer to the very same object in memory. Two separate lists with equal contents are == but not is. The idiomatic use of is is for singletons such as None, True, False and sentinel objects, as in if x is None. The pitfall is that CPython caches small integers and interns some strings, so a is b may be true for 256 and short strings but false for 1000 or strings built at runtime. Code that uses is to compare numbers or strings works by accident and fails unpredictably.

questions.title: Mutable default arguments
questions.prompt: How do mutable default arguments create surprising behavior?

expectedConcepts.label: Default values are evaluated once, when the function is defined
A mutable default like a list is shared across calls and accumulates state
Use None as the default and create a new object inside

questions.modelAnswer: Python evaluates default argument values once, when the def statement runs, not on every call. If the default is mutable, such as a list or dictionary, every call that relies on the default shares that same object. So def add(item, items=[]): items.append(item); return items returns [1] on the first call and [1, 2] on the second, leaking state between unrelated calls. The idiomatic fix is to use None as the default and create a fresh object inside: if items is None: items = []. Linters flag mutable defaults. The same once-only evaluation means a default like datetime.now() is frozen at definition time.

questions.title: The descriptor protocol and properties
questions.prompt: What is the descriptor protocol, and where do properties use it?

expectedConcepts.label: A descriptor is an object with __get__, __set__ or __delete__ stored on a class
Attribute access on instances calls the descriptor's methods
property, methods, classmethod, staticmethod and ORM fields are descriptors

questions.modelAnswer: A descriptor is any object that defines __get__, and optionally __set__ or __delete__, and is stored as a class attribute. When you access that attribute on an instance, Python does not just return the object; it calls its __get__ method, and assignments call __set__. This hook powers much of Python. The built-in property is a descriptor that calls your getter and setter functions, letting you add validation or computed values without changing the attribute syntax. Plain functions are descriptors too: __get__ is what turns them into bound methods with self filled in, and classmethod and staticmethod are descriptors. Libraries such as ORMs and dataclass fields use descriptors for typed, validated attributes.

questions.title: Calling blocking code from async functions
questions.prompt: How should an async Python function call blocking code safely?

expectedConcepts.label: Blocking calls inside a coroutine freeze the whole event loop
Offload blocking work with asyncio.to_thread or run_in_executor
Prefer async-native libraries; use process pools for CPU-heavy work

questions.modelAnswer: An asyncio event loop runs all coroutines on one thread, switching only at await points. If a coroutine calls blocking code, such as requests.get, time.sleep, a synchronous database driver or heavy computation, the whole loop freezes: no other request makes progress, timeouts fire and latency spikes. The best fix is an async-native library, such as httpx or aiohttp, asyncpg, or asyncio.sleep. When you must call blocking code, offload it with await asyncio.to_thread(func, args) or loop.run_in_executor, which runs it on a thread pool while the loop continues. For CPU-heavy work, threads do not help much because of the GIL, so use a process pool. asyncio's debug mode can warn about slow callbacks.

questions.title: Late binding in loop-created lambdas
questions.prompt: What is a closure, and how can late binding affect loop-created lambdas?

expectedConcepts.label: A closure is a function that remembers variables from its enclosing scope
Closures look up variables when called, so loop lambdas all see the final value
Bind the current value with a default argument or functools.partial

questions.modelAnswer: A closure is a function that captures variables from the scope where it was defined, so it can use them later. Python closures capture variables, not values: the name is looked up when the function runs. That creates a classic surprise: funcs = [lambda: i for i in range(3)] produces three functions that all return 2, because by the time they are called the loop has finished and i is 2. To capture the value at each iteration, bind it as a default argument, lambda i=i: i, which is evaluated at definition time, or use functools.partial, or create the function in a helper that takes i as a parameter.

questions.title: Duck typing and protocols
questions.prompt: What is duck typing, and how do protocols express structural typing?

expectedConcepts.label: Duck typing: objects are used by what methods they have, not their class
typing.Protocol lets type checkers verify structure without inheritance
Keeps code flexible and testable; runtime_checkable allows isinstance checks

questions.modelAnswer: Python traditionally uses duck typing: "if it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it is a duck".
