A function that calls obj.read() works with any object that has a read method, such as a file, a socket wrapper or a test fake, regardless of its class. typing.Protocol brings this idea to static type checking. You declare a protocol listing the methods and attributes needed, such as class Reader(Protocol): def read(self) -> bytes: ..., and type checkers like mypy accept any class that has a matching structure, without it inheriting from the protocol. This is structural typing, as opposed to nominal typing with abstract base classes. Adding @runtime_checkable allows isinstance checks, though only for method presence.

questions.title: Generator send and yield from
questions.prompt: What are generators' send and yield-from capabilities used for?

expectedConcepts.label: send passes a value into a paused generator as the result of yield
yield from delegates to a subgenerator and returns its return value
They enabled coroutines and pipelines; modern async uses async and await instead

questions.modelAnswer: A generator usually produces values with yield, but yield is also an expression. Calling gen.send(value) resumes the generator and makes the paused yield evaluate to that value, so the caller can push data in, which allows generator-based coroutines such as running averages or state machines that consume input. yield from subgen delegates to another generator: it forwards every yielded value out and every sent value or exception in, and evaluates to the subgenerator's return value. This makes it easy to compose generators into pipelines. Historically, asyncio was built on these mechanisms; today native async and await syntax replaced them for asynchronous code, but send and yield from remain useful for advanced generator pipelines.

questions.title: Import caching and circular imports
questions.prompt: How does Python import caching work, and how can circular imports occur?

expectedConcepts.label: Imported modules are cached in sys.modules and executed only once
A circular import sees a partially initialised module
Fix by restructuring, moving imports, or importing modules not names

questions.modelAnswer: The first time a module is imported, Python creates a module object, stores it in sys.modules, and executes the module's code top to bottom. Later imports anywhere simply return the cached object without running the code again. A circular import happens when module A imports B while A is still executing, and B in turn imports A: B receives the partially initialised A from the cache, so names defined later in A do not exist yet, causing ImportError or AttributeError, often depending on which module was imported first. Fixes include restructuring so shared code lives in a third module, importing inside the function that needs it, or importing the module rather than names from it.

questions.title: Virtual environments and pinned dependencies
questions.prompt: What is a virtual environment, and why should dependencies be pinned?

expectedConcepts.label: A virtual environment is an isolated interpreter with its own installed packages
Each project gets its own dependency versions without conflicts
Pin exact versions in a lock file for reproducible installs and controlled upgrades

questions.modelAnswer: A virtual environment is a self-contained directory with its own Python interpreter link and site-packages, created with python -m venv or tools like uv and Poetry. Packages installed there do not affect the system Python or other projects, so one project can use Django 4 and another Django 5 on the same machine. Pinning means recording the exact version of every dependency, including transitive ones, in a lock file such as requirements.txt generated by pip-compile, poetry.lock or uv.lock. Without pinning, a fresh install months later may pull new versions that break your code or introduce vulnerabilities. With a lock file, every developer, CI run and deployment installs the same set, and upgrades become deliberate, reviewed changes.

questions.title: Exception chaining
questions.prompt: How should exceptions be chained to preserve debugging context?

expectedConcepts.label: raise NewError from original sets __cause__ and keeps both tracebacks
Implicit chaining via __context__ happens when raising inside except
Wrap low-level errors in domain errors without losing the cause; use from None deliberately

questions.modelAnswer: When you catch a low-level exception and raise a more meaningful one, such as turning a KeyError into ConfigError, you want to keep the original cause. Writing raise ConfigError("missing database URL") from err sets the new exception's __cause__, and the traceback shows both, joined by "The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception". If you raise inside an except block without from, Python still records the original as __context__, but shows it as "during handling of the above exception, another exception occurred", which suggests an accident. Use raise ... from None only when the original is truly irrelevant noise. Never swallow exceptions with a bare except that loses the cause.

questions.title: Profiling a slow Python endpoint
questions.prompt: How would you profile a slow Python endpoint?

expectedConcepts.label: Measure first: reproduce the slow request and time it
Use profilers such as cProfile, py-spy or pyinstrument
Check database queries and external calls, often the real cause

questions.modelAnswer: First reproduce the slow request and measure it, so you know the baseline and can confirm improvements. Many slow endpoints are not slow in Python at all: tracing or query logging often shows they make dozens of database queries, the N+1 problem, or wait on slow external APIs, so check those first with APM tracing or the ORM's query log. To see where Python time goes, use a sampling profiler like py-spy, which can attach to a running production process with low overhead and produce flame graphs, or pyinstrument and cProfile in development. Look for the widest stacks, fix the biggest cost, and measure again.

questions.title: Multiprocessing start methods
questions.prompt: How do multiprocessing start methods affect process startup and state?

expectedConcepts.label: Start methods: fork, spawn and forkserver
fork copies the parent's memory; spawn starts a fresh interpreter and re-imports the main module
fork is fast but unsafe with threads and locks; spawn is slower but cleaner

questions.modelAnswer: multiprocessing can create worker processes in three ways. fork, historically the Linux default, copies the parent process with copy-on-write, so startup is fast and workers inherit already loaded modules and data. But it copies the state of locks and only the forking thread, so forking a process that has other threads, such as from a logging or database library, can deadlock or corrupt state. spawn, the default on Windows and macOS, starts a fresh Python interpreter that re-imports the main module and receives its arguments by pickling; it is slower and requires the if __name__ == "__main__" guard, but it is clean and predictable. forkserver forks from a clean helper process. Python 3.14 made forkserver the Linux default.

questions.title: Monkey patching and its risks
questions.prompt: What is monkey patching, and what risks does it introduce?

expectedConcepts.label: Monkey patching replaces attributes of modules or classes at runtime
Common in tests to stub dependencies, and for hotfixing libraries
Global, surprising side effects that break on upgrades and leak between tests

questions.modelAnswer: Monkey patching means modifying a module, class or object at runtime, for example replacing requests.get or a class method with your own function. Python allows it because attributes are dynamic. It is common and useful in tests, through unittest.mock.patch or pytest's monkeypatch fixture, to substitute a slow or external dependency, and sometimes to work around a bug in a third-party library. The risks: the change is global and invisible at the call site, so other code behaves unexpectedly; patches that are not undone leak between tests; you may patch the wrong name, since you must patch where the object is looked up; and patches break silently when the library's internals change. Prefer dependency injection where possible.

questions.title: Wheels versus source distributions
questions.prompt: How do package wheels differ from source distributions?

expectedConcepts.label: A wheel is a prebuilt, ready-to-install archive; an sdist contains source to be built
Wheels install quickly without compilers; platform tags mark compiled extensions
Publish wheels for common platforms plus an sdist as fallback

questions.modelAnswer: A source distribution, or sdist, is an archive of the package's source code and build configuration. Installing it means running the build backend on your machine, which for packages with C, C++ or Rust extensions requires compilers and system libraries, takes time and can fail. A wheel is a pre-built archive in the final installed layout: pip just unpacks it, which is fast and needs no compilers. Pure-Python wheels work everywhere, while wheels with compiled code have tags for Python version, operating system and architecture, such as manylinux x86_64 or macOS arm64. Maintainers publish wheels for common platforms, often built in CI, plus an sdist as a fallback for others.

questions.title: What 'static means in Rust
questions.prompt: What does 'static mean for a reference and for a trait object?

expectedConcepts.label: &'static T is a reference valid for the whole program
T: 'static as a bound means the type holds no non-static borrows, not that it lives forever
Common confusion; thread::spawn requires 'static, so move owned data or use Arc

questions.modelAnswer: On a reference, &'static T means the data lives for the entire run of the program, like string literals or leaked allocations. As a trait bound, T: 'static, or Box<dyn Trait + 'static>, means something different: the type contains no references with a shorter lifetime, so it could be kept as long as needed. Any owned type such as String, Vec<u8> or a struct of owned fields satisfies 'static, even though the value is dropped normally. This matters because std::thread::spawn and tokio::spawn require 'static closures: a spawned task might outlive the current stack frame, so it cannot borrow local variables. The fix is to move owned data into the closure, or share it with Arc.

questions.title: When to use Cow
questions.prompt: When should a Rust API use Cow?

expectedConcepts.label: Cow, clone-on-write, holds either borrowed or owned data
Useful when a function usually returns its input unchanged but sometimes must allocate
Avoids needless clones but adds API complexity

questions.modelAnswer: Cow, short for clone-on-write, is an enum that holds either a borrowed reference, Cow::Borrowed(&str), or an owned value, Cow::Owned(String). It fits functions that usually can return their input as is but occasionally need to modify it. For example, a function that escapes HTML can return the original &str with no allocation when there is nothing to escape, and allocate a new String only when it actually changes something. Callers can read either variant through Deref, or call into_owned when they need ownership. It is also used for configuration that may come from static defaults or runtime values. Use it where profiling shows allocations matter, since it makes signatures more complex.

questions.title: Ownership and borrowing with collections
questions.prompt: How do ownership and borrowing interact with collections?

expectedConcepts.label: Collections own elements; access borrows them
No push while holding a reference into a Vec
Use indices, collect changes, or entry and retain

questions.modelAnswer: A Vec, HashMap or other collection owns its elements: moving a value in transfers ownership, and dropping the collection drops them. Accessing elements gives borrows: iter() yields shared references, iter_mut() mutable ones, and into_iter() moves elements out. The borrow checker then prevents a classic bug from other languages: holding a reference to an element while pushing to the vector is rejected, because pushing may reallocate and leave the reference dangling. The same applies to modifying a map while iterating it. Idiomatic workarounds include storing indices or keys instead of references, collecting the changes into a separate list and applying them afterwards, using the entry API for maps, and methods like retain or drain.

questions.title: Holding a lock across an await point
questions.prompt: How can holding a lock across an await point cause trouble?

expectedConcepts.label: Holding a std Mutex guard across await blocks other tasks and can deadlock
std::sync guards are not Send, so the future cannot move between threads
Release the lock before awaiting, or use an async-aware mutex such as tokio::sync::Mutex

questions.modelAnswer: In async Rust, a task suspends at each .await and other tasks run on the same worker thread. If a task holds a std::sync::Mutex guard across an await, the lock stays held while it is suspended. Another task on the same thread that tries to lock it blocks the whole thread, which can deadlock the runtime or stall many tasks. The compiler often catches this, because std::sync::MutexGuard is not Send, so the future cannot be spawned on a multi-threaded runtime, producing a confusing error. The fix is to keep critical sections short and drop the guard before awaiting, often by moving the locked work into a small block or function. If a lock must be held across await, use an async-aware mutex such as tokio::sync::Mutex.

questions.title: Pinning and Pin
questions.prompt: What are pinning and Pin used for at a high level?

expectedConcepts.label: Pin guarantees a value will not be moved in memory again
Needed for self-referential types such as async futures that hold references to their own fields
Mostly hidden by Box::pin and pin! macros; Unpin types are unaffected:box:

questions.modelAnswer:
Rust normally moves values freely, by copying their bytes to a new location. That breaks self-referential types, values that contain pointers into themselves, because after a move those pointers point at the old location. The futures generated by async functions are often self-referential: a local variable and a reference to it, both stored in the future across an await. Pin

wraps a pointer and promises that the value behind it will never be moved again, so polling such a future is safe; Future::poll therefore takes Pin<&mut Self>. Most types are Unpin, meaning pinning does not restrict them. In everyday code you meet Pin through Box::pin or the pin! macro when storing or polling futures manually.

questions.title: Crates, modules and visibility
questions.prompt: How do crates and modules define visibility boundaries?

expectedConcepts.label: A crate is a compilation unit; modules organise code inside it
Items are private by default; pub, pub(crate) and pub(super) widen visibility
Keep the public API small and re-export a curated surface

questions.modelAnswer: A crate is Rust's unit of compilation and distribution: a library or binary package. Inside it, code is organised into a tree of modules with mod. Everything is private by default, visible only within its own module and its children. pub makes an item visible to anyone who can reach the module, pub(crate) limits it to the current crate, and pub(super) to the parent module. Struct fields have their own visibility, so a public struct can keep fields private and enforce invariants through constructors. Good libraries keep internal modules private and re-export a small, deliberate public API with pub use, so they can refactor internals without breaking users.

questions.title: Monomorphisation and binary size
questions.prompt: What is monomorphization, and how can it affect binary size?

expectedConcepts.label: Monomorphisation creates a separate copy of generic code for each concrete type
It makes generics zero-cost at runtime but increases code size and compile time
Reduce with dyn Trait, or a non-generic inner function wrapped by a thin generic one

questions.modelAnswer: When you call a generic function like fn process<T: Display>(x: T) with several types, the compiler generates a separate, specialised copy for each concrete type, such as process for i32, for String, and so on. Each copy is optimised for its type and calls are static, which is why Rust generics have no runtime overhead. The cost is that large generic functions used with many types multiply machine code, increasing binary size, compile times and instruction-cache pressure. Remedies include using dyn Trait when dynamic dispatch is acceptable, or the inner-function pattern: a thin generic wrapper converts its argument, for example with as_ref or into, then calls a non-generic function containing the bulk of the code. Tools like cargo bloat show which generics dominate.

questions.title: Converting errors between library layers
questions.prompt: How should a Rust program convert errors between library layers?

expectedConcepts.label: Per-layer error types; From lets ? convert
Libraries: thiserror enums; apps: anyhow
Add context and keep the source chain

questions.modelAnswer: Each layer usually has its own error type, so callers can handle failures in terms that make sense at that level, such as StorageError rather than an SQL driver error. Implementing From<LowerError> for HigherError lets the ? operator convert errors automatically as they propagate. Libraries typically define enums of meaningful variants, often with the thiserror crate to derive Display, Error and From, and keep the original error as the source so the full chain is available for debugging. Applications often use anyhow, which wraps any error and lets you add human context like "failed to load config from path". Avoid exposing third-party error types in a library's public API, since that ties users to that dependency's version.

questions.title: Channels versus shared mutable state in Rust
questions.prompt: How do channels compare with shared mutable state in Rust?

expectedConcepts.label: Channels send owned values between threads; shared state uses Arc with Mutex or RwLock
Ownership transfer means no locking on the data itself
Channels suit pipelines and actors; locks suit shared caches and counters

questions.modelAnswer: Rust supports both styles safely. With channels, such as std::sync::mpsc, crossbeam or tokio channels, threads send owned values to each other; ownership moves with the message, so the receiving thread has exclusive access and needs no lock, and the compiler stops the sender from using the value afterwards. This suits pipelines, worker pools and actor-style designs where one task owns some state and others send it requests. With shared state, data is wrapped in Arc<Mutex<T>> or Arc<RwLock<T>>, and every thread locks it to read or write. That is simpler for a shared cache, counter or configuration that many threads touch. The type system, through Send and Sync, prevents data races either way.

questions.title: FFI boundaries and Rust safety
questions.prompt: How can FFI boundaries complicate Rust's safety assumptions?

expectedConcepts.label: FFI calls into C or other languages are unsafe because the compiler cannot verify them
Foreign code can violate ownership, lifetimes, aliasing, thread safety and panic rules
Wrap FFI in a small safe abstraction that documents and checks invariants

questions.modelAnswer: Rust's guarantees only hold for code the compiler can check. Calling a C library through extern "C" functions is unsafe because the compiler cannot verify the foreign side: it may return null or dangling pointers, free memory Rust still uses, keep pointers longer than the borrow allowed, mutate data Rust assumes is immutable, call back from other threads, or expect a different memory layout. Panics must not unwind across the boundary, and ownership of allocations must be clear, with memory freed by the same allocator that created it. The standard practice is to confine raw FFI calls to a small module, generated with tools like bindgen, and wrap them in a safe Rust API that validates inputs, documents invariants and manages ownership with types like Drop guards.

questions.title: Cargo features for configurable libraries
questions.prompt: How do cargo features help build configurable libraries?

expectedConcepts.label: Features are named flags in Cargo.toml that enable optional code and dependencies
Users enable only what they need, reducing compile time and binary size
Features must be additive; feature combinations need testing

questions.modelAnswer: Cargo features are named switches declared in a crate's Cargo.toml. Code guarded by #[cfg(feature = "...")] is compiled only when the feature is enabled, and features can turn on optional dependencies. A library can offer, for example, a serde feature for serialisation support, a tls feature for HTTPS, or a choice of async runtime, so users who do not need them avoid the extra dependencies, compile time and binary size. A key rule is that features must be additive: Cargo unifies features across the whole dependency graph, so if two crates enable different features of your library, both are on, and enabling a feature must never break code that does not use it. Test combinations, for example with cargo hack.

questions.title: Cloning versus complex lifetimes
questions.prompt: What is the trade-off between cloning data and introducing complex lifetimes?

expectedConcepts.label: Borrowing with lifetimes avoids copies; cloning gives independent owned data
Lifetimes spread through structs and APIs and make code rigid
Clone or use Arc when cost is small and not hot; borrow in measured hot paths

questions.modelAnswer: Borrowing avoids copying data, but once a struct stores a reference it needs a lifetime parameter, and that lifetime spreads into every type and function that holds it. The data must outlive all of them, which makes the code harder to refactor, store, return or send to threads, and causes fights with the borrow checker. Cloning gives each owner an independent copy, so types become simple and flexible, at the cost of allocation and copying. For small data, configuration, or code outside hot paths, cloning, or sharing with Arc or Rc, which makes clones cheap reference-count increments, is usually the right call. In performance-critical paths, measured with a profiler, the complexity of borrowing can be worth it.

questions.title: Stack frames versus heap objects in the JVM
questions.prompt: What is the difference between stack frames and heap objects in the JVM?

expectedConcepts.label: Per-thread stack frames; shared heap objects
Frames pop on return; objects live until collected
Escape analysis; stack overflow versus OOM

questions.modelAnswer: Each Java thread has its own stack. Every method call pushes a frame containing that method's local variables, parameters and intermediate values; primitives are stored directly, and object variables hold references. When the method returns, its frame is popped instantly. Objects themselves, created with new, live on the heap, shared by all threads, and stay alive as long as something references them; the garbage collector reclaims them later. Too-deep recursion exhausts the stack with StackOverflowError, while too many live objects exhaust the heap with OutOfMemoryError. The JIT's escape analysis can sometimes avoid heap allocation for objects that never leave a method, replacing them with local values.

questions.title: Class loaders
questions.prompt: What are class loaders, and why can multiple class loaders matter?

expectedConcepts.label: Loaders load bytecode by parent delegation
Class identity is name plus loader
ClassCastException and redeploy leaks

questions.modelAnswer: The JVM loads classes lazily through class loaders, which locate bytecode in JARs, directories or elsewhere. They form a hierarchy, the bootstrap, platform and application loaders, and normally delegate to their parent first. Application servers, plugin systems and build tools create additional loaders to isolate components, so each web application or plugin can have its own versions of libraries. The key subtlety is that a class's identity is its name plus the loader that defined it: the same class loaded by two loaders is two different types, producing confusing errors like "ClassCastException: Foo cannot be cast to Foo". Loaders also cause memory leaks on redeploy if anything keeps a reference to an old loader's classes.

questions.title: synchronized versus ReentrantLock
questions.prompt: How do synchronized blocks and ReentrantLock compare?

expectedConcepts.label: Both give exclusion, visibility and reentrancy
ReentrantLock adds tryLock, timeouts and fairness
Unlock in finally; virtual-thread pinning

questions.modelAnswer: Both give mutual exclusion and the same memory-visibility guarantees, and both are reentrant, so a thread holding the lock can acquire it again. synchronized is built into the language: you mark a method or block, and the lock is released automatically when the block exits, even with an exception, so it is simple and hard to misuse. ReentrantLock is a library class with more features: tryLock to avoid waiting, timed and interruptible acquisition, optional fairness, and multiple Condition objects. The cost is that you must call unlock in a finally block yourself. Before Java 24, synchronized also pinned virtual threads to their carrier threads, which made ReentrantLock preferable in virtual-thread code.

questions.title: CompletableFuture and executor services
questions.prompt: What are CompletableFuture and executor services used for?

expectedConcepts.label: An ExecutorService manages a pool of threads that run submitted tasks
CompletableFuture composes asynchronous results with thenApply, thenCompose and allOf
Default common pool is shared; choose executors and handle exceptions explicitly

questions.modelAnswer: An ExecutorService decouples submitting work from how it runs: you submit tasks, and it manages a pool of threads, queues work, and returns Futures; you must size it appropriately and shut it down. CompletableFuture builds on that to compose asynchronous computations without blocking: you can transform a result with thenApply, chain another async call with thenCompose, combine results with thenCombine or allOf, and handle errors with exceptionally or handle. Pitfalls: async methods without an explicit executor run on the shared ForkJoinPool common pool, so blocking I/O there starves other users, exceptions are easy to lose if nobody observes the future, and long chains can be hard to debug. With virtual threads, simple blocking code is often clearer.

questions.title: Thread-pool starvation deadlock
questions.prompt: How can thread-pool starvation deadlock an application?

expectedConcepts.label: Tasks wait on tasks that cannot get a thread
A task blocks on a subtask in the same pool
Separate pools, async composition, thread dumps

questions.modelAnswer: A thread-pool starvation deadlock happens when every thread in a pool is busy waiting for work that can only run on that same pool. Classic example: a pool of 10 threads, and each task submits a subtask to the same pool and calls get() on it. Under load, all 10 threads are blocked waiting, the subtasks sit in the queue, and nothing ever progresses, without any lock cycle a deadlock detector would notice. The same occurs when request handlers block on calls that need the same bounded pool. Fixes include separate pools for dependent stages, composing asynchronously with CompletableFuture instead of blocking, ForkJoinPool for recursive tasks, and timeouts. A thread dump showing all pool threads parked in get() reveals it.

questions.title: HashMap versus ConcurrentHashMap
questions.prompt: How do HashMap and ConcurrentHashMap differ under concurrency?

expectedConcepts.label: HashMap is not thread-safe; ConcurrentHashMap supports concurrent access
Concurrent writes to HashMap can lose updates or corrupt the structure
Use atomic methods like computeIfAbsent and merge instead of check-then-act

questions.modelAnswer: HashMap has no synchronisation. If multiple threads modify it concurrently, updates can be lost, size can become wrong, and a resize happening concurrently can corrupt the internal structure; in old Java versions it could even create an infinite loop. ConcurrentHashMap is designed for concurrent use: reads are generally lock-free, and writes lock only a single bin, so many threads can update different keys in parallel, and iterators do not throw ConcurrentModificationException. However, sequences of operations are still not atomic: if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v) is a race. Use the atomic methods putIfAbsent, computeIfAbsent, compute and merge. ConcurrentHashMap also rejects null keys and values.

questions.title: Records and sealed classes
questions.prompt: How do records and sealed classes help model data?

expectedConcepts.label: Records are concise immutable data carriers with generated equals, hashCode and toString
Sealed classes restrict which classes may extend a type
Together with pattern matching in switch they give exhaustive, algebraic data types

questions.modelAnswer: A record, such as record Point(int x, int y) {}, declares a transparent, immutable data carrier in one line: the compiler generates the constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode and toString, and you can add validation in a compact constructor. Sealed classes and interfaces, declared with sealed and permits, restrict which classes may extend or implement them, so the hierarchy is closed and known. Combined with pattern matching in switch, available since Java 21, you can model alternatives like sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square, with each as a record, and the compiler checks that a switch handles every case. That gives Java algebraic data types, making illegal states unrepresentable and refactoring safer.

questions.title: try-with-resources
questions.prompt: What is try-with-resources, and how does it handle cleanup?

expectedConcepts.label: try-with-resources closes AutoCloseable resources automatically when the block exits
Resources close in reverse order, even when exceptions occur
Close failures are recorded as suppressed exceptions instead of hiding the original

questions.modelAnswer: try-with-resources is a form of try statement that declares resources, such as files, sockets, database connections or locks wrapped in AutoCloseable, in parentheses: try (var in = Files.newInputStream(path)) { ... }. When the block exits, normally or by exception, Java calls close on each resource automatically, in reverse order of declaration. It also handles a subtle problem with manual finally blocks: if the body throws and then close also throws, the original exception is kept as the primary error, and the close failure is attached as a suppressed exception, available through getSuppressed. That makes cleanup correct and concise, avoiding the resource leaks common in hand-written finally code.

questions.title: Memory leaks in garbage-collected Java
questions.prompt: What are common causes of memory leaks in garbage-collected Java?

expectedConcepts.label: A leak is objects that remain reachable but are no longer needed
Causes: static collections, unbounded caches, listeners, ThreadLocals and class loaders
Diagnose with heap dumps and dominator trees; use bounded caches and weak references

questions.modelAnswer: Garbage collection frees only unreachable objects, so Java leaks happen when objects stay reachable even though the program no longer needs them. Common causes: static maps or lists that keep growing; caches without size limits or expiry; listeners and callbacks registered but never removed; ThreadLocal values in pooled threads that are never cleared, especially in application servers; unclosed resources; and class loader leaks during redeploys. Symptoms are heap usage that climbs after every GC, more frequent collections and eventually OutOfMemoryError. Diagnose with heap dumps analysed in Eclipse MAT or VisualVM, looking at the dominator tree and the reference path keeping objects alive, and fix with bounded caches such as Caffeine, cleanup, or weak references.

questions.title: Heap dumps and thread dumps
questions.prompt: How do heap dumps and thread dumps help diagnose incidents?

expectedConcepts.label: Heap dump: objects; thread dump: thread stacks
Heap dumps for memory; thread dumps for hangs
Capture with jcmd; take several thread dumps

questions.modelAnswer: A heap dump is a snapshot of every object on the heap with its references. It answers memory questions: what is filling the heap, and what chain of references keeps it alive, analysed in tools like Eclipse MAT. Enable -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError so you get one automatically, but note dumps pause the JVM and may contain sensitive data. A thread dump lists every thread with its state, such as RUNNABLE, BLOCKED or WAITING, its stack trace and the locks it holds or waits for. It explains hangs, deadlocks, which the JVM reports explicitly, exhausted thread pools and lock contention. Take several thread dumps a few seconds apart with jcmd or jstack to see which threads are stuck versus just busy.

questions.title: Platform threads versus virtual threads
questions.prompt: What is the difference between a platform thread and a virtual thread?

expectedConcepts.label: Platform threads are OS threads; virtual are JVM-managed
Blocked virtual threads unmount from carriers
Not faster for CPU work; avoid pooling them

questions.modelAnswer: A platform thread is a thin wrapper around an operating system thread: it has a large stack, creating it is relatively expensive, and you can only have a few thousand, which is why servers used thread pools and asynchronous frameworks. Virtual threads, final since Java 21, are managed by the JVM. They are cheap to create, so you can start one per request, even millions. When a virtual thread blocks on I/O, the JVM unmounts it from its carrier platform thread, which then runs other virtual threads. This lets simple, blocking-style code scale like async code. Virtual threads do not make CPU-bound work faster, should not be pooled, and heavy ThreadLocal use or pinning can reduce their benefits.

questions.title: Propagating interruption in Java
questions.prompt: How should interruption be propagated in Java code?

expectedConcepts.label: Interruption is a cooperative request for a thread to stop
Blocking methods throw InterruptedException and clear the interrupted flag
Never swallow it: rethrow or restore the flag with Thread.currentThread().interrupt()

questions.modelAnswer: Java threads cannot be forcibly stopped safely; instead, another thread calls interrupt(), which is a polite request to stop. Blocking methods such as sleep, wait, join and BlockingQueue.take respond by throwing InterruptedException, and in doing so they clear the thread's interrupted flag. The most common bug is catching InterruptedException and ignoring it, which loses the cancellation request, so executors cannot shut down and tasks keep running. Correct handling is either to let the exception propagate by declaring it, or, if you cannot rethrow, to restore the flag with Thread.currentThread().interrupt() and then exit promptly. Long-running loops without blocking calls should check Thread.interrupted() periodically.

questions.title: Class initialisation order bugs
questions.prompt: What is class initialization order, and how can it cause bugs?

expectedConcepts.label: Static initialisers run in textual order
Overridable calls in constructors see null fields
Circular statics expose default values

questions.modelAnswer: When a class is first used, the JVM initialises it: static fields and static blocks run in the order they appear in the source. A static field that depends on another declared later sees that one's default value, null or zero, and circular static dependencies between two classes can expose half-initialised state. For objects, a constructor first runs the superclass constructor, then the subclass's field initialisers and constructor body. If the superclass constructor calls an overridable method, the subclass override runs before the subclass fields are initialised, so it sees null or zero, a classic source of NullPointerExceptions. Avoid calling overridable methods from constructors and keep static initialisation simple.

questions.title: Immutable objects in concurrent programs
questions.prompt: How do immutable objects help concurrent programs?

expectedConcepts.label: Immutable objects cannot change after construction
They can be shared between threads without locks, and final fields are safely published
Model updates as new objects; use records and defensive copies of mutable inputs

questions.modelAnswer: An immutable object's state cannot change after it is constructed: all fields are final, there are no setters, and any mutable inputs are defensively copied. Most concurrency bugs come from shared mutable state, so immutable objects eliminate them: any number of threads can read the same object at the same time without locks, there are no torn or inconsistent states, and the Java memory model guarantees that final fields are visible correctly once construction finishes. Updates are expressed by creating a new object, and a single reference to the current version can be swapped atomically, for example with AtomicReference. Records, String and the List.of collections are examples. The cost is extra allocation, which is usually cheap.

questions.title: Maven versus Gradle
questions.prompt: How do Maven and Gradle differ in build configuration style?

expectedConcepts.label: Maven uses declarative XML in pom.xml with a fixed lifecycle
Gradle uses a Kotlin or Groovy DSL with a flexible task graph
Maven is uniform and predictable; Gradle is faster with incremental builds and caching but can grow complex

questions.modelAnswer: Maven configures builds declaratively in an XML pom.xml file. It follows convention over configuration with a fixed lifecycle of phases, such as compile, test, package and install, and customisation happens through plugins bound to those phases. That makes Maven projects uniform and easy to understand, but unusual builds can be awkward. Gradle uses build scripts written in a Kotlin or Groovy DSL, modelling the build as a graph of tasks. It is more flexible and programmable, and faster for large projects thanks to incremental builds, the build cache and the daemon. The downside is that build logic can become real code that is hard to maintain, so teams should keep it in conventions and plugins.

questions.title: Dependency scopes and runtime packaging
questions.prompt: What is dependency scope, and how can it affect runtime packaging?

expectedConcepts.label: Scope controls on which classpaths a dependency appears
compile, provided or compileOnly, runtime and test scopes are packaged differently
Wrong scope causes NoClassDefFoundError at runtime or bloated, conflicting artifacts

questions.modelAnswer: A dependency's scope, in Maven terms, or configuration, in Gradle, determines where it is available. Compile scope, or implementation and api in Gradle, is on the compile and runtime classpaths and is packaged with the application. Provided, or compileOnly, is available for compiling but expected to be supplied by the environment, such as the servlet API in an application server, so it is not packaged. Runtime scope, such as a JDBC driver, is needed only when running. Test scope is only for tests. Mistakes are costly: marking something provided when nothing provides it gives NoClassDefFoundError in production, while packaging a provided library causes conflicts and bloated artifacts.

questions.title: Diagnosing high GC pause times
questions.prompt: How would you diagnose high GC pause times?

expectedConcepts.label: Enable GC logging and measure pause frequency, duration and cause
Causes: allocation rate, too-small heap, humongous objects, full GCs, collector choice
Reduce allocation, size the heap, tune or switch collector, such as G1 to ZGC

questions.modelAnswer: Start with data: enable unified GC logging with -Xlog:gc*, and look at how often pauses happen, how long they last, which collection type causes them, and the heap occupancy before and after. Correlate pauses with latency spikes. Common causes are a high allocation rate, which triggers frequent young collections; a heap too small for the live data set, so old-generation collections or full GCs happen; humongous allocations in G1; memory leaks steadily increasing live data; and explicit System.gc calls. Fixes include reducing allocation in hot paths, found with an allocation profiler such as JFR or async-profiler, sizing the heap correctly, fixing leaks, and for very low latency switching from G1 to ZGC or Shenandoah.

questions.title: null, undefined and absent properties
questions.prompt: What is the difference between null, undefined, and an absent property?

expectedConcepts.label: undefined means no value assigned; null is an intentional empty value
An absent property is not present at all, though reading it also gives undefined
Matters for JSON, spreading, and TypeScript exactOptionalPropertyTypes

questions.modelAnswer: undefined is JavaScript's default for "no value": an uninitialised variable, a missing function argument, or a function with no return. null is a value developers assign deliberately to mean "intentionally empty". An absent property is one that does not exist on the object at all; reading it also returns undefined, so obj.x === undefined cannot tell you whether x is missing or explicitly set to undefined, but "x" in obj or Object.hasOwn(obj, "x") can. The difference matters in practice: JSON.stringify drops undefined properties but keeps null, object spread copies an explicit undefined over an existing value, and APIs may treat null as "clear this field" versus absent as "leave unchanged". The ?? operator treats both null and undefined as missing.

questions.title: Lexical scope versus dynamic scope
questions.prompt: How does lexical scope differ from dynamic scope?

expectedConcepts.label: Lexical scope resolves names by where code is written; dynamic scope by the call stack at runtime
JavaScript variables are lexically scoped, which makes closures work
this behaves dynamically in ordinary functions, a common source of confusion

questions.modelAnswer: With lexical, or static, scope, a variable reference is resolved by where the code is written: a function can see variables from the blocks and functions that textually enclose it, no matter where it is called from. With dynamic scope, a reference is resolved by looking up the chain of active function calls at runtime, so the same function could see different variables depending on its caller. JavaScript variables declared with let, const, var and function parameters are lexically scoped, which is what makes closures predictable: a returned function keeps access to its defining scope. The notable exception that feels dynamic is this in ordinary functions, determined by how the function is called; arrow functions instead take this lexically.

questions.title: Promise.all, allSettled, race and any
questions.prompt: How do Promise.all, allSettled, race, and any differ?

expectedConcepts.label: All four combine several promises into one
all rejects on the first failure; allSettled waits for every outcome
race settles with the first to settle; any resolves with the first success

questions.modelAnswer: Each takes an iterable of promises and returns one promise. Promise.all fulfils with an array of all results if every promise fulfils, but rejects as soon as any one rejects, which suits steps that all must succeed, such as loading required data in parallel; the other operations keep running unless you cancel them. Promise.allSettled always waits for every promise and returns objects describing each fulfilled value or rejection reason, which suits batches where partial failure is acceptable. Promise.race settles with whichever promise settles first, success or failure, often used for timeouts. Promise.any fulfils with the first successful result and rejects with an AggregateError only if all fail, useful for trying redundant sources.

questions.title: Avoiding unhandled promise rejections
questions.prompt: How should rejected promises be handled to avoid unhandled rejections?

expectedConcepts.label: An unhandled rejection is a rejected promise with no catch handler
await inside try and catch, or attach .catch, and return or await every promise
Node crashes on unhandled rejections; use lint rules and global handlers as a last resort

questions.modelAnswer: When a promise rejects and nothing handles it, the error disappears from normal control flow: browsers log a warning, and since Node.js 15 the process crashes by default. They usually come from "floating" promises, async calls started without await, return or .catch, such as calling saveData() inside an event handler and forgetting to await it. Handle rejections where you can act on them: use await inside try and catch, or attach .catch to promise chains, and make sure functions return or await the promises they create so errors propagate to callers. Lint rules such as @typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises catch mistakes, and global unhandledrejection handlers should log and report as a last resort, not replace proper handling.

questions.title: Type narrowing versus type assertions
questions.prompt: What is the difference between type narrowing and type assertion in TypeScript?

expectedConcepts.label: Narrowing refines a type through checks the compiler understands
A type assertion tells the compiler to trust you, without any runtime check
Assertions can hide bugs; prefer narrowing or validation

questions.modelAnswer: Narrowing is the compiler following your control flow: after if (typeof x === "string"), or checks with instanceof, in, equality against a discriminant, or a user-defined type guard function, TypeScript knows x has a more specific type in that branch. The check really runs at runtime, so the narrowed type is backed by evidence. A type assertion, written value as Type or with the non-null operator !, simply tells the compiler "trust me, it is this type". Nothing is checked at runtime, so if you are wrong, the program fails later with a confusing error far from the cause. Prefer narrowing and runtime validation; reserve assertions for cases where you genuinely know more than the compiler, and keep them rare.

questions.title: Discriminated unions for safer state
questions.prompt: What are discriminated unions, and how can they make state handling safer?

expectedConcepts.label: A union of object types sharing a literal tag property
Switching on the tag narrows to the matching variant and its fields
Makes impossible states unrepresentable and enables exhaustiveness checks with never

questions.modelAnswer: A discriminated union is a union of object types that share a common property with a distinct literal value, the discriminant, for example type Request = { status: "loading" } | { status: "error"; error: Error } | { status: "success"; data: User }. When code checks request.status, TypeScript narrows the type, so data is only accessible in the success branch and error only in the error branch. Compare that with a single object with optional isLoading, error and data fields, which allows nonsense combinations such as loading with an error and data at once. Adding a default case that assigns the value to a variable of type never makes the compiler flag any switch that forgets to handle a newly added variant.

questions.title: unknown versus any
questions.prompt: What is the difference between unknown and any in TypeScript?

expectedConcepts.label: any disables type checking; unknown is the type-safe top type
Values of type unknown must be narrowed before use
Use unknown for external data and caught errors; avoid any because it spreads silently

questions.modelAnswer: Both can hold any value, but they behave oppositely. any switches type checking off: you can call methods, access properties and pass the value anywhere without errors, and any spreads silently through expressions, so bugs the compiler should catch slip through to runtime. unknown is the safe counterpart: you can assign anything to it, but you cannot do anything with it until you narrow it, with typeof, instanceof, a type guard or a validation library. That makes unknown the right type for data from outside, such as JSON responses, user input and caught errors, which TypeScript can type as unknown with useUnknownInCatchVariables. Reserve any for gradual migrations, and limit it with lint rules.

questions.title: Tree shaking and what prevents it
questions.prompt: What is tree shaking, and what can prevent it?

expectedConcepts.label: Tree shaking removes unused exports from the bundle
Relies on static ES module imports and exports
Blocked by CommonJS, side effects, dynamic access and barrel files

questions.modelAnswer: Tree shaking is a bundler optimisation, in tools like Rollup, esbuild, webpack and Vite, that removes code you import from but never use, so importing one function from a large library does not ship the whole library. It works because ES module imports and exports are static: the bundler can see exactly which names are used without running the code. It is prevented by CommonJS modules, whose require and module.exports are dynamic; by modules with top-level side effects, which the bundler must keep unless package.json declares "sideEffects": false; by dynamic property access on a namespace import; and by some patterns like class-based APIs with all methods attached. Barrel files that re-export everything can also defeat it in some setups.

questions.title: Cancelling obsolete network requests
questions.prompt: How should a frontend cancel obsolete network requests?

expectedConcepts.label: Obsolete responses can arrive late and overwrite newer results
AbortController signals fetch to cancel the request
Abort on new input or unmount; ignore AbortError; libraries handle this automatically

questions.modelAnswer: When a user types into a search box, each keystroke may start a request, and responses can arrive out of order: the result for "re" arriving after "react" overwrites the correct result with a stale one. Navigating away also leaves requests whose responses update unmounted components. The standard tool is AbortController: create one per request, pass its signal to fetch, and call abort when the request becomes obsolete, such as when a new query starts or in a React effect cleanup on unmount. Aborted fetches reject with an AbortError, which should be ignored rather than shown to the user. Data-fetching libraries such as TanStack Query handle cancellation and stale responses automatically.

questions.title: Type checking versus runtime validation
questions.prompt: What is the difference between type checking and runtime validation?

expectedConcepts.label: TypeScript types are erased at compile time and check only your own code
Runtime validation checks actual data at boundaries such as API responses and user input
Use schema libraries like Zod to validate and infer types from one definition

questions.modelAnswer: TypeScript's type checking happens at compile time and is erased from the JavaScript that runs. It proves your own code is consistent with the types you declared, but it cannot know what actually arrives from outside: a JSON response, local storage, URL parameters or user input. Writing const user = await res.json() as User is only a promise to the compiler; if the server sends something different, the program fails later in a confusing place. Runtime validation checks real data when it crosses a boundary, rejecting or handling unexpected shapes. Schema libraries such as Zod or Valibot let you define the schema once, validate data with parse, and infer the TypeScript type from the same schema, so types and checks never drift apart.

questions.title: Structured cloning versus JSON serialisation
questions.prompt: How does structured cloning differ from JSON serialization?

expectedConcepts.label: structuredClone deep-copies values using the structured clone algorithm
It supports Dates, Maps, Sets, typed arrays and circular references, which JSON cannot
Neither copies functions or class prototypes; JSON is for text exchange

questions.modelAnswer: JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x)) was a common deep-copy trick, but JSON only supports plain objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans and null. Dates become strings, Map, Set and typed arrays are lost or mangled, undefined and functions are dropped, NaN becomes null, and circular references throw an error. structuredClone, available in browsers and Node, uses the same structured clone algorithm as postMessage and IndexedDB: it correctly copies Dates, RegExps, Maps, Sets, ArrayBuffers and typed arrays, errors, and circular or shared references. It still cannot copy functions or DOM nodes, and class instances lose their prototype, becoming plain objects. Use structuredClone for in-memory copies and JSON for text exchange with servers and storage.

questions.title: Exposing types without leaking internals
questions.prompt: How can a package expose types without leaking internal implementation?

expectedConcepts.label: The public API is what the entry points and their declaration files export
Use package.json exports to block deep imports into internal files
Export narrow interfaces, not internal classes; check the API surface with tools

questions.modelAnswer: Everything a package's entry points export, including types in its generated .d.ts files, becomes part of its public API, and users will depend on it, so changing it later is a breaking change. Keep the surface intentional: export interfaces and types that describe what users need, rather than internal classes with all their private details; return opaque or branded types for handles; and mark internal items with @internal and strip them from declarations. Use the exports field in package.json to define exactly which entry points exist, which prevents users from importing deep internal files. Tools like API Extractor generate a report of the public API so reviewers notice accidental changes, which helps follow semantic versioning.

questions.title: Source maps for debugging production code
questions.prompt: How do source maps help debug minified production code?

expectedConcepts.label: A source map maps positions in bundled, minified code back to original source
Debuggers and error trackers use them to show readable stack traces
Upload them privately to error trackers rather than serving them publicly

questions.modelAnswer: Production JavaScript is bundled, transpiled from TypeScript and minified, so an error stack trace points to something like line 1, column 48213 of main.3f9a.js, with renamed variables. A source map is a JSON file that maps every position in the generated code back to the original file, line, column and name. Browser developer tools load source maps to show and step through your original source, and error-tracking services like Sentry use them to turn production stack traces into readable ones. Because source maps can reveal your full source code, many teams generate "hidden" source maps that are uploaded privately to the error tracker during the build and are not referenced or served publicly.

questions.title: Microbenchmarking C++ code correctly
questions.prompt: You want to compare two implementations of a hot C++ function. How do you write a trustworthy microbenchmark with a tool like Google Benchmark, and what mistakes make the numbers meaningless?

expectedConcepts.label: Many iterations in an optimised build, compared over repetitions
DoNotOptimize and ClobberMemory stop dead code elimination
Control noise: frequency scaling, pinned cores, realistic data
Tiny hot-cache inputs mislead; confirm with perf and end-to-end

questions.modelAnswer: Use a framework such as Google Benchmark, which runs the code enough iterations to get a stable time and reports statistics; ask for several repetitions and compare medians and spread, not a single run. Always benchmark an optimised build, -O2 or -O3 with the same flags as production, because a debug build measures different code. The most common mistake is that the compiler deletes the work: if a result is never used, dead code elimination removes it, or the compiler computes a constant input at compile time. benchmark::DoNotOptimize on the result and ClobberMemory prevent that. Control noise: disable CPU frequency scaling and turbo or at least record them, pin the process to an isolated core, and run on a quiet machine. Use realistic data: a tiny input that stays in L1 cache with perfectly predictable branches can make one version look faster than it will be in production. Finally, confirm the reason with perf stat, looking at cycles, cache misses and branch misses, and check that the win survives in an end-to-end benchmark.

questions.title: How the Go race detector works
questions.prompt: How does the Go race detector find data races, what can it miss, and how should you use it in CI?

expectedConcepts.label: Finds unsynchronised concurrent accesses where one is a write
keywords: at least one of them writ

expectedConcepts.label: ThreadSanitizer instrumentation tracks happens-before
Only races that execute are found; no false positives, but slow
Run it on all tests in CI and in a race-enabled staging build

questions.modelAnswer: A data race is two goroutines accessing the same memory at the same time without synchronisation, with at least one of them writing. Building with -race compiles the program with ThreadSanitizer instrumentation: every memory access and every synchronisation operation, such as channel operations, mutexes, WaitGroups and atomics, is recorded, and the runtime tracks happens-before relationships between goroutines. When two accesses conflict and neither happens before the other, it prints both stack traces and where the goroutines were created. It reports races that actually occur during that run, so it has essentially no false positives, but it cannot find races in code paths that did not execute or interleavings that did not happen, so a clean run is not a proof. It typically increases memory use five to ten times and execution time two to twenty times, so it is rarely used in production. Run all tests with -race in CI, write tests that really exercise concurrency, repeat them with the -count flag, and run a race-enabled build in a staging load test. Treat every report as a bug.
